# 2.48 Definition of Done

A new Instagram lead:

```text
Raj
+1403...
Hindi
Physiotherapy
```

should automatically become:

```text
Lead
 ↓
Identity Resolution
 ↓
Existing Customer C10028 found
 ↓
New lead attached
 ↓
New service interest attached
 ↓
Language preference confirmed
 ↓
Interaction timeline updated
 ↓
CRM synchronized
 ↓
Customer 360 refreshed
```

without creating duplicate customers.

The output of Phase 2 is therefore a trustworthy **Golden Customer Record**, which becomes the input for **Phase 3 — ConsentAI + Communication Preference + DNC + Suppression + Calling Eligibility**, one of the most critical components before we allow the outbound AI agent to place calls.

---

## 🧑 User — msg #39

next

---

## 🤖 Assistant — msg #40

# Phase 3 — ConsentAI + Communication Preferences + DNC + Suppression + Call Eligibility

This phase decides one critical thing before any outbound call is placed:

> **Are we allowed to contact this customer, by this channel, for this purpose, at this time?**

This must be a deterministic policy service. The LLM should never decide whether a marketing call is permitted.

## 3.1 Target architecture

```text
Lead / Customer
      ↓
ConsentAI
      ↓
Preference Engine
      ↓
DNC / Suppression
      ↓
Jurisdiction Rules
      ↓
Calling Window
      ↓
Frequency Cap
      ↓
Campaign Rules
      ↓
Risk / Complaint Check
      ↓
Eligibility Decision
      ↓
ALLOW / BLOCK / REVIEW
```

The service should return both the decision and the reason.

Example:

```json
{
  "allowed": false,
  "reason_code": "DNC_ACTIVE",
  "policy_version": "CALL-POLICY-3.2",
  "evaluated_at": "2026-08-24T..."
}
```

---

## 3.2 Consent domains

Do not maintain one generic `consent=true`.

Model consent independently by:

| Dimension | Examples |
|---|---|
| Channel | Phone, SMS, Email, WhatsApp |
| Purpose | Callback, transactional, marketing, survey |
| Brand | Brand A, Brand B |
| Organization | Parent company/tenant |
| Campaign | Specific campaign where needed |
| Geography | Canada, US, India, etc. |
| Duration | Active, expired |
| Source | Website, verbal call, paper, API |
| Status | Granted, denied, withdrawn |
| Evidence | Consent wording/version/timestamp |

This lets the system correctly represent:

**Phone callback = YES**

while:

**Marketing SMS = NO**

and:

**Email service notifications = YES**

---

# 3.3 Consent data model

Recommended table:

```text
CONSENT

consent_id
tenant_id
customer_id

channel
purpose
brand_id

status

GRANTED
DENIED
WITHDRAWN
EXPIRED

source

WEB
VOICE
SMS
EMAIL
STAFF
IMPORT
API

consent_text_version
consent_text_hash

effective_from
effective_until
withdrawn_at

campaign_id
interaction_id

evidence_reference

created_at
updated_at
```

Do not overwrite historical consent.

Store versions.

---

# 3.4 Consent evidence

For each consent event retain enough evidence to answer:

> When did the customer provide this permission, through what source, for what purpose, and under which wording?

Example:

```text
Customer: C10028

Channel:
PHONE

Purpose:
REQUESTED_CALLBACK

Status:
GRANTED

Source:
WEB_FORM

Text version:
CALLBACK-CONSENT-V4

Timestamp:
2026-08-24 10:32

Campaign:
PHYSIO-AUG-26
```

---

# 3.5 Preference vs consent

Keep these separate.

Customer preference:

> "I prefer SMS."

does **not automatically mean**:

> "I consent to marketing SMS."

Likewise:

> "Call me after 6 PM."

means a timing preference, not necessarily broad marketing consent.

Model:

```text
PREFERENCE
```

separately from:

```text
CONSENT
```

---

# 3.6 Communication preference model

Fields:

```text
customer_id

preferred_channel
secondary_channel

preferred_language

preferred_days[]
preferred_start_time
preferred_end_time

timezone

do_not_voicemail
sms_preferred
email_preferred

preferred_agent_type
human_only

notes
source
confidence
valid_from
valid_to
```

Example:

```text
Language:
Punjabi

Primary:
Phone

Secondary:
SMS

Best day:
Saturday

Time:
10:00–13:00

Voicemail:
No
```

---

# 3.7 DNC service

You need your own internal Do-Not-Call state even when external/jurisdictional rules also apply.

Table:

```text
DO_NOT_CONTACT

customer_id
channel

scope

ALL_MARKETING
PHONE_ONLY
SMS_ONLY
BRAND_ONLY
CAMPAIGN_ONLY

reason

CUSTOMER_REQUEST
COMPLAINT
LEGAL
ADMIN
RISK

effective_at
expires_at

source_interaction
created_by
```

---

# 3.8 Voice DNC handling

During any call, the customer may say:

> "Please don't call me anymore."

or:

> "Remove me from your list."

or:

> "Stop calling."

The conversation engine should detect this with extremely high priority.

Flow:

```text
Customer says DNC
      ↓
Intent = STOP_CONTACT
      ↓
Confirm only if genuinely ambiguous
      ↓
DNC API
      ↓
Suppression immediately active
      ↓
Campaign queues invalidated
      ↓
CRM updated
      ↓
Audit event
      ↓
Agent gracefully closes
```

Do not make the customer repeat themselves unnecessarily.

---

# 3.9 DNC intent examples

Test variants:

```text
Don't call again.
Stop calling me.
Take me off your list.
Remove my number.
I don't want marketing calls.
No more calls.
Please don't contact me.
Don't phone me, just email.
```

The last example is channel-specific.

Store:

```text
PHONE = BLOCKED
EMAIL = potentially still allowed according to policy/consent
```

---

# 3.10 Suppression engine

DNC is only one reason to suppress a call.

Suppression reasons can include:

```text
DNC
CONSENT_MISSING
CONSENT_WITHDRAWN
INVALID_PHONE
CUSTOMER_DECEASED
WRONG_NUMBER
COMPLAINT
LEGAL_HOLD
ALREADY_CONVERTED
CAMPAIGN_EXCLUSION
EMPLOYEE
TEST_ACCOUNT
FRAUD
HIGH_RISK
MAX_CONTACT_ATTEMPTS
TEMPORARY_PAUSE
```

---

# 3.11 Suppression table

```text
SUPPRESSION

suppression_id
customer_id
contact_point_id

scope
reason
severity

campaign_id
brand_id

start_at
end_at

source
created_by

status
```

Supports:

permanent suppression  
temporary suppression  
campaign-only suppression.

---

# 3.12 Call eligibility service

Main API:

```text
POST /eligibility/call
```

Request:

```json
{
  "customer_id": "C10028",
  "campaign_id": "CMP5001",
  "phone": "+14035551234",
  "purpose": "MARKETING"
}
```

Response:

```json
{
  "eligible": true,
  "earliest_call_time": "2026-08-24T18:00:00-06:00",
  "preferred_language": "Hindi",
  "reason_codes": [],
  "policy_version": "3.2"
}
```

---

# 3.13 Eligibility evaluation sequence

Recommended deterministic order:

```text
1. Customer exists?
2. Phone exists?
3. Phone valid?
4. Contact verified?
5. Customer DNC?
6. Number suppressed?
7. Required consent valid?
8. Consent expired?
9. Jurisdiction known?
10. Campaign approved?
11. Calling day allowed?
12. Calling time allowed?
13. Customer preferred time?
14. Frequency limit exceeded?
15. Retry limit exceeded?
16. Existing complaint?
17. Customer already converted?
18. Existing appointment?
19. Risk block?
20. Provider available?
21. Budget available?
22. CALL
```

Do the cheapest/highest-priority checks first where practical.

---

# 3.14 Hard block vs soft preference

Important distinction.

### Hard block

DNC  
required consent missing  
prohibited calling time  
invalid number.

The system must not call.

### Soft preference

Customer prefers evening.

Maybe morning calling is technically permissible, but the business should normally respect the preference.

Return:

```text
ELIGIBLE_BUT_NOT_PREFERRED
```

Then scheduler moves the call.

---

# 3.15 Decision model

Use:

```text
ALLOW
ALLOW_AT
BLOCK
MANUAL_REVIEW
```

Examples:

```text
ALLOW
```

Call now.

```text
ALLOW_AT 18:00
```

Wait until preferred/compliant window.

```text
BLOCK
reason=DNC
```

Never call.

```text
MANUAL_REVIEW
reason=CONSENT_CONFLICT
```

Require staff intervention.

---

# 3.16 Policy engine

Avoid hardcoding all rules deep inside Python if you anticipate many markets/tenants.

Possible approaches:

Simple early stage:

Python rule service.

More mature:

Open Policy Agent (OPA)

or a structured custom policy engine.

Policy example concept:

```text
IF
  purpose = marketing
AND
  phone_dnc = true
THEN
  decision = BLOCK
```

---

# 3.17 Policy versioning

Every eligibility decision needs:

```text
policy_id
policy_version
effective_date
decision
reason_code
```

Why?

Later someone may ask:

> Why was C10028 called on August 24?

You need to reconstruct the exact rules in force at that time.

---

# 3.18 Jurisdiction engine

Determine relevant jurisdiction using reliable fields such as:

customer address  
phone country  
declared country  
campaign region.

Do not use weak inference when the result affects legal eligibility.

Output:

```text
country
province_state
timezone
confidence
```

If uncertain:

```text
MANUAL_REVIEW
```

or apply conservative policy.

---

# 3.19 Timezone handling

Do not schedule using server timezone.

Store all timestamps consistently, usually UTC, while keeping the customer's IANA timezone.

Example:

```text
customer_timezone = America/Edmonton
```

Scheduler converts policy window correctly.

Handle daylight saving time automatically.

---

# 3.20 Calling windows

Configure policies per jurisdiction/campaign.

Example conceptual configuration:

```text
MONDAY:
09:00–20:00

TUESDAY:
09:00–20:00
...
```

This should be data-driven.

Don't place regulatory hours directly into LLM prompts.

---

# 3.21 Customer-specific call window

Policy may allow:

09:00–20:00.

Customer preference:

18:00–20:00.

Effective window:

```text
intersection(
 regulatory_window,
 campaign_window,
 customer_preference
)
```

Call during the intersection where possible.

---

# 3.22 Holiday calendar

Campaign scheduler should account for:

national holidays  
regional holidays  
tenant-defined closures.

Customer experience may justify avoiding some calls even when technically permissible.

Make holiday policies configurable.

---

# 3.23 Frequency capping

Critical customer-experience feature.

Track:

```text
calls_last_24h
calls_last_7d
calls_last_30d

sms_last_24h
email_last_7d

all_contacts_last_7d
```

Rules could include configurable thresholds such as:

```text
max outbound attempts per campaign
max voice contacts per period
cooldown after customer refusal
```

Exact values should come from business/compliance policy.

---

# 3.24 Cross-channel frequency

Don't look only at calls.

Customer may receive:

3 calls  
5 emails  
4 SMS messages.

That's still excessive.

Create:

```text
CONTACT_PRESSURE_SCORE
```

Inputs:

Voice  
SMS  
Email  
WhatsApp  
push  
human outreach.

---

# 3.25 Contact pressure score

Example conceptual calculation:

```text
Recent calls × weight
+
Recent SMS × weight
+
Recent email × weight
+
Recent unsuccessful attempts
+
Recent complaints
```

Then:

```text
LOW
MEDIUM
HIGH
EXCESSIVE
```

If excessive:

delay or block.

---

# 3.26 Retry strategy

Call attempts should have clear states:

```text
ATTEMPTED
CONNECTED
NO_ANSWER
BUSY
VOICEMAIL
FAILED
REJECTED
WRONG_NUMBER
```

Retry rules differ per outcome.

For example:

`NO_ANSWER`

may allow retry later.

`WRONG_NUMBER`

should suppress immediately after confirmation.

`DNC`

must not retry.

---

# 3.27 Customer-requested callback

If customer says:

> "Call tomorrow at 6."

Create:

```text
CALLBACK_REQUEST

customer_id
requested_at
callback_at
timezone
reason
preferred_language
agent_preference
status
```

Requested callbacks should be distinguished from general campaign calls.

---

# 3.28 Callback priority

Recommended ordering:

```text
Customer-requested callback
        ↓
Appointment-related call
        ↓
High-intent new lead
        ↓
Warm lead
        ↓
Marketing campaign
```

Use business rules, not arbitrary FIFO for everything.

---

# 3.29 Callback conflicts

What if:

Customer requests 6 PM

but:

campaign ends at 5 PM?

Do not silently ignore request.

Options:

Move to next permissible time  
send SMS asking for alternative  
human callback  
manual review.

---

# 3.30 Call queue cleanup

Critical edge case:

Customer enters DNC at 11:02.

Three calls are already queued for later.

You need event:

```text
consent.changed
or
dnc.created
```

Campaign workers must immediately invalidate queued jobs.

Don't rely only on eligibility checking at initial scheduling.

---

# 3.31 Re-check eligibility immediately before dialing

This is essential.

Check eligibility:

### First

when scheduling.

### Again

seconds before placing the call.

Because consent/DNC/status may have changed.

```text
Queue
 ↓
PRE-DIAL ELIGIBILITY
 ↓
Call
```

---

# 3.32 Complaint handling

A complaint should affect future eligibility.

Store:

```text
COMPLAINT

customer_id
category
severity
status
created_at
```

Possible action:

Low severity → flag.

High severity → temporary suppression.

Critical → block outbound activity pending review.

---

# 3.33 Wrong-number management

Agent:

> "Is this Sarah?"

Person:

> "No, you have the wrong number."

Do not keep calling.

Process:

```text
WRONG_NUMBER
↓
contact_point = invalid/suspect
↓
campaign suppression
↓
identity review
↓
CRM update
```

Do not expose unnecessary information about Sarah.

---

# 3.34 Deceased-customer scenario

If caller informs you the intended customer is deceased:

Immediately stop sales dialogue.

Mark:

```text
CUSTOMER_CONTACT_RESTRICTED
```

Then follow organizational policy for verification/data handling.

This is both customer-experience and governance-critical.

---

# 3.35 Sensitive circumstances

Examples:

bereavement  
medical distress  
severe complaint  
vulnerable customer situation.

The campaign engine should support:

```text
SENSITIVE_CONTACT_HOLD
```

rather than forcing a normal sales call.

---

# 3.36 AI disclosure tracking

Where disclosure is required or company policy mandates it, record:

```text
AI_DISCLOSURE

call_id
disclosure_version
timestamp
acknowledged
```

Example:

> "I'm the virtual assistant for ABC Clinic."

Don't try to deceive the caller into believing the system is human.

---

# 3.37 Recording consent

Treat call recording separately from call-contact permission.

Possible states:

```text
CALL_ALLOWED = YES
RECORDING_ALLOWED = NO
```

Your telephony/agent architecture must be able to honor that configuration.

---

# 3.38 Recording controls

Policy decision:

```text
record_call = true/false
```

If false:

Disable recording where technically possible.

Potentially restrict transcript retention as required by policy.

---

# 3.39 Preference updates during call

Customer:

> "Don't call during work. Evenings are better."

Voice agent invokes:

```text
update_contact_preference(
  channel="PHONE",
  time="EVENING"
)
```

Next campaign uses that information.

---

# 3.40 Language updates

Customer:

> "Please call me in Punjabi next time."

Update:

```text
preferred_voice_language = Punjabi
```

This feeds RouteAI later.

---

Recommended:

```text
POST /consents

POST /consents/{id}/withdraw

POST /dnc

POST /suppressions
GET  /customers/{id}/suppressions

POST /eligibility/call

POST /preferences/contact

POST /callbacks
```

Publish:

```text
consent.granted

consent.withdrawn
consent.expired

dnc.created
```

# 3.43 Technology options

Backend:

**FastAPI / Java Spring Boot**

Database:

**PostgreSQL**

Cache:

**Redis**

Policy:

**OPA** or custom deterministic engine.

Workflow:

**Temporal**

**n8n**

append-only event/audit storage.

# 3.44 Test strategy — consent

Test combinations:

| Call consent | Marketing consent | DNC | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| Yes | Yes | No | Evaluate further |
| Yes | No | No | Only appropriate permitted purpose |
| No | Yes | No | Policy-dependent; don't assume callable |
| No | No | No | Block marketing |
| Yes | Yes | Yes | BLOCK |
| Withdrawn | Yes | No | Block applicable purpose |
| Expired | Yes | No | Block/review |

Use your actual policy requirements for final expectations.

---

# 3.45 DNC test cases

Test:

Exact phrase  
paraphrase  
angry DNC  
polite DNC  
channel-specific DNC  
temporary request  
"Don't call today"  
"Don't call again"  
"Email me instead."

The system needs to distinguish:

```text
TEMPORARY_PREFERENCE
```

from:

```text
PERMANENT_DNC
```

without overinterpreting ambiguous wording.

---

# 3.46 Test-data matrix

Create synthetic customers:

```text
C001
Consent yes
DNC no
English
Calgary
```

```text
C002
Consent withdrawn
Punjabi
```

```text
C003
Phone DNC
Email allowed
```

```text
C004
No timezone
```

```text
C005
Shared household phone
```

```text
C006
High contact pressure
```

```text
C007
Complaint pending
```

```text
C008
Callback requested at exact time
```

---

# 3.47 Boundary-time testing

Test:

one second before allowed window  
exact start time  
exact end time  
one second after end.

Also:

DST start  
DST end  
midnight  
timezone change  
travelling customer if known.

These are common scheduling bugs.

---

# 3.48 Concurrency test

Scenario:

Eligibility service says ALLOW.

At exactly the same time:

customer withdraws consent.

Need transactional/event handling that minimizes races.

Most importantly:

**re-check at dial time.**

---

# 3.49 Fail-closed vs fail-open

For critical compliance checks:

If ConsentAI is unavailable:

### Do not call.

That's:

**fail closed.**

For some noncritical preference features:

If preference service fails, you may be able to continue using conservative defaults.

Classify dependencies accordingly.

---

# 3.50 Security testing

Test:

Unauthorized consent change  
DNC removal by unauthorized user  
tenant A accesses tenant B consent  
forged consent API request  
modified consent timestamp  
policy bypass  
direct campaign-call request bypassing eligibility.

Critical control:

Voice provider API calls should only originate after eligibility authorization.

---

# 3.51 Authorization

Roles:

```text
CUSTOMER
CALL_AGENT
CAMPAIGN_MANAGER
COMPLIANCE
ADMIN
SYSTEM_SERVICE
```

For example:

Campaign manager:

can create campaign.

Cannot arbitrarily remove DNC.

Compliance/admin role:

may perform controlled DNC correction with audit where policy permits.

---

# 3.52 Audit trail

Every decision:

```text
decision_id
customer_id
campaign_id
action

ALLOW/BLOCK

reason_codes

policy_version
inputs_hash
timestamp
service_version
```

This is valuable for investigations.

---

# 3.53 Observability

Metrics:

```text
eligibility_requests
eligibility_allowed
eligibility_blocked

blocked_dnc
blocked_consent
blocked_time
blocked_frequency
blocked_complaint

policy_latency

consent_withdrawals
preference_updates
```

---

# 3.54 Dashboard

### Compliance funnel

```text
10,000 Leads
   ↓
9,200 Valid Phone
   ↓
8,500 Consent Eligible
   ↓
8,250 Non-DNC
   ↓
7,900 Frequency Eligible
   ↓
7,600 Time Eligible
   ↓
7,600 Callable
```

This tells operations why leads aren't entering campaigns.

---

# 3.55 Alerts

Trigger alerts for:

Sudden increase in DNC  
high complaint rate  
ConsentAI unavailable  
eligibility latency high  
unexpected policy version  
DNC suppression failure  
campaign attempting blocked customers.

---

# 3.56 Quality KPIs

Track:

**DNC enforcement accuracy**

Target: effectively 100% for deterministic blocks.

**Consent decision accuracy**

**Call-window compliance**

**Frequency-cap compliance**

**Preference adherence**

**False-block rate**

**Manual-review rate**

**Policy-engine availability**

---

# 3.57 Edge case — human user manually initiates call

Staff clicks:

**Call customer**

Do not bypass ConsentAI.

Flow:

```text
Human UI
  ↓
Eligibility API
  ↓
ALLOW/BLOCK
  ↓
Dial
```

One centralized enforcement service for both AI and humans reduces policy gaps.

---

# 3.58 Edge case — CSV import contains "consent=yes"

Do not automatically trust poorly evidenced imports.

Store:

```text
source = CSV_IMPORT
evidence_quality = UNKNOWN
```

Apply import validation and policy.

Potentially:

```text
MANUAL_REVIEW
```

---

# 3.59 Edge case — customer asks for service callback after previously DNC

This requires careful distinction between:

**general marketing DNC**

and:

**customer-initiated service request**.

Don't automatically erase historical DNC.

Create purpose-specific, evidence-backed authorization for the requested interaction, subject to applicable policy.

---

# 3.60 Edge case — user changes phone

Do not blindly transfer consent/DNC state to a newly entered phone when the policy depends on the contact point.

Model:

Customer-level restrictions

and:

Contact-point-level permissions

separately.

---

# 3.61 Edge case — phone number reassigned

When confidence suggests number ownership changed:

Mark verification stale.

Reverify.

Avoid revealing previous customer's information.

---

# 3.62 Governance

Every policy needs:

```text
policy_owner
business_owner
compliance_owner

version
effective_from
review_date
jurisdiction
```

Policy changes should pass:

```text
Draft
→ Review
→ Test
→ Approval
→ Staging
→ Production
```

---

# 3.63 Policy regression tests

Suppose policy V3 changes.

Before deployment run:

```text
10,000 historical eligibility scenarios
```

Compare:

V2 decisions  
vs  
V3 decisions.

Investigate every unexpected delta.

This is exactly where **PolicyAI + TestAI + GovernAI** connect.

---

# 3.64 Definition of Done

Phase 3 should not be considered complete until:

```text
Consent capture               PASS
Consent versioning            PASS
Withdrawal                    PASS

Channel-specific permission   PASS
Purpose-specific permission   PASS

DNC                            PASS
Suppression                    PASS

Calling window                 PASS
Timezone                       PASS
DST                            PASS

Frequency caps                 PASS
Callback handling              PASS

Pre-dial revalidation          PASS

Policy versioning              PASS
Audit                          PASS

RBAC                           PASS
Tenant isolation               PASS

Fail-closed behavior           PASS

Performance                    PASS
Chaos/failure testing          PASS

Dashboard                      PASS
Alerts                         PASS
UAT                            PASS
```

### Phase 3 output

The campaign engine can now safely ask:

```text
Can I call C10028?
```

and receive:

```text
YES

Purpose:
Requested consultation

Phone:
+1...

Language:
Hindi

Earliest call:
18:00 America/Edmonton

Maximum remaining attempts:
2

Recording:
Policy evaluation required

AI disclosure:
Required

Policy:
CALL-POLICY-V3.2
```

or:

```text
NO

Reason:
PHONE_DNC

Effective:
2026-08-24

Action:
SUPPRESS
```

The next phase is **Phase 4 — Lead Validation + Enrichment + FraudAI + Data Quality**, where the system determines whether the lead is genuine, reachable, complete, duplicate/suspicious, and sufficiently trustworthy before sending it into segmentation and scoring.

## 🤖 Assistant — msg #42

# Phase 4 — Lead Validation + Enrichment + FraudAI + Data Quality

This phase turns a raw lead into a **trusted, enriched, scored-for-quality record** before segmentation, outreach, and Voice AI execution. The goal is to stop bad data, spam, duplicates, unreachable contacts, and suspicious activity from polluting downstream campaigns.

## 4.1 Target flow

```text
Lead Created
   ↓
Schema Validation
   ↓
Phone Validation
   ↓
Email Validation
   ↓
Identity Cross-Check
   ↓
Duplicate Detection
   ↓
Fraud/Bot Detection
   ↓
Source Validation
   ↓
Optional Enrichment
   ↓
Data Quality Scoring
   ↓
Trust Score
   ↓
VALID / REVIEW / REJECT
```

## 4.2 Core modules

| Module | Purpose |
|---|---|
| ValidateAI | Validate fields and formats |
| ContactAI | Phone/email/contact validation |
| IdentityAI | Cross-check identity signals |
| DedupeAI | Duplicate/near-duplicate detection |
| FraudAI | Bot, fake lead, abuse, malicious activity |
| EnrichAI | Add business/contextual attributes |
| DataQualityAI | Completeness, validity, consistency |
| TrustAI | Overall lead trust score |
| ReviewQueue | Manual review for ambiguous cases |

## 4.3 Phone validation

Normalize to E.164 first.

Examples:

```text
4035551234
(403) 555-1234
+1 403-555-1234
```

become:

```text
+14035551234
```

Validate:

country code, plausible length, line type when available, carrier metadata when available, disposable/temporary patterns where detectable, blocked/suppressed status, verification status, duplicate usage.

Do not assume a technically valid number means the person owns it.

## 4.4 Email validation

Use several levels:

```text
Syntax
→ Domain
→ MX/domain health
→ Disposable-domain check
→ Optional mailbox validation
```

Store result separately:

```text
email_validity = VALID / INVALID / UNKNOWN
email_risk = LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH
```

Avoid rejecting a genuine lead just because an external provider cannot confidently verify the mailbox.

## 4.5 Identity consistency checks

Compare:

```text
name
phone country
email domain
address
form location
IP region where appropriate
CRM data
previous customer identity
```

Example:

```text
Country selected = Canada
Phone = +91
Address = Calgary
IP region = India
```

This is not automatically fraud.

It becomes:

```text
IDENTITY_INCONSISTENCY
confidence = medium
```

and may require further verification depending on use case.

## 4.6 Duplicate detection

Use deterministic and fuzzy matching.

Strong signals:

```text
same verified phone
same verified email
same external CRM ID
```

Moderate:

```text
same phone + similar name
same email + similar name
same address + similar name
```

Weak:

```text
similar name only
```

Possible outcomes:

```text
NEW
EXACT_DUPLICATE
LIKELY_DUPLICATE
POSSIBLE_DUPLICATE
NOT_DUPLICATE
```

## 4.7 Duplicate edge cases

Customer submits same form three times.

Solution:

Use `submission_id`, idempotency key, and customer identity matching.

Customer uses work and personal email.

Solution:

Same customer can have multiple contact points.

Family members share phone.

Solution:

Do not auto-merge based on phone alone.

## 4.8 FraudAI signals

Look for:

high submission velocity, repeated same IP/device, identical form patterns, impossible timestamps, fake/random strings, suspicious disposable emails, same phone across hundreds of leads, rotating names with same number, known abusive source, malformed automation attempts, bot-like behavior, referral abuse, incentive farming, repeated CAPTCHA failures.

Example features:

```text
submissions_1m
submissions_1h
same_phone_count
same_email_count
same_device_count
same_ip_count
form_completion_time
captcha_score
domain_risk
phone_risk
historical_fraud_count
```

## 4.9 Fraud score

Example:

```text
0–29   LOW
30–59  MEDIUM
60–79  HIGH
80–100 CRITICAL
```

Action:

```text
LOW      → continue
MEDIUM   → limited workflow/review
HIGH     → manual review
CRITICAL → reject/block
```

Do not let the LLM override this.

## 4.10 Bot protection

Use layered controls:

Cloudflare Turnstile, rate limiting, honeypot field, device/IP velocity, behavioral signals, form-timing checks, request signatures for trusted APIs.

CAPTCHA alone is not enough.

## 4.11 Source validation

Each lead should know where it came from:

```text
source
medium
campaign
partner
form_id
landing_page
referrer
utm
external_lead_id
```

For partner/API leads, validate webhook/API authenticity.

Use:

API keys, OAuth where applicable, HMAC signatures, IP allowlisting where appropriate, timestamp/replay protection.

## 4.12 Enrichment

Enrichment should be optional and purpose-driven.

For B2C:

general location, timezone, language preference, service area, contactability metadata.

For B2B:

company, industry, employee band, geography, website, role/title when lawfully sourced and relevant.

Do not enrich simply because data is available.

## 4.13 Enrichment priority

Use this order:

```text
Customer-provided
→ verified internal data
→ connected CRM
→ trusted external source
→ inference
```

Store provenance.

Example:

```text
employee_count = 250
source = CRM
confidence = high
```

or:

```text
company_industry = wellness
source = inferred
confidence = 0.61
```

## 4.14 Data quality dimensions

Score:

| Dimension | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Completeness | Required fields available |
| Validity | Format/domain/phone correct |
| Accuracy | Evidence suggests values are correct |
| Consistency | Fields don't contradict each other |
| Uniqueness | Not an unresolved duplicate |
| Freshness | Recently confirmed |
| Provenance | Source is known |
| Verifiability | Can be independently verified |

## 4.15 Data quality score

Example:

```text
Completeness  95
Validity      100
Consistency   80
Uniqueness    90
Freshness     100
Provenance    95

Overall = 93
```

Keep the underlying dimensions. Do not expose only one composite score.

## 4.16 Trust score

A separate trust score can combine:

```text
contact validity
identity consistency
source reputation
fraud score
duplicate confidence
verification evidence
historical interaction quality
```

Example:

```text
Lead Trust Score = 87/100
```

Reason codes:

```text
+ verified phone
+ known campaign source
+ previous CRM match
- email not verified
```

## 4.17 Lead decision

At the end:

```text
VALID
VALID_WITH_WARNINGS
MANUAL_REVIEW
REJECTED
```

Example output:

```text
lead_id = L10092
phone_valid = true
email_valid = unknown
duplicate = false
fraud_score = 8
data_quality = 94
trust_score = 89
status = VALID
```

## 4.18 APIs

Recommended:

```text
POST /validation/lead
POST /validation/phone
POST /validation/email

POST /identity/check

POST /duplicates/check

POST /fraud/evaluate

POST /enrichment/run

GET /leads/{id}/quality
GET /leads/{id}/trust
```

## 4.19 Event model

Emit:

```text
lead.validation.started
lead.validation.completed
lead.validation.failed

duplicate.detected

fraud.detected
fraud.review_required

lead.enriched

data_quality.updated
trust_score.updated
```

## 4.20 Technical stack

Backend:

FastAPI / Spring Boot.

Database:

PostgreSQL.

Cache/velocity counters:

Redis.

Optional stream:

Kafka/Redpanda later.

External validation:

provider abstraction.

Fraud rules:

custom rules first.

ML later if justified.

## 4.21 Rule engine before ML

Start with deterministic rules.

Example:

```text
IF same_phone_count_1h > threshold
AND device_count > threshold
THEN fraud_signal = VELOCITY_ABUSE
```

Then later introduce supervised models once you have actual labels.

Avoid building FraudAI with no historical truth data.

## 4.22 Fraud model later

Possible models:

logistic regression, XGBoost/LightGBM, isolation forest for anomaly support.

Features:

velocity, source reputation, contact validity, duplicate count, device diversity, historical conversions, chargeback/fraud history where applicable.

## 4.23 Human review queue

Show:

```text
Lead
Fraud score
Trust score
Duplicate candidates
Conflicting fields
Source
Evidence
Recommended action
```

Reviewer actions:

Approve, Reject, Merge, Request verification, Escalate.

Every action must be audited.

## 4.24 Testing — phone

Test:

valid Canada, valid US, valid India, invalid country code, too short, too long, extension, spaces, Unicode input, landline, mobile, VoIP, duplicated number, shared family number.

## 4.25 Testing — email

Test:

valid, invalid syntax, typo domain, disposable domain, internationalized domain, uppercase, plus alias, duplicate email, blank email.

## 4.26 Testing — fraud

Create scenarios:

```text
1 normal submission
100 submissions/min same IP
100 different names same phone
same email across multiple accounts
disposable emails
bot-like 0.2-second completion
repeated failed CAPTCHA
known trusted API partner
```

## 4.27 Testing — enrichment

Test:

provider success, provider timeout, conflicting enrichment, stale data, no match, wrong company match, partial result.

Never overwrite verified customer data with weaker enrichment.

## 4.28 Edge case — external validator outage

Do not lose the lead.

Use:

```text
validation_status = PENDING
```

Queue retry.

Proceed only according to risk level and policy.

## 4.29 Edge case — phone valid but unreachable

Validity and reachability differ.

Store:

```text
phone_valid = true
phone_reachable = unknown
```

After call attempts:

```text
phone_reachable = false/likely_false
```

## 4.30 Edge case — real customer looks suspicious

Example:

frequent form submissions because customer repeatedly changed appointment preference.

Do not auto-ban solely on velocity.

Use contextual rules and historical customer identity.

## 4.31 Edge case — malicious lead targets another person

Someone enters another person's phone number intentionally.

Mitigation:

verification, source analysis, consent evidence, cautious first-call disclosure, low-information opening until identity is established.

## 4.32 Edge case — invalid data corrected later

Maintain history.

Example:

```text
email_old = wrong@example
email_new = correct@example.com
```

Preserve:

who changed, why, when, source.

## 4.33 Security controls

Protect validation endpoints from abuse.

Use:

authentication, rate limiting, API quotas, request signatures, tenant isolation, secrets management, input sanitization, safe logging.

Do not log raw sensitive values unnecessarily.

## 4.34 Observability

Track:

```text
validation_success_rate
phone_invalid_rate
email_invalid_rate
duplicate_rate
fraud_rate
manual_review_rate
enrichment_success_rate
provider_latency
provider_failure_rate
data_quality_average
trust_score_distribution
```

## 4.35 Alerts

Alert when:

fraud spikes, duplicate rate spikes, external validator fails, suspicious source appears, manual-review queue grows, trust scores drop suddenly, enrichment provider latency degrades.

## 4.36 Reporting

Dashboard examples:

**Lead Quality Funnel**

```text
10,000 submitted
↓
9,400 schema-valid
↓
9,000 contact-valid
↓
8,700 nonduplicate
↓
8,550 low-fraud
↓
8,300 trusted
↓
8,100 ready for segmentation
```

**Source Quality**

| Source | Leads | Valid % | Fraud % | Conversion later |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Google | 1,000 | 94% | 1% | — |
| Instagram | 2,000 | 88% | 4% | — |
| Partner A | 500 | 70% | 12% | — |

Later, connect source quality with actual conversion.

## 4.37 QA acceptance criteria

A lead can move forward only when minimum thresholds are satisfied.

Example:

```text
schema_valid = true
phone_or_email_valid = true
fraud != CRITICAL
duplicate_status resolved
consent evidence available where required
data_quality >= configured threshold
```

Exact thresholds should be business-specific.

## 4.38 Definition of Done

Phase 4 is complete when:

```text
Phone validation             PASS
Email validation             PASS
Normalization                PASS
Duplicate detection          PASS
Fraud rules                  PASS
Bot protection               PASS
Source verification          PASS
Enrichment                   PASS
Data quality scoring         PASS
Trust scoring                PASS
Manual review                PASS
Audit                        PASS
Security                     PASS
Performance                  PASS
Failure recovery             PASS
Monitoring                   PASS
Dashboards                   PASS
UAT                          PASS
```

### Phase 4 output

A lead should now look like:

```text
Lead: L10092
Customer: C10028

Source:
Instagram / Physio-Aug

Phone:
VALID

Email:
VALID

Duplicate:
NO

Fraud:
6/100 — LOW

Data Quality:
96/100

Trust:
91/100

Preferred language:
Hindi

Consent:
Eligible for requested callback

Status:
READY_FOR_SEGMENTATION
```

The next phase is **Phase 5 — SegmentAI + Persona + Cohort Management**, where we organize customers into actionable groups using needs, language, behavior, source, timing, value, intent, service interest, geography, lifecycle stage, and eventually AI-driven clustering.

## 🤖 Assistant — msg #44

# Phase 5 — SegmentAI + Persona + Cohort Management

This phase turns clean leads into **actionable customer groups** so that the platform can choose the right campaign, language, call script, service, timing, voice agent, and follow-up strategy.

The objective is not just “segment by age or city.” It is to create dynamic segmentation using **need, intent, behavior, preference, channel, language, source, engagement, timing, value, risk, and lifecycle stage**.

## 5.1 Target flow

```text
Validated Lead / Customer 360
        ↓
Feature Builder
        ↓
Rule-Based Segmentation
        ↓
Persona Assignment
        ↓
Behavioral Cohorts
        ↓
Need-Based Segments
        ↓
Value / Intent Segments
        ↓
Language / Channel Segments
        ↓
Campaign Eligibility
        ↓
Segment-specific Call Strategy
```

## 5.2 Core SegmentAI modules

| Module | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Segment Rules | Deterministic segmentation |
| Persona Engine | Human-readable customer archetypes |
| Cohort Engine | Time/behavior-based groups |
| Feature Builder | Creates reusable customer features |
| Dynamic Segment Engine | Re-evaluates membership continuously |
| Segment Versioning | Tracks rule/model changes |
| Segment Explainability | Why customer belongs to segment |
| Segment QA | Tests membership accuracy |
| Segment Analytics | Conversion/quality by segment |

## 5.3 Segment dimensions

Start with these major dimensions.

### Lifecycle

```text
Prospect
New Lead
Qualified Lead
Appointment Pending
Customer
Repeat Customer
Lapsed Customer
Former Customer
Referral
```

### Intent

```text
High Intent
Medium Intent
Low Intent
Researching
Price Shopping
Ready to Book
Callback Requested
```

### Need

```text
Physiotherapy
Dental
Massage
Yoga
Corporate Wellness
Senior Wellness
Stress Management
Other
```

### Language

```text
English
French
Hindi
Punjabi
Tamil
Telugu
Multilingual
Code-Switching
```

### Contact preference

```text
Phone
SMS
Email
WhatsApp
Human Only
```

### Timing

```text
Morning
Afternoon
Evening
Weekend
Immediate Callback
Specific Time
```

### Price behavior

```text
Price Sensitive
Value Focused
Quality Focused
Convenience Focused
Premium
Unknown
```

### Engagement

```text
Highly Engaged
Moderately Engaged
Passive
Dormant
Reactivated
```

### Source

```text
Google
Instagram
Facebook
LinkedIn
Referral
Website
Partner
Existing CRM
```

## 5.4 Customer can belong to multiple segments

Do not force one segment only.

Example:

```text
C10028

High Intent
Physiotherapy
Hindi
Evening
Price Sensitive
Instagram Lead
Requested Callback
```

This is more useful than one generic persona label.

## 5.5 Segment membership table

Recommended structure:

```text
SEGMENT_MEMBERSHIP

customer_id
segment_id
membership_status
score
confidence
source
reason_codes
valid_from
valid_to
segment_version
```

Example:

```text
customer = C10028
segment = HIGH_INTENT
score = 91
reason = appointment_request + callback_request
```

## 5.6 Rule-based segmentation first

Start simple.

Example:

```text
IF
 intent = BOOK_APPOINTMENT
 OR callback_requested = true
THEN
 segment = HIGH_INTENT
```

Another:

```text
IF
 preferred_language = Hindi
 AND code_switching = true
THEN
 segment = HINDI_ENGLISH_MULTILINGUAL
```

Another:

```text
IF
 price_objection_count >= 2
 OR price_sensitivity_score > 70
THEN
 segment = PRICE_SENSITIVE
```

Rule-based segmentation is easier to explain and validate.

## 5.7 Feature builder

Create reusable features from Customer 360.

Examples:

```text
days_since_last_interaction
calls_last_30d
forms_last_30d
sms_responses
appointment_requests
booking_history
average_call_duration
preferred_language
preferred_time
price_objection_count
competitor_mentions
last_sentiment
lead_score
intent_score
service_fit_score
```

Do not recompute everything independently inside every model.

## 5.8 Persona engine

Create business-friendly personas.

Example:

### Persona P01 — Ready-to-Book

Characteristics:

```text
High intent
Specific service
Requested appointment
Valid contact
Clear timing preference
```

Call strategy:

```text
Short discovery
Confirm need
Check availability
Book
```

### Persona P02 — Price-Conscious Researcher

Characteristics:

```text
Interested
Repeated price questions
Competitor comparison
No urgency
```

Call strategy:

```text
Understand value criteria
Explain relevant options
Avoid aggressive selling
Offer trial/package
```

### Persona P03 — Multilingual Family Decision Maker

Characteristics:

```text
Preferred mother tongue
Asking for self + family
Multiple service needs
```

Call strategy:

```text
Preferred language
Need separation
Family-member context
Cross-service recommendation
```

## 5.9 Persona table

| Persona | Need | Intent | Typical objection | Agent strategy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ready-to-Book | Clear | High | Availability | Fast booking |
| Researcher | General | Medium | Trust/info | Education |
| Price Sensitive | Clear | Medium | Cost | Value/package |
| Time Sensitive | Clear | High | Schedule | Availability first |
| Family Buyer | Multiple | Medium/High | Fit | Multi-need discovery |
| Existing Customer | Known | Medium | Convenience | Personalized |
| Reactivation | Historical | Low/Medium | Relevance | Re-engage softly |
| Corporate Buyer | B2B | Medium/High | ROI | Business case |

## 5.10 Cohorts

Cohorts answer temporal questions.

Examples:

```text
Leads created this week
Customers acquired in August
Instagram leads from Campaign A
Customers who booked within 24 hours
Customers contacted within 5 minutes
Customers who did not answer first call
Customers who converted after SMS follow-up
```

These are crucial for analysis.

## 5.11 Cohort schema

```text
COHORT

cohort_id
name
definition
start_date
end_date
version
```

Membership:

```text
COHORT_MEMBER
customer_id
cohort_id
joined_at
```

## 5.12 Dynamic segmentation

Some segments change automatically.

Example:

Customer today:

```text
LOW_INTENT
```

Then submits appointment request.

Immediately:

```text
HIGH_INTENT
```

Use events:

```text
appointment.requested
lead.score.updated
preference.changed
call.completed
```

to trigger reevaluation.

## 5.13 Event-driven architecture

```text
Customer event
     ↓
Feature update
     ↓
Segment evaluator
     ↓
Membership changes
     ↓
segment.entered
segment.exited
```

Then campaign engine reacts.

Example:

```text
segment.entered = HIGH_INTENT
      ↓
priority callback campaign
```

## 5.14 Segment explainability

Every membership should answer:

> Why is this customer in this segment?

Example:

```text
Segment:
PRICE_SENSITIVE

Reasons:
- Said "too expensive"
- Asked for lower-cost package
- Compared competitor price

Confidence:
0.91
```

This becomes important for ExplainAI.

## 5.15 Explicit vs inferred segments

Customer explicitly says:

> "Evenings are better."

Store:

```text
EVENING_PREFERENCE
source = CUSTOMER_EXPLICIT
```

AI infers:

```text
LIKELY_PRICE_SENSITIVE
source = MODEL_INFERENCE
confidence = .68
```

Never blur the two.

## 5.16 Need-based segmentation

Create hierarchical categories.

Example:

```text
Healthcare
 ├── Dental
 ├── Physiotherapy
 ├── Chiropractic
 ├── ENT
 └── Massage

Wellness
 ├── Yoga
 ├── Meditation
 ├── Senior Yoga
 ├── Kids Yoga
 └── Corporate Wellness
```

This supports broad and granular campaigns.

## 5.17 Location segmentation

Examples:

```text
Canada
 └── Alberta
      └── Calgary
           ├── NW
           ├── NE
           ├── SW
           └── SE
```

Keep geography separate from language, ethnicity, or inferred identity.

## 5.18 Channel segmentation

Example:

```text
PHONE_PREFERRED
SMS_PREFERRED
EMAIL_PREFERRED
WHATSAPP_PREFERRED
HUMAN_ONLY
DIGITAL_ONLY
```

This drives outreach strategy.

## 5.19 Timing segmentation

Use explicit and learned data.

Examples:

```text
MORNING_RESPONDER
EVENING_RESPONDER
WEEKEND_RESPONDER
BUSINESS_HOURS_ONLY
```

Do not infer from tiny samples.

Require enough history.

Example:

```text
minimum answered calls >= 3
```

before declaring a behavioral preference.

## 5.20 Engagement segmentation

Potential score:

```text
form completion
email click
SMS reply
call answer
appointment request
website revisit
```

Then:

```text
HIGH
MEDIUM
LOW
DORMANT
```

But avoid overweighting channel activity that merely reflects automation.

## 5.21 Competitor segments

Examples:

```text
CURRENT_COMPETITOR_CUSTOMER
COMPETITOR_PRICE_SHOPPER
SWITCHING_CANDIDATE
COMPETITOR_LOYAL
```

Capture competitor evidence from calls.

Do not fabricate competitive status from weak inference.

## 5.22 Objection-based segments

Useful categories:

```text
PRICE_OBJECTION
TRUST_OBJECTION
TIME_OBJECTION
LOCATION_OBJECTION
QUALITY_CONCERN
HUMAN_PREFERENCE
AI_RESISTANCE
```

These can directly alter the call script.

## 5.23 Script adaptation

Example:

```text
Customer Segment:
HIGH_INTENT + EVENING + HINDI
```

Agent configuration:

```text
Language = Hindi
Opening = short
Discovery = minimal
CTA = appointment
Availability = evening first
```

Another:

```text
PRICE_SENSITIVE + RESEARCHER
```

Agent:

```text
Language = preferred
Discovery = deeper
Explain value
Discuss options
Avoid early booking pressure
```

## 5.24 Segment → provider routing

SegmentAI can later inform RouteAI.

Example:

```text
Punjabi + multilingual
→ Sarvam candidate

English + premium quality
→ LiveKit/Retell candidate
```

But RouteAI should still consider cost, availability, compliance, and current quality.

## 5.25 Segment → campaign mapping

Create:

```text
SEGMENT_CAMPAIGN_RULE
```

Example:

| Segment | Campaign |
|---|---|
| High Intent | Immediate/priority callback |
| No Answer | Retry |
| Price Sensitive | Value offer |
| Existing Customer | Loyalty |
| Lapsed | Reactivation |
| Corporate Buyer | Human sales |
| DNC | None |

## 5.26 Manual segment overrides

Admins may occasionally need to override segment membership.

Store:

```text
manual_override = true
reason
user_id
timestamp
expiration
```

Do not silently let models overwrite explicit authorized overrides.

## 5.27 AI-driven clustering later

Once you have enough customer data, use exploratory clustering.

Possible tools:

HDBSCAN  
K-means  
Gaussian Mixture Models.

Input features:

```text
intent
engagement
service interests
contact patterns
preferences
objections
conversion behavior
```

Use clustering primarily for discovery.

Do not automatically push unknown clusters into production campaigns.

## 5.28 Embedding-based persona discovery

Transcript summaries can be embedded to identify recurring themes.

Example clusters:

```text
"wants evening appointment"
"concerned about price"
"asking for family service"
"needs online service"
```

Use these to discover new segmentation rules.

## 5.29 Segment drift

Segment populations change.

Example:

```text
PRICE_SENSITIVE
10% → 32% in 2 months
```

Could indicate:

pricing issue  
campaign targeting change  
economic shift  
competitor activity.

DriftAI should eventually monitor this.

## 5.30 Segment versioning

Suppose:

`HIGH_INTENT v1`

used:

appointment request only.

v2 adds:

callback requested + service-specific inquiry.

Store:

```text
segment_definition_version
```

so historical reports remain reproducible.

## 5.31 API design

Recommended:

```text
POST /segments
GET /segments

GET /segments/{id}

POST /segments/{id}/evaluate

GET /customers/{id}/segments

POST /customers/{id}/segments/override

GET /cohorts
POST /cohorts

GET /segments/{id}/performance
```

## 5.32 Event catalog

```text
segment.created
segment.updated
segment.entered
segment.exited

persona.assigned
persona.changed

cohort.created
cohort.member_added

segment.drift_detected
```

## 5.33 Technology stack

Rules:

Python/FastAPI initially.

Data:

PostgreSQL.

Feature computation:

SQL + Python.

Cache:

Redis.

Analytics:

dbt later if warehouse grows.

ML:

scikit-learn  
XGBoost  
HDBSCAN.

Visualization:

Metabase / Superset / Power BI.

## 5.34 Testing — rules

For every segment create:

positive cases  
negative cases  
boundary cases  
missing-data cases.

Example:

High Intent:

```text
booking request = yes
→ membership YES
```

```text
browsed page only
→ membership NO
```

## 5.35 Segment conflict testing

Customer might simultaneously be:

```text
HIGH_INTENT
PRICE_SENSITIVE
HUMAN_ONLY
```

This is valid.

Create priority rules only when actions conflict.

For example:

`HUMAN_ONLY` overrides AI outbound calling.

## 5.36 Edge case — insufficient data

New lead:

```text
Name + phone only
```

Do not over-classify.

Use:

```text
UNKNOWN_INTENT
UNKNOWN_PRICE_SENSITIVITY
```

rather than inventing values.

## 5.37 Edge case — contradictory behavior

Customer:

> "Price doesn't matter."

Later:

> "That's too expensive."

Keep history.

Possible current state:

```text
price_sensitivity = MEDIUM
confidence = .62
```

rather than declaring a fixed permanent trait.

## 5.38 Edge case — segment churn

Customer repeatedly enters/leaves a segment due to tiny score changes.

Use hysteresis.

Example:

Enter HIGH_INTENT at:

```text
score >= 80
```

Exit only when:

```text
score < 70
```

This avoids oscillation.

## 5.39 Edge case — customer becomes DNC

DNC is not simply another marketing segment.

Compliance restrictions should override segmentation.

```text
DNC
→ campaign eligibility BLOCK
```

even if:

```text
HIGH_INTENT = true
```

## 5.40 Edge case — AI inference based on sensitive attributes

Do not create questionable segments such as inferred race, religion, health condition, political belief, or similar sensitive profiling for marketing.

Use explicit business-relevant preferences and needs.

## 5.41 QA metrics

Measure:

```text
segment_precision
segment_recall
manual_override_rate
unknown_rate
segment_stability
segment_transition_rate
campaign_conversion_by_segment
complaint_rate_by_segment
```

For rule-based segments, precision/recall can be measured against manually labeled test sets.

## 5.42 Test dataset

Create at least 500 synthetic customers spanning:

```text
high/medium/low intent
different languages
different services
different call windows
price sensitivities
existing/new customers
different acquisition channels
different engagement patterns
DNC
human-only
multiple needs
```

Expected segment labels should be manually defined.

## 5.43 Validation process

```text
Rules designed
→ Product review
→ Data review
→ QA dataset
→ Automated evaluation
→ Business UAT
→ Shadow mode
→ Production
```

Shadow mode is useful.

Let SegmentAI calculate segments without triggering campaigns initially.

Compare against human judgement.

## 5.44 Monitoring

Dashboard:

```text
Customers per segment
New entrants
Exits
Segment growth
Conversion
Call connect
Booking
Revenue
Complaints
DNC rate
Cost/customer
```

## 5.45 Segment performance

Example:

| Segment | Calls | Connect | Booking | Conversion |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| High Intent | 1,000 | 72% | 45% | 32% |
| Researcher | 1,500 | 60% | 19% | 10% |
| Price Sensitive | 900 | 64% | 16% | 8% |

Now you can optimize scripts and campaigns by customer type.

## 5.46 ReportAI connection

Executives can ask:

> Which customer segment generates the most revenue?

Marketing:

> Which source creates High-Intent leads?

Sales:

> Which personas need human follow-up?

Product:

> Which segment is requesting services we don't offer?

## 5.47 Security

Segment membership itself can become sensitive information.

Protect:

RBAC  
tenant isolation  
audit  
data minimization.

Don't expose all inferred traits to every salesperson.

## 5.48 Explainability record

Example:

```text
Customer C10028

Segment:
READY_TO_BOOK

Confidence:
0.94

Reasons:
Requested appointment
Provided preferred time
Asked provider availability

Version:
SEG-READY-BOOK-v3
```

## 5.49 Definition of Done

Phase 5 is complete when:

```text
Rule-based segments          PASS
Persona assignment           PASS
Multi-segment membership     PASS
Dynamic reevaluation         PASS
Cohort engine                PASS
Explainability               PASS
Versioning                   PASS
Overrides                    PASS
Conflict handling            PASS
DNC override                 PASS
Security                     PASS
Synthetic test suite         PASS
Shadow validation            PASS
Monitoring                   PASS
Dashboards                   PASS
UAT                          PASS
```

### Phase 5 output

A customer might now look like:

```text
Customer:
C10028

Segments:
HIGH_INTENT
PHYSIOTHERAPY
HINDI
EVENING
PRICE_SENSITIVE
INSTAGRAM
CALLBACK_REQUESTED

Persona:
READY_TO_BOOK_WITH_PRICE_CONCERN

Recommended campaign:
HIGH_INTENT_CALLBACK

Script profile:
SHORT_DISCOVERY + VALUE_EXPLANATION

Preferred call window:
18:00–20:00

Status:
READY_FOR_SCORING
```

The next phase is **Phase 6 — ScoreAI**, where we build the full lead, intent, fit, urgency, engagement, conversion, appointment, churn, price-sensitivity, complaint-risk, AI-confidence, and next-action scoring framework—including formulas, ML progression, explainability, calibration, test data, monitoring, drift, validation, and edge cases.

## 🤖 Assistant — msg #46

# Phase 6 — ScoreAI: Lead + Intent + Fit + Conversion + Risk + Confidence Scoring

Phase 5 tells us **what kind of customer this is**. Phase 6 answers:

> **How strong is this opportunity, what is likely to happen next, how confident are we, and why?**

A key design rule: **do not create one mysterious “AI Score = 87.”** Maintain separate, explainable scores for different business decisions.

---

## 6.1 ScoreAI architecture

```text
Customer 360
    +
Lead
    +
Segments
    +
Form
    +
Campaign
    +
Call History
    +
Preferences
    +
Needs
    +
Appointments
    +
Feedback
    +
Interaction History
         ↓
     Feature Store
         ↓
 ┌────────┼────────────────────────────────┐
 ↓        ↓          ↓          ↓          ↓
Lead    Intent      Fit      Engagement   Urgency
Score   Score       Score      Score       Score
 ↓        ↓          ↓          ↓          ↓
 ├────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
 ↓        ↓          ↓          ↓          ↓
Booking Conversion Show     Churn     Complaint
Score     Score     Score    Score       Risk
                    ↓
              Decision Engine
                    ↓
             ExplainAI / NextAI
                    ↓
      Campaign / Agent / Human / Nurture
```

---

# 6.2 Score catalog

I would start with these scores.

| Score | Question answered | Range |
|---|---|---:|
| Lead Quality | Is this a useful lead? | 0–100 |
| Data Trust | Can we trust the lead data? | 0–100 |
| Intent | How interested are they? | 0–100 |
| Need Strength | How clearly do they need something? | 0–100 |
| Service Fit | How well do we meet that need? | 0–100 |
| Engagement | How engaged are they? | 0–100 |
| Urgency | How soon might they act? | 0–100 |
| Conversion | Likelihood of becoming customer | 0–100 |
| Booking | Likelihood of appointment booking | 0–100 |
| Show | Likelihood of attending | 0–100 |
| Price Sensitivity | Price resistance | 0–100 |
| Upsell | Adjacent-service opportunity | 0–100 |
| Churn | Existing-customer churn probability | 0–100 |
| Competitor Risk | Likelihood competitor wins | 0–100 |
| Complaint Risk | Potential dissatisfaction | 0–100 |
| Contactability | Probability of successful contact | 0–100 |
| AI Confidence | Confidence in AI-derived fields | 0–100 |

Some are predictive. Others are descriptive/rule-based.

Keep that distinction.

---

# 6.3 Start rules-based

For an early-stage platform with limited historical data, don't pretend ML knows your customers.

Example Lead Quality Score:

```text
Valid phone                    +15
Valid email                    +10
Specific service selected      +10
Callback requested             +15
Appointment intent             +20
Preferred contact time         +5
Preferred language             +5
Required consent/evidence      +10
Trusted acquisition source     +10
-----------------------------------
Maximum                        100
```

This is simple, testable and explainable.

---

# 6.4 Intent Score

Signals might include:

### Strong positive

```text
"Book me."
"When is the next appointment?"
"Can I come tomorrow?"
"Please call me tonight."
```

### Medium

```text
"Tell me about your program."
"What does it cost?"
"How does this work?"
```

### Weak

```text
"Just browsing."
"Send information."
```

### Negative

```text
"Not interested."
"I didn't request this."
"Stop calling."
```

Example rules:

```text
Appointment request             +35
Requested callback              +20
Specific service                +10
Specific date/time              +15
Asked price                     +5
Asked availability              +10
Competitor comparison            +5
```

But:

```text
Not interested                  -50
Wrong number                   BLOCK
DNC                            BLOCK
```

DNC is **not merely a negative score**. It is a policy block.

---

# 6.5 Need Strength Score

Measure how clearly the requirement is established.

Example:

```text
Explicit need                  +40
Specific desired outcome       +20
Specific constraints           +10
Urgency expressed              +15
Repeated confirmation          +15
```

Compare:

> "I'm interested in wellness."

Need strength may be 30.

versus:

> "I need an evening physiotherapy appointment this week."

Need strength may be 95.

---

# 6.6 Service Fit Score

Inputs:

```text
Need match
Service availability
Location
Schedule
Language
Delivery preference
Price range
Eligibility
Provider availability
```

Conceptually:

```text
Fit =
Need match          30%
Availability        20%
Schedule            15%
Location            10%
Language            10%
Delivery preference 10%
Price fit            5%
```

Weights should be validated using business data.

---

# 6.7 Engagement Score

Potential inputs:

```text
Form completed
Returned to website
Answered call
SMS reply
Email response
Requested callback
Call duration
Appointment action
```

Use recency decay.

Interaction from yesterday should generally matter more than one from six months ago.

Concept:

```text
effective_signal =
raw_signal × recency_weight
```

---

# 6.8 Don't reward meaningless engagement

A 20-minute call is not automatically better than a two-minute successful booking.

Avoid:

```text
longer call = better lead
```

Instead measure meaningful engagement:

questions answered, need clarified, CTA accepted, appointment action, explicit follow-up.

---

# 6.9 Urgency Score

Signals:

```text
"today"
"tomorrow"
"this week"
"as soon as possible"
```

versus:

```text
"maybe next year"
"just researching"
```

Example:

| Timing | Score |
|---|---:|
| Today | 100 |
| 1–3 days | 90 |
| This week | 80 |
| This month | 60 |
| 1–3 months | 40 |
| Unknown | 30 |
| No plan | 10 |

Don't infer emergency severity from a marketing conversation.

---

# 6.10 Price Sensitivity Score

Signals:

```text
"too expensive"
"any discount?"
"competitor charges $50"
"do you have cheaper package?"
```

But also:

> "What does it cost?"

should **not** automatically mean price-sensitive.

Price inquiry ≠ price objection.

Separate:

```text
PRICE_INQUIRY
PRICE_OBJECTION
PRICE_REJECTION
```

---

# 6.11 Contactability Score

Useful for outbound calling.

Features:

```text
previous answer rate
preferred call time
valid phone
recent callback request
voicemail history
busy history
call rejection history
```

Example:

```text
Customer answers evenings 4/5 times
```

could produce:

```text
Evening contactability = HIGH
Morning contactability = LOW
```

This later feeds campaign scheduling.

---

# 6.12 Booking Score

Predict:

> Probability that this lead will book an appointment.

Inputs might include:

Intent  
need strength  
availability match  
urgency  
engagement  
previous booking behavior  
service fit  
price objection.

Output:

```text
booking_probability = 0.82
```

Keep probability distinct from a 0–100 business score if needed.

---

# 6.13 Show Score

After booking:

> How likely are they to actually attend?

Potential signals:

booking lead time  
previous no-shows  
confirmation response  
rescheduling frequency  
appointment reminder engagement.

Use carefully. Don't use questionable demographic proxies.

Output can determine reminder strategy rather than whether someone deserves service.

---

# 6.14 Conversion Score

Predict:

```text
Lead → Paying Customer
```

Potential features:

```text
intent
need strength
service fit
engagement
urgency
price sensitivity
competitor risk
booking probability
contactability
```

Initially use a rule score.

Later train against actual conversions.

---

# 6.15 Upsell / Cross-sell Score

Customer says:

> "I'm booking yoga, but my mother is looking for a senior program."

Potential:

```text
Primary conversion opportunity
+
Secondary service opportunity
```

Calculate:

```text
need-service match
explicit interest
eligibility
timing
relationship/context
```

Do not cross-sell merely because an AI model predicts vulnerability or sensitive traits.

---

# 6.16 Competitor Risk

Signals:

```text
Existing competitor
Competitor satisfaction
Competitor price
Switching intent
Contract commitment
Feature comparison
```

Example:

```text
Competitor Risk = 78
```

Reasons:

```text
Currently uses competitor
Likes competitor price
No major complaint
Low switching urgency
```

---

# 6.17 Complaint Risk

Potential signals:

repeated unresolved issues  
negative sentiment  
multiple transfers  
repeated failed calls  
broken promises  
incorrect booking  
customer frustration.

Do not equate accent, language, speech pattern or demographic characteristics with complaint risk.

---

# 6.18 Churn Score

For existing customers:

```text
Reduced engagement
Cancellation
Repeated complaints
Service dissatisfaction
Price concerns
Competitor mentions
Failed support interactions
```

Then NextAI can recommend:

human follow-up, retention offer, service recovery.

---

# 6.19 AI Confidence Score

This one is different.

Suppose AI extracts:

```text
preferred_time = evening
```

Customer explicitly said:

> "Call me after six."

Confidence:

```text
0.99
```

But AI infers:

```text
price_sensitive = true
```

from vague language.

Confidence:

```text
0.58
```

Store confidence **per extracted fact**, not just one global number.

---

# 6.20 Feature provenance

Every feature should know its source.

Example:

```text
feature:
preferred_language

value:
Hindi

source:
CALL-90881

type:
CUSTOMER_EXPLICIT

confidence:
1.0
```

versus:

```text
feature:
price_sensitivity

value:
HIGH

source:
MODEL_INFERENCE

confidence:
0.67
```

This greatly improves governance.

---

# 6.21 Score storage model

```text
SCORE

score_id
customer_id
lead_id

score_type
score_value
probability

model_type
RULE / ML / LLM

model_id
model_version

feature_version

confidence

reason_codes

calculated_at
expires_at
```

Never overwrite historical scores.

---

# 6.22 Reason codes

Example:

```text
INTENT_APPOINTMENT_REQUEST
CALLBACK_REQUESTED
SPECIFIC_SERVICE
SPECIFIC_TIME
PRICE_OBJECTION
COMPETITOR_MENTION
NO_RECENT_ENGAGEMENT
```

Reason codes are much easier to govern and report than free-text explanations alone.

---

# 6.23 ExplainAI integration

For every important score:

```text
Score
 ↓
Top positive drivers
 ↓
Top negative drivers
 ↓
Confidence
 ↓
Model version
```

Example:

> **Conversion: 76/100**

Positive:

+ requested appointment  
+ requested evening callback  
+ high service fit.

Negative:

− price objection  
− competitor comparison.

---

# 6.24 Score bands

Example:

```text
80–100  VERY HIGH
60–79   HIGH
40–59   MEDIUM
20–39   LOW
0–19    VERY LOW
```

But don't apply the same thresholds to every score.

A complaint-risk score requires different action thresholds from intent.

---

# 6.25 Score → action mapping

Example:

| Intent | Fit | Action |
|---|---|---|
| High | High | Priority call |
| High | Low | Alternative service/human |
| Medium | High | Nurture/call |
| Low | High | Low-pressure nurture |
| Low | Low | Don't waste call capacity |

Add consent/policy checks above everything.

---

# 6.26 Score orchestration

Recommended order:

```text
Data Quality
 ↓
Trust
 ↓
Contactability
 ↓
Intent
 ↓
Need Strength
 ↓
Service Fit
 ↓
Engagement
 ↓
Urgency
 ↓
Booking
 ↓
Conversion
 ↓
NextAI
```

Some scores can run in parallel.

---

# 6.27 ML progression

Use four maturity stages.

### Stage 1 — Rules

Transparent.

Fast.

Best for MVP.

### Stage 2 — Classical ML

Logistic regression.

Excellent baseline for conversion/booking.

### Stage 3 — Gradient boosting

XGBoost / LightGBM.

Useful for nonlinear interactions.

### Stage 4 — More advanced approaches

Only if justified by volume and measurable uplift.

Don't jump to deep learning because the platform is called AI.

---

# 6.28 Training labels

Define outcomes clearly.

Booking model:

```text
label=1
if appointment booked within defined observation window
```

Conversion model:

```text
label=1
if lead became qualified paying customer within defined window
```

Show model:

```text
label=1
if appointment attended
```

Bad labels create bad ScoreAI.

---

# 6.29 Avoid label leakage

Do not train booking prediction using information only known **after** booking.

Example bad feature:

```text
appointment_confirmation_status
```

when predicting whether an appointment will be booked.

Create feature snapshots as of decision time.

---

# 6.30 Train/validation/test split

Prefer temporal splits for production-like evaluation.

Example:

```text
Train:
Jan–Apr

Validation:
May

Test:
June
```

rather than randomly mixing future and past events.

This better approximates deployment.

---

# 6.31 Evaluation metrics

For classification:

AUC-ROC  
PR-AUC  
precision  
recall  
F1.

For probability models:

Brier score  
calibration curve  
log loss.

For business:

conversion uplift  
booking uplift  
cost/booking  
revenue/customer  
calls saved.

---

# 6.32 Calibration

If model says:

```text
80% probability
```

then approximately 80% of similarly scored cases should convert over time.

That's calibration.

A model can rank customers well while producing poor probabilities.

Monitor both.

---

# 6.33 Threshold optimization

Don't automatically use:

```text
0.50
```

as the decision threshold.

Choose thresholds according to:

cost of call  
agent capacity  
value of conversion  
false-positive cost  
customer experience.

---

# 6.34 Human review zone

Example:

```text
0–30      low priority
31–69     automated/nurture
70–90     priority
91–100    high priority
```

For risk scores, define review zones separately.

Ambiguous/high-impact decisions can go to humans.

---

# 6.35 Cold-start problem

New customer:

No call history.

No purchase history.

No behavioral history.

Don't return artificial certainty.

Use:

form intent  
source  
explicit preferences  
service request  
campaign information.

And return:

```text
confidence = LOW
```

---

# 6.36 Missing-data handling

Do not automatically convert:

```text
unknown income → zero income
```

or:

```text
unknown price sensitivity → low sensitivity
```

Use explicit missing indicators where appropriate.

---

# 6.37 Score expiration

Scores become stale.

Example:

Intent score from six months ago may be irrelevant.

Store:

```text
calculated_at
valid_until
```

Recalculate on meaningful events.

---

# 6.38 Real-time score updates

Events:

```text
form.submitted
call.completed
preference.changed
appointment.requested
appointment.cancelled
complaint.created
```

trigger relevant rescoring.

Don't recalculate every model after every insignificant event.

---

# 6.39 Testing — rules

For every score create:

positive case  
negative case  
boundary case  
missing data  
conflicting data.

Example:

```text
appointment_request=true
```

must increase intent according to documented rule.

---

# 6.40 ML test data

Build historical-like synthetic records:

```text
customer
source
intent
service
language
call_history
engagement
objections
appointment
conversion
```

Use synthetic data for pipeline testing.

Do not use synthetic performance as proof of model accuracy.

Real model validation requires real labeled outcomes.

---

# 6.41 Edge case — high score but DNC

Example:

```text
Conversion = 98
Intent = 95
DNC = TRUE
```

Result:

```text
DO NOT CALL
```

PolicyAI always outranks ScoreAI.

---

# 6.42 Edge case — high intent but low fit

Customer desperately wants a service you don't provide.

```text
Intent = 96
Fit = 12
```

Don't sell something inappropriate.

Next action:

```text
alternative service
human review
or transparent unavailable response
```

---

# 6.43 Edge case — low confidence

```text
Intent = 82
Confidence = 41
```

Treat differently from:

```text
Intent = 82
Confidence = 97
```

NextAI should incorporate confidence.

---

# 6.44 Edge case — contradictory signals

Customer:

> "I'm very interested."

but repeatedly refuses booking and asks not to follow up yet.

Maintain different dimensions:

```text
Service Interest = HIGH
Purchase Readiness = LOW
Contact Permission = LIMITED
```

Don't force everything into Intent.

---

# 6.45 Edge case — model gaming

Sales staff may learn that entering:

```text
urgent=true
```

creates higher priority.

Track:

who generated each feature  
manual override rates  
suspicious score manipulation.

Govern manual inputs.

---

# 6.46 Bias testing

Check whether performance differs across relevant evaluation groups such as language or region when appropriate.

Metrics:

false-positive rate  
false-negative rate  
calibration  
booking-prediction error.

Do not automatically force equal outcomes where underlying contexts legitimately differ; investigate the causes and business impact.

---

# 6.47 DriftAI integration

Monitor:

feature drift  
score drift  
prediction drift  
performance drift  
calibration drift.

Example:

```text
Average Conversion Score

May = 58
June = 59
July = 74
```

Investigate unexpected jumps.

---

# 6.48 Shadow deployment

Before scores affect campaign priority:

```text
Model
 ↓
Shadow Mode
 ↓
Generate scores
 ↓
No automated decisions
 ↓
Compare actual outcomes
```

Run for an appropriate evaluation period.

Then activate gradually.

---

# 6.49 Champion/challenger

Production:

```text
Champion:
Logistic Regression v3

Challenger:
XGBoost v1
```

Compare:

accuracy  
calibration  
conversion uplift  
fairness  
latency  
cost.

Don't replace champion solely because challenger has slightly higher AUC.

---

# 6.50 ScoreAI APIs

```text
POST /scores/calculate

GET /customers/{id}/scores

GET /leads/{id}/scores

GET /scores/{id}/explanation

POST /scores/recalculate

GET /models/{id}/performance
```

Example response:

```json
{
  "intent": {
    "score": 91,

  },

    "score": 74,

    "band": "HIGH"
  }
}
```

# 6.51 Feature Store

At modest scale:

PostgreSQL + well-designed feature tables may be sufficient.

Later consider:

Feast or a custom feature platform.

Feature example:

```text
customer_id
feature_name
value
event_time
computed_at
source
version
```

The key is **point-in-time correctness**.

Track:

```text
model_id
model_name
version
training_dataset
features
metrics
owner
approval
deployment
rollback_version
```

Possible tool:

MLflow.

# 6.53 Experiment tracking

For ML:

MLflow or Weights & Biases.

Track:

parameters  
features  
data version  
metrics  
artifacts.

# 6.54 Monitoring dashboard

### Score distribution

```text
Intent
0–20       8%
21–40     17%
41–60     29%
61–80     31%
81–100    15%
```

### Outcome

```text
Score Band → Actual Conversion
```

Example:

| Conversion score | Actual conversion |
|---|---:|
| 0–20 | 3% |
| 21–40 | 9% |
| 41–60 | 22% |
| 61–80 | 47% |
| 81–100 | 74% |

If this relationship deteriorates, investigate calibration/drift.

# 6.55 Business monitoring

Track:

```text
calls saved through prioritization
conversion uplift
appointments/call
revenue/call
cost/conversion
human review volume
complaint rate
```

ScoreAI is useful only if it improves outcomes without damaging customer experience or governance.

---

# 6.56 Score-level SLA

Example operational requirements:

```text
Rules score:
<100 ms

Realtime ML score:
<300 ms

Batch rescoring:
defined by campaign requirements
```

Don't call an LLM synchronously for every deterministic scoring rule.

---

# 6.57 Security

Protect:

model endpoints  
feature data  
score history  
explanations.

Use:

RBAC  
service authentication  
tenant isolation  
encryption  
audit logging.

Prevent arbitrary score editing.

# 6.58 Audit record

For every score used in a decision:

```text
customer
score
value
model
model_version
feature_version
timestamp
reason_codes
decision_id
```

Then six months later you can reconstruct:

> Why was this customer prioritized?

# 6.59 ScoreAI regression suite

Before deployment:

```text
Golden scoring dataset
        ↓
Old model
        ↓
New model
        ↓
Compare
```

Investigate:

large score changes  
segment-specific deterioration  
calibration degradation  
risk/fairness changes.

# 6.60 Failure handling

If ML scoring service fails:

Do not crash customer acquisition.

Possible fallback:

```text
ML score unavailable
       ↓
rules-based fallback
       ↓
confidence = reduced
       ↓
log incident
```

For high-risk decisions, fail conservatively.
