# Phase 7 — CampaignAI / Outbound Campaign Orchestration

This phase converts eligible, scored leads into controlled outbound campaigns. It is where **who to call, when to call, how often to retry, which agent/provider to use, what budget to spend, and when to stop** are decided.

## 7.1 Target architecture

```text
Eligible Leads
   ↓
Audience Builder
   ↓
Campaign Definition
   ↓
Priority Rules
   ↓
Schedule + Timezone
   ↓
Budget + Frequency Caps
   ↓
Pre-call Eligibility Check
   ↓
Queue / Workflow Engine
   ↓
RouteAI
   ↓
Telephony + Voice Provider
   ↓
Call Outcome
   ↓
Retry / Follow-up / Stop
   ↓
CRM + Analytics + QA
```

## 7.2 Campaign object

Core fields:

```text
campaign_id
tenant_id
name
purpose
status

audience_definition
segment_ids

agent_profile
script_version
language_strategy

start_date
end_date
timezone_strategy

daily_call_limit
max_concurrency
max_attempts

retry_policy
voicemail_policy
sms_fallback
human_transfer_policy

budget_total
budget_daily
cost_per_lead_limit

priority
provider_strategy

created_by
approved_by
policy_version
```

## 7.3 Campaign lifecycle

```text
DRAFT
  ↓
REVIEW
  ↓
APPROVED
  ↓
SCHEDULED
  ↓
ACTIVE
  ↓
PAUSED
  ↓
COMPLETED
```

Other terminal states:

```text
CANCELLED
BLOCKED
BUDGET_EXHAUSTED
COMPLIANCE_HOLD
```

Never allow `DRAFT → ACTIVE` directly for production campaigns.

## 7.4 Audience selection

Campaign audience can use:

**Segments + Scores + Need + geography + language + campaign source + service + lifecycle + contactability + consent eligibility.**

Example:

```text
Segment = HIGH_INTENT
AND
Service = PHYSIOTHERAPY
AND
IntentScore >= 80
AND
Contactability >= 60
AND
City = Calgary
AND
CALL_ELIGIBLE = TRUE
```

Important: create an **audience snapshot** at campaign execution time, but still re-check eligibility immediately before dialing.

## 7.5 Audience exclusion rules

Always exclude:

```text
DNC
suppressed
invalid phone
already converted
active complaint
existing appointment where campaign no longer applies
fraud/high-risk lead
campaign exclusion
contact pressure exceeded
```

## 7.6 Campaign types

Support:

| Campaign | Example |
|---|---|
| Immediate lead callback | Form submission |
| Qualification | New lead |
| Appointment booking | High-intent |
| Reminder | Upcoming appointment |
| No-show recovery | Missed appointment |
| Reactivation | Lapsed customer |
| Renewal | Existing service |
| Feedback | Post-service |
| Cross-sell | Related service |
| Win-back | Former customer |
| Event campaign | Webinar/open house |
| B2B outreach | Corporate prospects |

Each campaign type should have different retry and script policies.

## 7.7 Priority model

Example:

```text
P0 Requested callback
P1 Appointment-related
P2 High-intent new lead
P3 Warm lead
P4 Reactivation
P5 General marketing
```

Within priority, use:

```text
intent_score
+
urgency
+
contactability
+
service_fit
+
lead_age
```

Do not prioritize customers solely because they are predicted to spend more if that creates inappropriate or unfair exclusion.

## 7.8 Lead freshness

For inbound leads, recency matters.

Create:

```text
lead_age_minutes
lead_age_hours
lead_age_days
```

Fresh high-intent leads may receive higher operational priority, subject to consent and calling-window policy.

## 7.9 Scheduling engine

Inputs:

```text
customer timezone
customer preference
campaign window
jurisdiction window
holiday policy
agent/provider capacity
priority
requested callback time
```

Calculate:

```text
next_eligible_call_at
```

## 7.10 Exact callback scheduling

If customer says:

> "Call me Tuesday at 6 PM."

Store:

```text
requested_callback_at
timezone
source_interaction
```

This gets higher priority than general campaign optimization.

## 7.11 Best-time-to-call optimization

Initially use explicit preference.

Later use historical behavior:

```text
answer rate by weekday/hour
conversion rate by weekday/hour
callback success
```

Example:

```text
Tuesday evening:
answer = 72%

Tuesday morning:
answer = 31%
```

Then rank eligible windows.

Never violate calling policy just because the prediction says another time performs better.

## 7.12 Queue architecture

For modest volume:

**Redis + Temporal**

At larger scale:

**Kafka/Redpanda + Temporal + Redis**

Example workflow:

```text
Campaign
  ↓
Generate call jobs
  ↓
Priority Queue
  ↓
Worker
  ↓
Pre-dial policy
  ↓
Provider
```

## 7.13 Durable orchestration

Temporal is useful because calls involve:

```text
schedule
wait
retry
timeout
callback
provider response
human transfer
CRM update
SMS follow-up
```

These are durable long-running workflows.

n8n is useful for secondary automations, but I would not make it the authoritative campaign scheduler at scale.

## 7.14 Concurrency management

Set:

```text
tenant_limit
campaign_limit
provider_limit
telephony_limit
global_limit
```

Effective concurrency:

```text
min(
tenant,
campaign,
provider,
telephony,
global
)
```

This protects infrastructure and vendor quotas.

## 7.15 Rate limiting

Track:

```text
calls/minute
calls/hour
API requests/sec
provider limits
```

Use token bucket or leaky bucket mechanisms where appropriate.

## 7.16 Campaign budget control

Track:

```text
daily_budget
campaign_budget
provider_budget
tenant_budget
```

Before every call:

```text
estimated_call_cost
+
current_spend
<= budget
```

Otherwise:

```text
BUDGET_HOLD
```

## 7.17 Cost reservation

Useful at scale.

Before call:

```text
reserve estimated cost
```

After call:

```text
actual cost
release difference
```

This prevents concurrency from overspending a tight budget.

## 7.18 Retry engine

Retry depends on outcome.

### No answer

May retry later.

### Busy

Retry at another appropriate time.

### Voicemail

Apply campaign voicemail policy.

### Wrong number

Stop.

### DNC

Stop permanently for applicable scope.

### Technical provider failure

Retry using provider/fallback logic without counting it as a customer contact attempt where policy permits.

## 7.19 Retry policy object

```text
max_attempts
minimum_gap
maximum_gap
backoff_strategy

retry_on:
 NO_ANSWER
 BUSY
 TEMP_PROVIDER_FAILURE

do_not_retry_on:
 DNC
 WRONG_NUMBER
 NOT_INTERESTED
```

## 7.20 Backoff strategies

Support:

```text
fixed
linear
exponential
next-preferred-window
```

For sales outreach, `next-preferred-window` is often more customer-friendly than aggressive exponential retries.

## 7.21 Contact-attempt ledger

Store every attempt:

```text
attempt_id
lead_id
campaign_id

attempt_number

scheduled_at
dialed_at

provider

result
duration
reason

counts_toward_frequency_cap
```

## 7.22 Voicemail handling

Campaign can choose:

```text
DO_NOT_LEAVE
LEAVE_STANDARD
LEAVE_PERSONALIZED
SMS_INSTEAD
```

Test voicemail detection carefully; answering-machine detection is imperfect.

Do not reveal sensitive information in voicemail.

## 7.23 Answering-machine detection edge case

False positive:

real person classified as voicemail.

False negative:

voicemail classified as human.

Mitigation:

confidence threshold + script designed to recover gracefully.

## 7.24 Call abandonment / pickup latency

If a customer answers, don't leave them hearing silence while the agent initializes.

Measure:

```text
answer_to_agent_audio_latency
```

Pre-warm agent sessions where justified.

## 7.25 Number pool management

Maintain:

```text
phone_number_id
country
region
provider
campaign
health_status
reputation_status
usage
```

Avoid random aggressive number rotation simply to evade caller reputation systems.

Manage numbers legitimately and consistently.

## 7.26 Caller identity configuration

Support:

business identity  
brand name  
location where appropriate  
campaign mapping.

For multi-brand environments:

```text
Brand A → Number Pool A
Brand B → Number Pool B
```

## 7.27 Provider health checks

Before routing calls:

```text
provider_status
API latency
call failure rate
regional availability
capacity
```

If unhealthy:

RouteAI selects alternative.

## 7.28 Call launch contract

Campaign worker should send a standard internal request:

```json
{
  "call_job_id": "CJ1009",
  "customer_id": "C10028",
  "campaign_id": "CMP2003",
  "agent_profile": "physio-hindi-v3",
  "language": "hi",
  "phone": "+1...",
  "priority": "HIGH"
}
```

Voice gateway maps this to Retell/Vapi/Bolna/LiveKit/etc.

## 7.29 Idempotent dialing

Use:

```text
call_job_id
idempotency_key
```

If workflow retries because of network failure, it should not place two simultaneous calls.

## 7.30 Pre-dial policy check

This is mandatory.

```text
Job ready
 ↓
ConsentAI
 ↓
DNC
 ↓
suppression
 ↓
call window
 ↓
frequency
 ↓
complaint/risk
 ↓
budget
 ↓
CALL
```

Do not trust eligibility calculated hours earlier.

## 7.31 Mid-campaign policy change

Suppose compliance changes a rule while campaign is running.

New calls must use:

```text
current effective policy
```

not stale cached approval.

Maintain policy cache with short TTL/event invalidation.

## 7.32 Pause capability

Campaign managers need:

```text
PAUSE
RESUME
STOP
```

Pause should:

stop new dialing  
preserve workflow state  
not kill already-connected calls unless explicitly required.

## 7.33 Emergency kill switch

Need global controls:

```text
STOP ALL OUTBOUND
STOP TENANT
STOP CAMPAIGN
STOP PROVIDER
STOP AGENT VERSION
STOP LANGUAGE
```

Access must be tightly controlled and audited.

## 7.34 Automated kill conditions

Examples:

```text
complaint rate > threshold
DNC rate spikes
call failure rate > threshold
unsafe response detected
booking errors spike
provider latency unacceptable
budget anomaly
```

Possible action:

```text
AUTO_PAUSE
```

then human review.

## 7.35 Campaign approval workflow

Recommended:

```text
Marketing creates
 ↓
Business owner reviews
 ↓
Policy/consent checks
 ↓
QA validates agent/script
 ↓
Approval
 ↓
Schedule
```

Higher-risk campaigns can require additional review.

## 7.36 Script assignment

Campaign references:

```text
conversation_template_id
prompt_version
agent_version
service_catalog_version
```

Never silently change active campaigns to a new untested prompt.

## 7.37 Campaign-specific variables

Example:

```text
brand_name
service_name
location
offer
campaign_reason
callback_context
```

Do not copy and edit prompts manually across 200 agents.

Use templates + structured variables.

## 7.38 Multilingual routing

Campaign may specify:

```text
language_strategy =
 CUSTOMER_PREFERENCE_FIRST
```

Then:

Hindi → relevant agent stack  
Punjabi → relevant agent stack  
English → default stack.

Fallback:

customer can switch language mid-call.

## 7.39 Human transfer configuration

Campaign defines:

```text
transfer_allowed
transfer_queue
business_hours
fallback_number
maximum_wait
```

If transfer unavailable:

offer callback rather than leaving caller hanging.

## 7.40 Campaign outcomes

Standardize outcomes:

```text
CONNECTED
QUALIFIED
BOOKED
CALLBACK_REQUESTED
INFO_SENT
NOT_INTERESTED
NO_ANSWER
BUSY
VOICEMAIL
WRONG_NUMBER
DNC
TRANSFERRED
FAILED_TECHNICAL
FAILED_POLICY
```

Provider-specific statuses map into these.

## 7.41 Disposition intelligence

Post-call model can derive:

```text
primary_outcome
secondary_outcomes[]
confidence
```

Example:

```text
primary = CALLBACK_REQUESTED
secondary = PRICE_OBJECTION
```

## 7.42 Testing — campaign creation

Test:

valid configuration

zero budget

## 7.43 Testing — scheduling

## 7.44 Testing — retry

## 7.45 Testing — concurrency

```text
1,000
```

## 7.46 Testing — budget

Create campaign test personas:

| Human-only | Don't use AI call |

Campaign controls are high-risk.

## 7.55 Campaign comparison

Example:

| Campaign | Connect | Booking | DNC | Cost/customer |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|

## 7.57 Campaign-level edge cases

| Edge case | Solution |
|---|---|
| Same lead in two campaigns | Priority/conflict resolver |
| Customer books while queued | Cancel future jobs |
| Customer withdraws consent | Purge/invalidate queue |
| Provider unavailable | RouteAI fallback |
| Budget reached mid-call | Complete active call, stop new calls |
| Campaign paused while queued | Freeze dispatch |
| Agent version recalled | Disable affected jobs |
| Customer changes timezone | Recompute schedule |
| Customer requests exact callback | Promote callback job |
| Duplicate event | Idempotent processing |

## 7.58 Campaign conflict resolver

Example:

Customer qualifies for:

`General Marketing`

and:

Choose:

```text
Requested Callback
```

and suppress lower-priority duplicate outreach.

Store:

```text
conflict_decision
reason
```

# Phase 8 — PolicyAI: Pre-Call Decision Engine + Runtime Guardrails

Phase 7 created a queued outbound call. Phase 8 is the final **authorization gate** before any voice provider or telephony system is allowed to dial.

The central principle:

> **LLM decides how to converse. PolicyAI decides whether an action is permitted.**

PolicyAI should therefore control not only the initial call, but also recording, language behavior, tool execution, booking, SMS/email follow-up, transfers, discounts, data collection, and sensitive conversation paths.

---

## 8.1 Target architecture

```text
CampaignAI
    ↓
Call Job
    ↓
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│          PolicyAI            │
│                              │
│ Consent                      │
│ DNC / Suppression            │
│ Purpose                      │
│ Jurisdiction                 │
│ Time / Day                   │
│ Frequency                    │
│ Customer Preference          │
│ Campaign                     │
│ Recording                    │
│ AI Disclosure                │
│ Data / Privacy               │
│ Risk                         │
│ Budget                       │
│ Agent / Model                │
│ Tool Permissions             │
└──────────────┬───────────────┘
               ↓
        Policy Decision
               ↓
 ┌────────┬─────────┬──────────┐
 ALLOW   ALLOW_WITH  REVIEW   BLOCK
          CONTROLS
               ↓
          Voice Gateway
               ↓
 Retell / Vapi / Bolna / LiveKit /
 Ultravox / other provider
```

---

# 8.2 Four policy decisions

Do not use only Boolean `true/false`.

Use:

```text
ALLOW
ALLOW_WITH_CONTROLS
MANUAL_REVIEW
BLOCK
```

For example:

```json
{
  "decision": "ALLOW_WITH_CONTROLS",
  "controls": {
    "recording": false,
    "language": "hi",
    "max_call_seconds": 600,
    "sms_followup": true,
    "human_transfer": true
  }
}
```

This makes PolicyAI much more useful.

---

# 8.3 Policy domains

Create separate policy families.

| Policy domain | Controls |
|---|---|
| ContactPolicy | Whether contact can occur |
| ConsentPolicy | Required authorization |
| DNCPolicy | Suppression |
| TimePolicy | When calling is permitted |
| FrequencyPolicy | Contact pressure |
| CampaignPolicy | Campaign eligibility |
| RecordingPolicy | Recording/transcription |
| DisclosurePolicy | AI/recording disclosures |
| LanguagePolicy | Language handling |
| PrivacyPolicy | Information accessible |
| DataPolicy | Data collection/storage |
| ToolPolicy | Which APIs agent may call |
| BookingPolicy | Appointment operations |
| PaymentPolicy | Payment-related operations |
| DiscountPolicy | Offers/discount authority |
| TransferPolicy | Human escalation |
| RiskPolicy | High-risk situations |
| ModelPolicy | Approved AI models |
| ProviderPolicy | Approved voice vendors |
| CostPolicy | Spending limits |

---

# 8.4 Policy hierarchy

Policies can conflict.

Define precedence explicitly.

Recommended conceptual order:

```text
LAW / REGULATORY REQUIREMENT
          ↓
ORGANIZATION POLICY
          ↓
PRIVACY / SECURITY
          ↓
CUSTOMER CONSENT
          ↓
CUSTOMER DNC
          ↓
CUSTOMER EXPLICIT PREFERENCE
          ↓
TENANT / BRAND POLICY
          ↓
CAMPAIGN POLICY
          ↓
AI OPTIMIZATION
```

AI optimization should never override higher-level controls.

---

# 8.5 Policy-as-code

For an MVP:

```text
FastAPI
+
Python rules
+
PostgreSQL policy configuration
```

As complexity grows, consider a policy engine such as OPA.

Conceptual rule:

```text
IF
 purpose = MARKETING
AND
 customer.phone_dnc = TRUE

THEN
 decision = BLOCK
reason = DNC_ACTIVE
```

Another:

```text
IF
 call_allowed = TRUE
AND
 recording_allowed = FALSE

THEN
 decision = ALLOW_WITH_CONTROLS
recording = FALSE
```

---

# 8.6 Policy request

Every proposed action should create a policy request.

```json
{
  "tenant_id": "T100",
  "customer_id": "C10028",
  "campaign_id": "CMP900",
  "action": "OUTBOUND_CALL",
  "purpose": "REQUESTED_CALLBACK",
  "channel": "VOICE",
  "phone": "+1...",
  "requested_at": "...",
  "agent_id": "PHYSIO-HI-V5"
}
```

---

# 8.7 Policy response

Return structured data.

```json
{
  "decision": "ALLOW_WITH_CONTROLS",
  "decision_id": "PD98282",
  "reason_codes": [
    "CONSENT_VALID",
    "CALL_WINDOW_VALID",
    "FREQUENCY_VALID"
  ],
  "controls": {
    "recording": false,
    "ai_disclosure": true,
    "preferred_language": "Hindi",
    "max_duration_seconds": 900
  },
  "policy_version": "2026.08.24"
}
```

---

# 8.8 Reason codes

Standardize them.

Examples:

```text
CONSENT_VALID
CONSENT_MISSING
CONSENT_EXPIRED

DNC_ACTIVE

TIME_WINDOW_BLOCK
HOLIDAY_BLOCK

FREQUENCY_LIMIT

CAMPAIGN_NOT_APPROVED

INVALID_PHONE

CUSTOMER_COMPLAINT

RECORDING_NOT_ALLOWED

PROVIDER_NOT_APPROVED

AGENT_VERSION_BLOCKED

MODEL_NOT_APPROVED

BUDGET_EXCEEDED
```

Avoid returning only:

```text
"Not allowed."
```

Operations needs to know why.

---

# 8.9 Pre-dial decision sequence

Recommended:

```text
Call Job
 ↓
Customer exists?
 ↓
Contact point valid?
 ↓
Campaign active?
 ↓
Campaign approved?
 ↓
Consent valid?
 ↓
DNC?
 ↓
Suppression?
 ↓
Jurisdiction resolved?
 ↓
Calling window?
 ↓
Customer preference?
 ↓
Frequency cap?
 ↓
Complaint/risk hold?
 ↓
Agent approved?
 ↓
Provider approved?
 ↓
Budget?
 ↓
ALLOW
```

---

# 8.10 Double authorization

Check PolicyAI:

### Gate 1

When call is scheduled.

### Gate 2

Immediately before dialing.

```text
Campaign
   ↓
PolicyAI
   ↓
Queue
   ↓
wait 3 hours
   ↓
PolicyAI AGAIN
   ↓
Dial
```

This solves many race conditions.

---

# 8.11 Short-lived authorization token

A useful architecture is for PolicyAI to issue:

```text
CALL_AUTH_TOKEN
```

Containing:

```text
decision_id
customer_id
campaign_id
phone_hash
agent_id
provider
allowed_actions
issued_at
expires_at
```

Voice Gateway only accepts calls carrying a valid authorization.

---

# 8.12 Why this matters

Otherwise a developer could accidentally call:

```text
Twilio.create_call()
```

directly.

Instead enforce:

```text
Campaign
   ↓
PolicyAI
   ↓
Voice Gateway
   ↓
Telephony
```

No policy authorization → no outbound dial.

---

# 8.13 Runtime PolicyAI

Policy enforcement should continue after the call starts.

Example:

```text
CALL STARTED
      ↓
AI disclosure
      ↓
conversation
      ↓
customer requests booking
      ↓
BookingPolicy
      ↓
appointment API
```

Every important action can be independently authorized.

---

# 8.14 Tool-level authorization

Suppose voice agent has tools:

```text
get_availability()
book_appointment()
cancel_appointment()
send_sms()
send_email()
apply_discount()
update_customer()
transfer_call()
```

Don't give unrestricted access.

PolicyAI evaluates:

```text
Agent
 ↓
Tool Gateway
 ↓
PolicyAI
 ↓
Tool
```

---

# 8.15 Tool permission matrix

| Tool | AI | Human | Additional control |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Search availability | Yes | Yes | customer context |
| Book appointment | Yes | Yes | confirmation |
| Cancel appointment | Limited | Yes | verification |
| Send SMS | Yes | Yes | channel eligibility |
| Update preference | Yes | Yes | audit |
| Add DNC | Yes | Yes | immediate |
| Remove DNC | No | Restricted | authorized process |
| Apply discount | Limited | Yes | threshold |
| Refund | Usually restricted | Authorized staff | approval |
| Delete customer | No | Restricted | privacy workflow |

---

# 8.16 Tool argument validation

LLM says:

```text
book_appointment(
 customer=C10028,
 date="tomorrow",
 service="physio"
)
```

Tool Gateway should convert and validate:

```text
customer exists
service valid
slot valid
location valid
customer confirmed
slot still available
```

before execution.

Never trust raw LLM arguments.

---

# 8.17 Appointment confirmation policy

Before booking:

Agent should verify critical fields.

Example:

```text
Service
Location
Date
Time
Customer
```

Then:

```text
Customer confirmation
        ↓
BookingPolicy
        ↓
Booking API
```

This prevents hallucinated bookings.

---

# 8.18 Idempotent tool calls

Voice agent:

```text
book()
```

network times out.

LLM retries.

Without protection:

two appointments.

Use:

```text
transaction_id
idempotency_key
```

so:

```text
same request
→ same result
```

---

# 8.19 Recording policy

Evaluate independently:

```text
CALL_ALLOWED
```

and:

```text
RECORDING_ALLOWED
```

Possible:

```text
Call = YES
Recording = NO
Transcription = LIMITED
```

Voice Gateway needs to enforce this technically.

---

# 8.20 Transcript policy

Separate:

```text
record_audio
create_transcript
store_transcript
retain_transcript
use_for_training
use_for_analytics
```

These are not necessarily equivalent permissions.

---

# 8.21 Data minimization

Agent Context API should return only what is required.

Bad:

```text
entire customer database record
```

Better:

```text
first_name
preferred_language
service_interest
callback_reason
appointment_context
```

PolicyAI can define accessible fields.

---

# 8.22 Field-level policy

Example:

Voice sales agent:

```text
CAN READ
first_name
service_interest
language
appointment

CANNOT READ
internal complaint notes
unrelated historical data
payment details
other sensitive records
```

This becomes important for healthcare deployments.

---

# 8.23 Healthcare policy layer

For dental, physiotherapy, ENT, chiropractic, massage, etc., distinguish:

```text
Administrative Conversation
```

from:

```text
Clinical Conversation
```

AI voice agent may appropriately handle:

appointments, clinic hours, location, general service information, administrative FAQs.

Clinical diagnosis, emergency interpretation, treatment decisions, or medication advice require a separate safety design and appropriate professional oversight.

---

# 8.24 Intent classification before sensitive actions

Classify:

```text
ADMIN
BOOKING
BILLING
GENERAL_INFORMATION
CLINICAL
URGENT
COMPLAINT
DNC
```

Then route accordingly.

Example:

```text
CLINICAL
   ↓
restricted response
   ↓
human/appropriate clinic workflow
```

---

# 8.25 Emergency detection

Healthcare voice agents need an emergency/escalation pathway defined by the clinic.

Potential signals should trigger:

```text
URGENT_RISK
   ↓
stop sales/normal booking flow
   ↓
approved emergency guidance/escalation
   ↓
log event
```

Do not let the sales conversation continue normally.

---

# 8.26 Language policy

Customer preference:

```text
Punjabi
```

Agent can switch.

But PolicyAI can also specify:

```text
approved_languages
```

because the organization may have validated scripts only for certain languages.

Example:

```text
English → approved
Hindi → approved
Punjabi → approved
Tamil → not validated
```

If unsupported:

human transfer or approved fallback.

---

# 8.27 Translation risk

Never assume machine translation preserves:

medical terminology, pricing, consent language, contractual terms.

Maintain validated language templates for high-impact statements.

---

# 8.28 AI disclosure

Policy can return:

```text
ai_disclosure_required = TRUE
```

Agent opening:

> "I'm the virtual assistant for ABC Clinic."

Record:

```text
disclosure_version
timestamp
```

---

# 8.29 Dynamic policy during conversation

Customer says:

> "Stop calling me."

Immediately:

```text
DNC event
 ↓
Policy state changes
 ↓
future outreach blocked
```

Customer says:

> "Text me instead."

Potentially:

```text
PHONE preference changes
SMS eligibility separately evaluated
```

Don't assume SMS permission.

---

# 8.30 Offer policy

Suppose agent wants to offer:

```text
20% discount
```

Policy:

```text
AI can offer ≤10%

>10%
→ human approval
```

Tool call:

```text
apply_discount(20)
```

returns:

```text
DENIED
reason=DISCOUNT_AUTHORITY_EXCEEDED
```

---

# 8.31 Price integrity

Agent should retrieve price from:

```text
Pricing API
```

not from model memory.

Architecture:

```text
Customer asks price
      ↓
Voice Agent
      ↓
Pricing Tool
      ↓
Current price
      ↓
Agent response
```

This prevents stale/hallucinated pricing.

---

# 8.32 Promotion policy

Validate:

```text
offer active?
customer eligible?
campaign eligible?
location eligible?
expiration?
usage limit?
```

before speaking as if a promotion is available.

---

# 8.33 Service policy

Similar architecture:

```text
Service Catalog
```

is authoritative for:

service name, description, duration, location, availability, general eligibility rules, current price references.

LLM converts structured facts into natural conversation.

---

# 8.34 Provider policy

You may use multiple providers:

Retell  
Vapi  
Bolna  
LiveKit  
Ultravox  
Sarvam  
others.

Maintain:

```text
PROVIDER_POLICY
```

Example:

```text
provider
approved_use_case
approved_region
approved_data_class
approved_language
recording_allowed
healthcare_approved
status
```

RouteAI cannot select a provider that PolicyAI rejects.

---

# 8.35 Model policy

Similarly:

```text
MODEL_POLICY

model_id
provider
approved_use_cases
data_classes
region
version
status
```

This allows:

```text
Model A → general sales
Model B → healthcare admin
Model C → prohibited for sensitive data
```

---

# 8.36 Prompt policy

Prompts should also be governed artifacts.

Store:

```text
prompt_id
version
owner
approved_use_case
approved_languages
risk_level
approved_at
status
```

Campaign uses only:

```text
APPROVED
```

prompt versions.

---

# 8.37 Policy versioning

Never overwrite production policy.

```text
CALL-POLICY-v1
CALL-POLICY-v2
CALL-POLICY-v3
```

Every decision records the version.

---

# 8.38 Policy deployment

Use:

```text
DRAFT
 ↓
PEER REVIEW
 ↓
COMPLIANCE REVIEW
 ↓
TEST
 ↓
SHADOW
 ↓
APPROVED
 ↓
PRODUCTION
```

Emergency rollback:

```text
v5
 ↓
problem
 ↓
v4
```

---

# 8.39 Policy simulation

Before activating a new rule, replay historical traffic.

Example:

```text
100,000 historical call decisions
          ↓
Policy V4
          ↓
Policy V5
          ↓
Decision comparison
```

Report:

```text
V4 allowed 70,000
V5 allowed 65,200

4,800 newly blocked
```

Then investigate why.

---

# 8.40 Golden policy dataset

Build a manually validated set.

Example:

| Scenario | Expected |
|---|---|
| Active DNC | BLOCK |
| Missing required consent | BLOCK |
| Valid callback | ALLOW |
| Outside permitted window | ALLOW_AT/BLOCK |
| Recording prohibited | Allow call, no recording |
| Agent not approved | BLOCK |
| Customer asks DNC mid-call | Update + stop marketing |
| Unauthorized discount | BLOCK tool |

Start with 500–1,000 scenarios and grow it.

---

# 8.41 Boundary tests

Test exact boundaries:

```text
08:59:59
09:00:00
20:00:00
20:00:01
```

plus:

DST change  
leap year  
month-end  
year-end  
holiday transitions.

---

# 8.42 Race-condition test

Scenario:

```text
12:00:00 PolicyAI = ALLOW

12:00:01 Customer DNC entered

12:00:02 Worker attempts dial
```

Pre-dial reauthorization must return:

```text
BLOCK
```

---

# 8.43 Policy cache

Policy calls can be frequent.

Use cache carefully.

Good cache candidates:

static service configuration  
approved provider list  
agent metadata.

Avoid long-lived caching for:

DNC  
consent withdrawal  
active complaint  
call eligibility.

Use event-based invalidation.

---

# 8.44 Fail-closed design

Critical services:

```text
Consent unavailable
DNC unavailable
Policy engine unavailable
```

should generally result in:

```text
DO NOT INITIATE NEW OUTBOUND CALL
```

until safely resolved.

This is preferable to uncontrolled outreach.

---

# 8.45 Circuit breaker

If PolicyAI becomes unstable:

```text
error rate rises
      ↓
circuit breaker
      ↓
pause new campaigns
      ↓
alert operations
```

Do not let thousands of workers hammer a failed policy service.

---

# 8.46 Policy performance

Because PolicyAI sits on critical paths:

Target architecture for simple decisions should aim for low latency.

Monitor:

```text
P50
P95
P99
error rate
timeout rate
```

Optimize deterministic rules rather than involving an LLM.

---

# 8.47 Policy audit record

Store:

```text
decision_id
tenant_id
customer_id
campaign_id

action
decision

reason_codes

input_snapshot_hash
policy_version

controls

timestamp
latency
```

This creates reconstructable evidence.

---

# 8.48 Security

PolicyAI itself is a high-value target.

Protect:

service-to-service authentication  
mTLS where appropriate  
RBAC  
API authorization  
rate limits  
network isolation  
secret management  
immutable audit.

Prevent:

policy bypass  
policy modification  
forged authorization tokens.

---

# 8.49 Policy change authorization

Roles:

```text
Policy Author
Reviewer
Compliance Approver
Production Deployer
Auditor
```

For higher-risk environments, separate these responsibilities.

---

# 8.50 Observability dashboard

Show:

```text
Policy decisions/min
ALLOW %
BLOCK %
REVIEW %
```

Block reasons:

```text
DNC
Consent
Time
Frequency
Campaign
Risk
Provider
Agent
Budget
```

Technical:

```text
Latency
Timeout
Errors
Cache hit
Version distribution
```

---

# 8.51 Anomaly detection

Example:

Normal:

```text
DNC blocks = 2%
```

Suddenly:

```text
DNC blocks = 0%
```

That might not be good news.

It could indicate a broken integration.

Alert on unusual **drops as well as spikes**.

---

# 8.52 PolicyAI + GovernAI

GovernAI should answer:

```text
Who owns this policy?
Who approved it?
When?
Why?
What version?
What systems use it?
What risk does it control?
When is review due?
```

This becomes the governance control plane.

---

# 8.53 PolicyAI + RiskAI

RiskAI detects signals.

PolicyAI makes deterministic decisions.

Example:

```text
RiskAI:
complaint_risk = HIGH

        ↓

PolicyAI:
human_review_required = TRUE
```

Keep detection and authorization logically separate.

---

# 8.54 PolicyAI + ExplainAI

Operations sees:

```text
CALL BLOCKED
```

ExplainAI presents:

```text
Reason:
Customer requested no further phone calls.

Policy:
PHONE-DNC-v4

Applied:
Aug 24

Recommended action:
No outbound voice contact.
```

No need to expose raw internal rule code to normal users.

---

# 8.55 PolicyAI + TestAI

Every new policy automatically triggers:

```text
Unit tests
Regression tests
Golden dataset
Historical replay
Boundary tests
Conflict tests
Performance tests
```

Production deployment should fail if critical tests fail.

---

# 8.56 Policy conflict engine

Example:

Customer:

```text
preferred_time = 18:00
```

Campaign:

```text
ends = 17:00
```

Policy should produce:

```text
NO_VALID_WINDOW
```

rather than arbitrarily selecting one.

Another:

```text
Customer requested callback
+
marketing DNC
```

requires purpose-specific policy evaluation rather than simply deleting either fact.

---

# 8.57 Edge cases

| Edge case | Policy response |
|---|---|
| DNC added after queueing | BLOCK |
| Consent withdrawn | BLOCK applicable action |
| Customer changes channel | Re-evaluate new channel |
| Recording denied | Continue without recording if allowed |
| Provider becomes prohibited | Route elsewhere |
| Prompt recalled | Block agent version |
| Unsupported language | Fallback/human |
| Appointment already booked | Stop redundant sales campaign |
| Pricing API unavailable | Don't invent price |
| Tool timeout | Safe retry/idempotency |
| Duplicate call job | Reject duplicate |
| Policy service down | Fail closed |
| Emergency intent | Exit normal sales path |

---

# 8.58 Definition of Done

Phase 8 should not pass until:

```text
Contact Policy             PASS
Consent Policy             PASS
DNC Policy                 PASS
Suppression                PASS
Time Policy                PASS
Frequency Policy           PASS
Jurisdiction               PASS

Recording Policy           PASS
Transcript Policy          PASS
Disclosure Policy          PASS

Privacy Policy             PASS
Data Minimization          PASS

Tool Authorization         PASS
Booking Policy             PASS
Pricing Policy             PASS
Offer Policy               PASS
Transfer Policy            PASS

Provider Policy            PASS
Model Policy               PASS
Prompt Policy              PASS

Policy Versioning          PASS
Approval Workflow          PASS
Simulation                 PASS
Golden Dataset             PASS
Regression Testing         PASS

Runtime Authorization      PASS
Pre-Dial Authorization     PASS
Authorization Token        PASS

Fail Closed                PASS
Circuit Breaker            PASS

RBAC                       PASS
Audit                      PASS
Monitoring                 PASS
Alerts                     PASS
Rollback                   PASS
UAT                        PASS
```

## Phase 8 output

Our customer call now reaches the gateway with a controlled authorization package:

```text
Customer:
C10028

Action:
OUTBOUND CALLBACK

Policy Decision:
ALLOW_WITH_CONTROLS

Purpose:
Requested physiotherapy consultation

Language:
Hindi

Calling window:
18:00–20:00

AI disclosure:
REQUIRED

Recording:
NOT ALLOWED

Booking:
ALLOWED WITH CONFIRMATION

SMS:
SEPARATE ELIGIBILITY CHECK REQUIRED

Discount:
Maximum agent authority = configured limit

Clinical advice:
RESTRICTED

Human transfer:
ALLOWED

Provider:
Must satisfy healthcare/data policy

Agent:
PHYSIO-HINDI-V5 — APPROVED

Policy version:
POLICY-2026.08-V4

Authorization:
SHORT-LIVED

Status:
AUTHORIZED_FOR_ROUTE
```

This leads into the particularly important **Phase 9 — RouteAI + Voice/Telephony Abstraction Layer**: dynamically selecting among Retell, Vapi, Bolna, LiveKit, Ultravox, Sarvam and telephony providers based on **voice quality, mother-tongue quality, latency, reliability, geography, healthcare/data requirements, cost, current outages, concurrency and historical success**, with automatic fallback and provider-independent APIs.

## 🤖 Assistant — msg #52

# Phase 9 — RouteAI + Voice/Telephony Abstraction Layer

Now we reach the actual voice infrastructure.

The objective is to prevent the entire platform from becoming dependent on one provider. Retell, Vapi, Bolna, LiveKit, Ultravox, Sarvam, STT/TTS vendors, LLMs, and telephony providers should sit behind your own **Voice Gateway + RouteAI**.

> **PolicyAI says whether the call may happen. RouteAI decides the best approved way to execute it.**

## 9.1 Target architecture

```text
CampaignAI
    ↓
PolicyAI
    ↓
RouteAI
    ↓
Voice Gateway
    │
    ├──────── Voice Agent Platforms ────────┐
    │                                       │
    ├── Retell Adapter                      │
    ├── Vapi Adapter                        │
    ├── Bolna Adapter                       │
    ├── LiveKit Adapter                     │
    ├── Ultravox Adapter                    │
    └── Custom Voice Adapter                │
                                            │
    ├──────── Speech / Model Layer ─────────┤
    │                                       │
    ├── Sarvam / multilingual speech        │
    ├── ElevenLabs / TTS                    │
    ├── Deepgram / STT                      │
    ├── OpenAI / other approved LLM         │
    └── self-hosted models where justified │
                                            │
    └──────── Telephony Layer ──────────────┘
         ├── Twilio
         ├── Telnyx
         ├── Plivo
         ├── SIP trunk
         └── other approved carrier
```

The important part is the abstraction—not the specific vendor list.

---

# 9.2 Why multi-provider architecture matters

If you directly write:

```python
retell.create_call(...)
```

throughout your applications, migration becomes painful.

Instead:

```python
voice_gateway.create_call(...)
```

Then RouteAI decides:

```text
Voice platform
Telephony provider
STT
TTS
LLM
Voice
Region
Fallback
```

This gives you portability.

---

# 9.3 RouteAI decision dimensions

Route using at least:

| Dimension | Why |
|---|---|
| Language | Mother-tongue quality |
| Accent | Natural conversation |
| Geography | Latency/telephony |
| Use case | Sales vs booking vs support |
| Data classification | Privacy |
| Policy | Approved providers |
| Quality | Historical QA |
| Reliability | Current health |
| Latency | Conversation quality |
| Cost | FinOps |
| Tool calling | Booking/API reliability |
| Concurrency | Capacity |
| Availability | Provider outage |
| Customer preference | Voice/language |
| Campaign | SLA requirements |

---

# 9.4 Provider registry

Maintain:

```text
VOICE_PROVIDER

provider_id
provider_name

capabilities
languages
regions

supports_inbound
supports_outbound
supports_transfer
supports_tools
supports_recording
supports_sip
supports_streaming

quality_score
latency_score
reliability_score

cost_profile

security_status
compliance_status

health_status
```

Do not hardcode these capabilities inside prompts.

---

# 9.5 Telephony registry

Separate voice-agent platform from telephony.

```text
TELEPHONY_PROVIDER

provider_id

countries
number_types
sip_support
outbound_support
inbound_support

pricing

concurrency_limit
rate_limit

health_status
quality_score
```

This allows:

```text
Voice platform A
+
Telephony provider B
```

instead of treating them as one inseparable product.

---

# 9.6 Canonical Voice API

Create your internal API:

```text
POST /voice/calls
```

Example:

```json
{
  "customer_id": "C10028",
  "campaign_id": "CMP2003",
  "phone": "+1...",
  "language": "hi",
  "agent_profile": "physio-v5",
  "purpose": "requested_callback",
  "authorization_id": "PD98282"
}
```

Internal caller does not specify Retell/Vapi unless intentionally forcing a provider.

---

# 9.7 RouteAI response

Example:

```json
{
  "route_id": "R9928",
  "voice_platform": "provider-A",
  "telephony": "carrier-B",
  "speech_profile": "hindi-premium",
  "region": "ca-central",
  "fallback_route": "R9929"
}
```

This is recorded before call initiation.

---

# 9.8 Provider adapter interface

Standardize:

```text
create_call()
end_call()

transfer_call()

send_dtmf()

get_call()

get_transcript()

get_recording()

update_agent()

handle_webhook()
```

Every provider adapter implements the same contract.

---

# 9.9 Canonical call states

Providers will return different status names.

Normalize into:

```text
QUEUED
INITIATING
RINGING
ANSWERED
CONNECTED
TRANSFERRING
COMPLETED

NO_ANSWER
BUSY
VOICEMAIL
REJECTED
FAILED
CANCELLED
```

Downstream systems should never need to understand every vendor's terminology.

---

# 9.10 Canonical event model

Normalize vendor webhooks:

```text
voice.call.created
voice.call.ringing
voice.call.answered
voice.call.connected

voice.turn.started
voice.turn.completed

voice.tool.requested
voice.tool.completed
voice.tool.failed

voice.transfer.started
voice.transfer.completed

voice.call.completed
voice.call.failed
```

---

# 9.11 Webhook gateway

Architecture:

```text
Provider
   ↓
Webhook Gateway
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Signature Verification
   ↓
Replay Protection
   ↓
Provider Adapter
   ↓
Canonical Event
   ↓
Event Bus
```

Never expose provider webhook payloads directly to business logic.

---

# 9.12 Webhook security

Validate:

```text
signature
timestamp
provider
event ID
request origin where appropriate
```

Protect against:

forged webhook  
replay attack  
duplicate delivery  
out-of-order events.

---

# 9.13 Webhook idempotency

Providers may send the same event multiple times.

Use:

```text
provider_event_id
```

or a calculated idempotency fingerprint.

Result:

```text
event received twice
→ processed once
```

---

# 9.14 Out-of-order event problem

You might receive:

```text
CALL_COMPLETED
```

before:

```text
CALL_CONNECTED
```

due to network delays.

Use event timestamps and a call-state machine.

Do not blindly update status based on arrival order.

---

# 9.15 Route score

Start with deterministic weighted scoring.

Concept:

```text
Route Score =

Language Quality      25%
Reliability           20%
Latency               15%
Task Success          15%
Tool Reliability      10%
Cost                   5%
Customer Experience    5%
Operational Fit        5%
```

Weights vary by use case.

---

# 9.16 Healthcare routing weights

For a clinic, I would prioritize:

```text
Policy/security
Reliability
Speech quality
Tool correctness
Latency
Language
Cost
```

over simply choosing the cheapest provider.

A failed appointment booking costs much more than a few cents of voice infrastructure.

---

# 9.17 Mother-tongue routing

Suppose:

```text
Customer language:
Punjabi
```

RouteAI evaluates approved candidates:

```text
Provider A
Punjabi QA = 72

Provider B
Punjabi QA = 91

Provider C
Punjabi QA = 83
```

Assuming policy/reliability requirements are met:

```text
Provider B
```

wins.

Do this from measured QA data—not vendor marketing claims.

---

# 9.18 Language benchmark

Build your own test corpus.

For every important language:

```text
100–500 test utterances
```

Cover:

names  
dates  
times  
addresses  
clinic terminology  
numbers  
prices  
service names  
mixed-language speech.

---

# 9.19 Code switching

Your target customer may say:

> "Mujhe physio appointment chahiye, but evening mein after six."

The system should handle:

```text
Hindi
+
English
```

without forcing the caller to restart.

Test:

Hindi-English  
Punjabi-English  
French-English  
other business-relevant combinations.

---

# 9.20 STT quality metrics

Don't evaluate only generic Word Error Rate.

Measure:

```text
WER
```

plus critical-entity accuracy:

```text
Name accuracy
Phone accuracy
Email accuracy
Date accuracy
Time accuracy
Address accuracy
Service accuracy
Medication/clinical terminology where applicable
```

For appointment agents, **time/date accuracy** may matter more than overall WER.

---

# 9.21 Critical Entity Error Rate

Create:

```text
CEER
```

Critical Entity Error Rate.

Example:

Customer says:

> Tuesday at 6:30.

Agent hears:

> Thursday at 6:30.

That's much more serious than a minor grammar transcription error.

Track separately.

---

# 9.22 TTS quality

Evaluate:

naturalness  
pronunciation  
emotion appropriateness  
pace  
clarity  
accent  
language authenticity  
name pronunciation  
numeric pronunciation.

For healthcare:

avoid voices that sound overly promotional.

---

# 9.23 Voice quality score

Example:

```text
Naturalness            20
Pronunciation           20
Language authenticity   20
Clarity                 15
Pacing                  10
Interruption handling   10
Consistency              5
---------------------------
Total                   100
```

Use human raters plus automated metrics where useful.

---

# 9.24 Latency decomposition

Don't monitor one vague "latency" metric.

Break down:

```text
Customer stops speaking
        ↓
VAD delay
        ↓
STT finalization
        ↓
LLM first token
        ↓
Tool call if required
        ↓
TTS first audio
        ↓
Network delivery
```

Measure each component.

---

# 9.25 Key voice latency metric

Track:

```text
END_OF_USER_SPEECH
→
FIRST_AGENT_AUDIO
```

P50 / P95 / P99.

This is one of the most important customer-experience metrics.

---

# 9.26 Interruption / barge-in

Customer:

> "Actually, wait—"

Agent must stop talking.

Architecture needs:

```text
VAD
↓
barge-in detection
↓
cancel TTS
↓
preserve conversation state
↓
listen
```

Test aggressively.

---

# 9.27 False interruption

Background sound:

TV  
child speaking  
door noise.

System incorrectly stops.

Measure:

```text
false_barge_in_rate
```

---

# 9.28 Silence handling

Customer becomes silent.

Use states:

```text
SHORT_SILENCE
MEDIUM_SILENCE
LONG_SILENCE
```

Agent might say:

> "Are you still there?"

After defined retries:

gracefully close.

Do not repeatedly nag the customer.

---

# 9.29 Background noise

Test:

car  
office  
street  
restaurant  
TV  
children  
speakerphone  
Bluetooth  
poor cellular connection.

Your polished lab demo is not representative of production.

---

# 9.30 Echo

Speakerphone can create:

```text
agent hears itself
```

Potentially causing bizarre loops.

Test echo cancellation and provider behavior.

---

# 9.31 Turn-taking metrics

Track:

```text
interruptions
agent-over-talk
customer-over-talk
silence duration
turn duration
agent monologue duration
```

High-quality voice AI is not just a good TTS voice.

---

# 9.32 Provider health service

Continuously track:

```text
API availability
call success
connection success
STT failures
TTS failures
tool failures
latency
webhook delay
```

Produce:

```text
HEALTHY
DEGRADED
UNHEALTHY
```

---

# 9.33 Circuit breaker

If provider failure spikes:

```text
Provider A
failure > threshold
       ↓
Circuit breaker OPEN
       ↓
Route new calls elsewhere
```

Don't wait for the vendor status page.

---

# 9.34 Automatic failover

Example:

```text
Primary:
Provider A

Secondary:
Provider B

Tertiary:
Provider C
```

If call initiation fails before customer connection:

RouteAI can try the next approved route.

---

# 9.35 Critical rule: don't duplicate calls

Suppose:

Provider A API times out.

You don't know whether the call was created.

Do NOT immediately call through Provider B.

First:

```text
query Provider A
or
wait for reconciliation
```

Otherwise customer may receive two simultaneous calls.

Use:

```text
global_call_id
idempotency
provider reconciliation
```

---

# 9.36 Mid-call provider failure

Harder problem.

If voice provider fails during an active call, seamless migration may not be feasible.

Fallback options:

graceful reconnect  
telephony transfer  
human takeover  
callback  
SMS follow-up.

Define per use case.

---

# 9.37 Telephony failover

Voice provider and telephony provider can fail independently.

Example:

```text
Voice AI healthy
Twilio degraded
```

Route:

```text
Voice AI
+
alternative approved carrier
```

where architecture/provider integrations support it.

---

# 9.38 SIP strategy

For more control and enterprise deployments, consider SIP abstraction.

```text
Carrier
 ↓
SIP
 ↓
Voice Gateway
 ↓
Voice AI
```

This can reduce dependence on bundled telephony.

---

# 9.39 Phone number abstraction

Internally use:

```text
NUMBER_POOL
```

not:

```text
twilio_number
```

Schema:

```text
number_id
e164
country
region
brand
provider
status
reputation
capabilities
```

---

# 9.40 Caller-number selection

Route based on:

country  
brand  
campaign  
service location  
customer geography  
number health.

Don't randomly rotate numbers merely to evade reputation controls.

---

# 9.41 Number health

Monitor:

```text
answer rate
spam complaints
carrier rejection
failure rate
customer complaints
```

A degraded number can be removed from rotation.

---

# 9.42 Agent abstraction

Create:

```text
AGENT_PROFILE
```

rather than provider-specific agent IDs.

Example:

```text
PHYSIO-BOOKING-HINDI-V5
```

maps to:

```text
Retell agent ...
Vapi assistant ...
Bolna agent ...
LiveKit configuration ...
```

Same business behavior, different execution backend.

---

# 9.43 Agent configuration

Canonical profile:

```text
agent_profile_id
business_role
language
voice_profile
prompt_version
toolset
knowledge_base
policy_profile
transfer_profile
quality_profile
```

Provider adapter translates it.

---

# 9.44 Voice profile abstraction

```text
VOICE_PROFILE

language
gender/presentation where business-appropriate
accent
pace
tone
TTS_provider
TTS_voice
```

Don't reference vendor-specific voice IDs throughout application logic.

---

# 9.45 LLM abstraction

Similarly:

```text
LLM Gateway
```

with:

```text
generate()
stream()
tool_call()
```

Route models based on:

latency  
quality  
cost  
data policy  
availability.

---

# 9.46 STT abstraction

```text
SpeechRecognitionGateway
```

Potentially routes among approved STT providers.

This becomes especially useful for multilingual requirements.

---

# 9.47 Full route object

One call route might be:

```text
Voice orchestration:
LiveKit

Telephony:
Carrier A

STT:
Provider B

LLM:
Model C

TTS:
Provider D

Language:
Hindi

Region:
Canada

Fallback:
Route-2
```

Another call could use a more bundled platform.

---

# 9.48 Cost model

Track each component.

```text
telephony_cost
STT_cost
LLM_cost
TTS_cost
voice_platform_cost
recording_cost
storage_cost
```

Then:

```text
total_call_cost
```

---

# 9.49 Cost per successful outcome

Much more important than cost/minute.

Measure:

```text
Cost / Connected Call
Cost / Qualified Lead
Cost / Appointment
Cost / Customer
```

A $0.15 call that fails is more expensive than a $0.50 call that books reliably.

---

# 9.50 RouteAI optimization objective

Do not optimize:

```text
MIN(cost)
```

Use something closer to:

```text
MAX(
 quality
 × reliability
 × task_success
 × policy_fit
)
while respecting cost constraints
```

---

# 9.51 Route learning

Initially:

rules + weighted score.

Later:

multi-armed bandit can potentially optimize routes.

For example:

```text
Hindi + healthcare booking + Canada
```

learns which approved route produces the best:

```text
booking success
quality
latency
cost
```

Keep exploration constrained by governance.

---

# 9.52 Route explainability

Every selection should say why.

Example:

```text
Route selected:
Provider B

Reasons:
Hindi QA = 94
Current health = HEALTHY
P95 latency = 720ms
Booking success = 81%
Policy = APPROVED
Cost = within campaign limit
```

This is important for debugging.

---

# 9.53 Shadow routing

Before changing providers:

```text
Current route = A
Candidate = B
```

Use offline/replay testing where feasible.

Then limited traffic:

```text
95% A
5% B
```

Gradually increase after validation.

Maintain your own scorecard.

Create reusable recordings:

```text
names
```

Test:

Customer:

Validate:

```text
 ↓

 ↓
```

# 9.60 Distributed tracing

One call should have:

```text
trace_id
```

connecting:

```text
Campaign
→ Policy
→ Route
→ Telephony
→ Voice
→ STT
→ LLM
→ Tool
→ Booking
→ CRM
```

Use OpenTelemetry.

# 9.62 Provider-specific dashboards

Track each provider:

```text
calls
connection rate
failure rate
P50/P95 latency
STT quality
tool success
booking success
transfer success
customer satisfaction
cost
```

# 9.63 SLOs

Example categories:

```text
Call initiation success
Voice availability
Turn latency

Booking correctness
```

# 9.64 Alerts

Examples:

# 9.65 Security

Store provider API keys in:

Vault / cloud secret manager.

Never:

prompt  
source code  
frontend  
logs.

Use:

secret rotation  
least privilege

---

# 9.66 Data boundary

For each provider document:

```text
What data is sent?
Where?
Why?
How long retained?
Is audio retained?
Is transcript retained?
Can training use it?
Which region?
Can retention be disabled?
```

This becomes part of VendorAI/GovernAI later.

---

# 9.67 Provider outage runbook

Example:

```text
Alert
 ↓
Confirm degradation
 ↓
Circuit breaker
 ↓
Stop new routing
 ↓
Activate approved secondary
 ↓
Reconcile uncertain calls
 ↓
Monitor secondary
 ↓
Incident report
 ↓
Root-cause analysis
```

---

# 9.68 Never retry uncertain calls blindly

This deserves its own production rule.

If API request timed out:

```text
UNKNOWN_CALL_STATE
```

First reconcile using:

provider call ID, idempotency key, webhook history, phone/campaign context.

Only redial after determining no active call exists.

---

# 9.69 RouteAI test cases

```text
English + healthy providers
Hindi + multilingual provider
Punjabi + provider A degraded
Policy blocks provider B
Provider C over concurrency
Telephony A outage
Cost budget exceeded
Primary route fails
All providers fail
Unknown language
Customer changes language
```

Expected route must be predetermined.

---

# 9.70 All-providers-fail case

Do not endlessly retry.

Return:

```text
VOICE_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE
```

Then:

```text
reschedule
human callback
SMS/email fallback if independently eligible
```

The next phase is the heart of the product: **Phase 10 — ConversationAI + Call Script Engine**. That is where we build the complete customer conversation: greeting → AI disclosure → mother-tongue detection/switching → identity/context → permission to continue → need discovery → primary/secondary/hidden needs → service explanation → FAQ → pricing → objections → likes/dislikes → competitor discussion → recommendations → appointment → cross-sell → feedback → next action → closing, including interruptions, silence, angry customers, hallucination controls, prompt design, state machine, RAG, memory, tools, testing and conversation-quality scoring.

next

---

## 🤖 Assistant — msg #54

# Phase 10 — ConversationAI + Call Script Engine + Customer Discovery

This is the core layer that determines how the Voice AI actually behaves during the call.

The goal is not simply to create a script. It is to build a **controlled conversational state machine** that can speak naturally, switch to the customer's preferred language, understand needs, explain relevant services, discover additional needs, capture objections and preferences, execute tools safely, and produce structured customer intelligence.

## 10.1 Target conversation architecture

```text
CALL CONNECTED
      ↓
Greeting
      ↓
AI / Brand Disclosure
      ↓
Right Person?
      ↓
Language Detection / Preference
      ↓
Permission to Continue
      ↓
Context of Call
      ↓
Primary Need Discovery
      ↓
Clarifying Questions
      ↓
Pain / Goal / Expected Outcome
      ↓
Preference Discovery
      ↓
Service Explanation
      ↓
Customer Reaction
      ↓
Likes / Dislikes
      ↓
Pricing / Availability
      ↓
Objection Handling
      ↓
Competitor Discussion
      ↓
Other Needs Discovery
      ↓
Service Matching
      ↓
Next Best Action
      ↓
Book / Transfer / Callback / Information
      ↓
Feedback
      ↓
Confirmation
      ↓
Close
      ↓
Post-Call Intelligence
```

---

# 10.2 Do not build one giant prompt

The first design rule is:

**Do not put the entire conversation into one huge system prompt.**

Use controlled states.

```text
S00_CALL_START
S01_GREETING
S02_DISCLOSURE
S03_IDENTITY
S04_LANGUAGE
S05_PERMISSION
S06_CONTEXT
S07_PRIMARY_NEED
S08_NEED_DISCOVERY
S09_PREFERENCE
S10_SERVICE_EXPLANATION
S11_REACTION
S12_PRICE
S13_OBJECTION
S14_COMPETITOR
S15_OTHER_NEEDS
S16_RECOMMENDATION
S17_CTA
S18_BOOKING
S19_TRANSFER
S20_FEEDBACK
S21_CONFIRMATION
S22_CLOSE
S23_POST_CALL
```

Each state has:

```text
Goal
Allowed questions
Required information
Allowed tools
Prohibited actions
Exit conditions
Fallback
Escalation
QA checks
```

---

# 10.3 State definition example

### `S07_PRIMARY_NEED`

Goal:

Understand why the customer requested contact.

Agent might ask:

> “What are you mainly looking for help with?”

Allowed outputs:

```text
primary_need
service_interest
reason_for_contact
```

Required before exit:

At least one confirmed need or explicit “just gathering information.”

Allowed tools:

```text
get_service_catalog()
```

Not allowed:

booking yet, aggressive upsell, inventing treatment/service claims.

Exit:

```text
need_confirmed
OR
customer_declines_discovery
```

---

# 10.4 Opening strategy

The opening should be short.

For a form-generated lead:

> “Hi Raj, I’m the virtual assistant from ABC Clinic. You recently asked us to contact you about physiotherapy. Is now a good time for a quick conversation?”

This establishes:

identity  
brand  
AI disclosure  
reason  
permission.

Do not begin with a long promotional script.

---

# 10.5 Wrong-person handling

Agent:

> “May I speak with Raj?”

Person:

> “No, this is his mother.”

Do not reveal:

service interest  
medical/clinic details  
appointment information

unless policy allows and identity/context is properly established.

Safe response:

> “Thanks. I’ll avoid discussing the request. Is there a better time or way for Raj to contact us?”

Record:

```text
outcome = WRONG_PERSON
customer_reached = false
```

---

# 10.6 Language discovery

Use both:

1. stored preference;
2. conversational detection.

Example:

Customer begins:

> “Haan boliye.”

Agent can recognize Hindi.

But if confidence is not strong:

> “Would you prefer Hindi or English?”

Store:

```text
detected_language
preferred_language
language_confidence
language_switch_count
code_switching
```

---

# 10.7 Mother-tongue strategy

The requirement is not simply translation.

The agent needs:

natural terminology  
proper cultural pacing  
correct number/date pronunciation  
code-switching  
service terminology.

Example:

> “Mujhe Tuesday evening mein appointment chahiye, around 6:30.”

The agent should interpret:

```text
date = next Tuesday
time ≈ 18:30
language = Hindi-English mixed
intent = appointment
```

Then explicitly confirm before booking.

---

# 10.8 Never infer ethnicity from language

Important governance rule:

```text
language_preference != ethnicity
```

Language should be used for communication quality, not sensitive profiling.

---

# 10.9 Customer context injection

Before conversation:

```text
Customer Context API
```

returns only minimum necessary information.

Example:

```json
{
  "first_name": "Raj",
  "preferred_language": "Hindi",
  "service_interest": "physiotherapy",
  "lead_source": "website",
  "callback_reason": "pricing and availability",
  "preferred_time": "evening"
}
```

Avoid feeding the entire CRM history into the model.

---

# 10.10 Permission to continue

Even when customer requested contact:

> “Is now still a good time?”

Possible responses:

### Yes

Continue.

### No

Ask:

> “What time would work better?”

Create callback.

### “Make it quick.”

Set:

```text
conversation_mode = EXPRESS
```

Agent shortens discovery.

---

# 10.11 Conversation modes

Useful feature:

```text
EXPRESS
STANDARD
DETAILED
HUMAN_TRANSFER
```

### Express

Customer rushed.

Focus:

need → answer → CTA.

### Standard

Normal flow.

### Detailed

Customer wants more explanation.

This avoids forcing every caller through the same 15-question conversation.

---

# 10.12 Primary need discovery

Capture:

```text
primary_need
desired_outcome
pain_point
urgency
current_solution
```

Example customer:

> “I’m looking for physio because I have shoulder discomfort and I want an evening appointment.”

Structured output:

```text
primary_need = physiotherapy
desired_outcome = appointment
schedule_preference = evening
```

For healthcare, avoid having the sales agent infer diagnosis.

---

# 10.13 Secondary needs

Ask naturally:

> “Is there anything else that’s important when choosing the clinic?”

Possible discoveries:

location  
price  
language  
provider gender preference where appropriate  
schedule  
parking  
online service  
insurance/admin questions.

These become structured preferences.

---

# 10.14 Need taxonomy

Maintain a taxonomy.

Example:

```text
SERVICE_NEED
SCHEDULING_NEED
PRICE_NEED
LOCATION_NEED
LANGUAGE_NEED
ACCESSIBILITY_NEED
PAYMENT_NEED
INFORMATION_NEED
HUMAN_SUPPORT_NEED
OTHER_SERVICE_NEED
```

This makes analytics much cleaner.

---

# 10.15 Explicit vs inferred needs

Customer says:

> “I need weekend appointments.”

```text
source = CUSTOMER_EXPLICIT
confidence = 1.0
```

AI thinks:

> “likely price-sensitive.”

```text
source = AI_INFERENCE
confidence = 0.61
```

Never combine them as equivalent facts.

---

# 10.16 Preference discovery

Track dimensions such as:

```text
Language
Contact channel
Call time
Appointment time
Location
Provider
Delivery mode
Price sensitivity
Quality priority
Convenience priority
Service frequency
Commitment preference
```

Do not interrogate customers.

Ask only what is relevant.

---

# 10.17 Adaptive questioning

If customer already submitted:

```text
preferred_time = Evening
```

don't ask:

> “What time do you prefer?”

Ask:

> “You mentioned evenings on the form. Is that still your preference?”

This improves experience and verifies the data.

---

# 10.18 Service explanation architecture

The LLM should not invent service facts.

Architecture:

```text
Customer Need
     ↓
Service Catalog Tool
     ↓
Approved Information
     ↓
LLM natural-language explanation
```

Service Catalog might provide:

```text
service_name
description
duration
delivery_mode
locations
price
current_offer
availability
approved_claims
restrictions
```

---

# 10.19 Explain only what matters

Customer wants evening physiotherapy.

Don't explain every clinic service.

Use:

```text
Need → Service Match → Relevant Explanation
```

Example:

> “Based on what you mentioned, our evening physiotherapy appointments may be the most relevant option. I can check available times for you.”

---

# 10.20 Response length control

Voice agents often talk too much.

Implement:

```text
max_response_words
```

by state.

Example:

Opening: 20–35 words.

Service explanation: 40–80 words.

Booking confirmation: concise.

Customer can ask for more detail.

---

# 10.21 Agent monologue monitoring

Track:

```text
agent_turn_duration
agent_words_per_turn
long_monologue_count
```

A high-quality call should feel conversational.

Set alert if agent repeatedly speaks for 60+ seconds without inviting interaction.

---

# 10.22 Likes/dislikes extraction

Customer:

> “I like that you have evening appointments, but the monthly package is expensive.”

Extract separately:

```text
LIKE
attribute = evening_availability
strength = high

DISLIKE
attribute = price
strength = high
```

Never store simply:

```text
sentiment = mixed
```

That loses business intelligence.

---

# 10.23 Reaction tracking

After explaining a service, ask:

> “How does that sound so far?”

Then classify:

```text
POSITIVE
NEUTRAL
UNCERTAIN
NEGATIVE
```

with reasons.

Example:

```text
reaction = POSITIVE
reason = schedule fit
```

---

# 10.24 Objection engine

Standard categories:

```text
PRICE
TRUST
TIMING
LOCATION
SERVICE_FIT
COMPETITOR
DECISION_DELAY
FAMILY_APPROVAL
HUMAN_PREFERENCE
AI_RESISTANCE
QUALITY
CONTRACT
OTHER
```

Capture:

```text
objection_type
objection_text
severity
resolved
resolution
```

---

# 10.25 Price objection flow

Customer:

> “That seems expensive.”

Do not immediately discount.

Flow:

```text
Acknowledge
 ↓
Understand comparison
 ↓
Clarify priorities
 ↓
Explain relevant value
 ↓
Check available approved options
 ↓
Offer only valid option
```

If discount exists:

use Pricing/Promotion API.

---

# 10.26 Don't argue

If customer says:

> “Competitor X is cheaper.”

Don't say:

> “They are worse.”

Better:

> “Understood. If price is an important factor, I can explain the options we currently offer so you can compare them.”

Capture competitor intelligence.

---

# 10.27 Competitor tracking

Store:

```text
competitor_name
competitor_service
competitor_price
competitor_like
competitor_dislike
switching_intent
```

But do not make defamatory or unverifiable claims about competitors.

---

# 10.28 Additional-needs discovery

Near the end:

> “Besides what we discussed, is there anything else you or your family are looking for help with?”

This can reveal:

secondary service  
family need  
corporate need  
future need.

Do not turn this into aggressive cross-selling.

---

# 10.29 Need → service matching

Example:

```text
Customer:
Interested in regular yoga

Other need:
Mother needs gentle program

        ↓

RecommendAI

        ↓

Possible:
Senior Yoga

        ↓

Service Catalog Validation

        ↓

Agent asks permission to explain
```

---

# 10.30 Cross-sell permission

A useful policy:

Don't immediately launch another pitch.

Ask:

> “We do have a related option that may fit that need. Would you like a quick overview?”

Customer says no:

Stop.

Track:

```text
cross_sell_declined = true
```

---

# 10.31 Pricing flow

Never let LLM rely on memory.

```text
Customer asks price
       ↓
Pricing Tool
       ↓
Current Price
       ↓
Agent
```

Retrieve:

price  
tax  
discount  
expiration  
terms.

---

# 10.32 Pricing edge case

Pricing API fails.

Wrong:

> “I think it’s around $80.”

Correct:

> “I’m unable to retrieve the current price right now. I can arrange a follow-up or transfer you.”

Never guess.

---

# 10.33 FAQ / RAG

Use RAG for informational questions:

clinic hours  
parking  
service description  
general preparation information  
location  
policies.

Architecture:

```text
Question
 ↓
Intent/Risk classifier
 ↓
Allowed informational query?
 ↓
RAG
 ↓
Grounding validation
 ↓
Response
```

---

# 10.34 RAG confidence

If retrieval confidence is poor:

```text
ABSTAIN
```

rather than hallucinate.

Example:

> “I don’t have a reliable answer for that. I can connect you with the clinic.”

---

# 10.35 Healthcare safety classification

Every user turn can optionally receive:

```text
ADMINISTRATIVE
SERVICE_INFO
CLINICAL
URGENT
PAYMENT
COMPLAINT
DNC
```

If:

```text
CLINICAL
```

use approved restricted pathway.

If:

```text
URGENT
```

use clinic-approved escalation pathway.

---

# 10.36 Tool calling

Available tools may include:

```text
get_customer()
get_service()
get_price()
get_location()
get_provider()
get_availability()
book()
reschedule()
cancel()
send_sms()
send_email()
create_callback()
transfer()
update_preference()
set_dnc()
```

Every tool goes through the Tool Gateway and PolicyAI.

---

# 10.37 Critical-field confirmation

Before executing high-impact operations:

Confirm:

```text
customer
service
location
provider if relevant
date
time
price if transaction
```

Example:

> “Just to confirm, you’d like physiotherapy at the NW clinic next Tuesday at 6:30 PM. Is that correct?”

Only then book.

---

# 10.38 Conversation memory

Use three levels.

### Turn memory

Current conversation.

### Session memory

Current call context.

### Long-term customer memory

Only approved persistent preferences/facts.

Don't persist every casual statement forever.

---

# 10.39 Memory schema

Store structured facts:

```text
fact
source
confidence
explicit_or_inferred
effective_from
expires_at
```

Example:

```text
preferred_language = Hindi
source = customer explicit
```

Better than feeding entire historical transcripts every call.

---

# 10.40 Contradiction handling

Previous preference:

`Evening`

Customer now says:

> “Morning works better these days.”

Agent:

> “Sure, I’ll use mornings as your current preference.”

Update history instead of creating conflicting values.

---

# 10.41 Barge-in handling

Agent:

> “Our physiotherapy program—”

Customer:

> “Actually I just want the price.”

System:

```text
detect interruption
stop TTS
update intent = PRICE
switch state → PRICE
```

Do not resume the old monologue.

---

# 10.42 Topic switching

Conversation should support non-linear movement.

Example:

```text
NEED
→ PRICE
→ LOCATION
→ PRICE
→ BOOKING
```

Maintain state stack/context.

Don't force customer back through a rigid questionnaire.

---

# 10.43 Tangent handling

Customer asks something unrelated.

Agent can briefly respond if in scope, then return:

> “Coming back to your appointment request…”

If out of scope:

politely redirect.

---

# 10.44 Silence

Example strategy:

```text
3 sec → wait
6 sec → “Are you still there?”
10+ sec → second prompt
prolonged → graceful close/callback option
```

Tune using production data.

---

# 10.45 Customer says “hello?” repeatedly

Likely latency/problem.

Detect:

```text
repeated_hello
```

This can trigger a technical-quality flag.

Agent:

> “Sorry for the delay—I’m here.”

Track for QA.

---

# 10.46 Customer angry

Detect frustration but don't rely only on sentiment model.

Signals:

explicit complaint  
raised voice  
repeated correction  
negative words  
multiple failures.

Action:

```text
de-escalate
stop sales pitch
offer human transfer
```

---

# 10.47 AI resistance

Customer:

> “Are you a bot?”

Agent should answer transparently.

> “Yes, I’m the virtual assistant for ABC Clinic. I can help with service information and booking, or connect you with a person.”

Track:

```text
AI_RESISTANCE
```

If customer wants human:

transfer.

---

# 10.48 Customer asks to stop

Highest-priority intent:

```text
DNC / STOP_CONTACT
```

Interrupt all sales states.

```text
set_dnc()
→ confirmation
→ close
```

---

# 10.49 No interest

Customer:

> “Not interested.”

Don't immediately launch objection handling every time.

Possible response:

> “Understood. Would you prefer that we simply close this inquiry?”

Respect the answer.

---

# 10.50 Feedback collection

At end of appropriate calls:

> “Was there anything we could have explained better?”

Capture:

```text
feedback_text
feedback_category
sentiment
service_issue
agent_issue
price_issue
```

Optional CSAT:

1–5.

Do not make the closing exhausting.

---

# 10.51 Next-action states

Conversation can result in:

```text
BOOKED
CALLBACK
HUMAN_TRANSFER
INFO_SENT
NURTURE
NOT_INTERESTED
DNC
WRONG_NUMBER
FOLLOW_UP
NO_ACTION
```

Every call needs one primary disposition.

---

# 10.52 Confirmation

Before ending, summarize:

> “You’re booked for Tuesday at 6:30 PM at the NW location, and I’ll send the confirmation by SMS.”

This reduces downstream disputes.

---

# 10.53 Closing

Good:

> “Thanks, Raj. Your appointment is confirmed. Have a good evening.”

Avoid repeating the sales pitch.

---

# 10.54 Post-call structured extraction

Immediately after the call:

```text
Transcript
 ↓
Post-Call AI
 ↓
Structured extraction
```

Capture:

```text
Primary need
Secondary need
Other need
Language
Intent
Likes
Dislikes
Preferences
Objections
Competitor
Sentiment
Price reaction
Trust
Questions
Unanswered questions
Outcome
Appointment
Next action
Feedback
AI confidence
```

---

# 10.55 Customer-intelligence output example

```text
Customer: C10028

Primary Need:
Physiotherapy

Secondary:
Evening availability

Other Need:
Senior wellness for mother

Language:
Hindi + English

Likes:
Evening appointments
Nearby location

Dislikes:
Package price

Main Objection:
Price

Competitor:
XYZ Physio

Competitor Like:
Lower advertised price

Intent:
High

Outcome:
Trial appointment booked

Preferred future contact:
Evening

Next Action:
SMS confirmation

Conversation sentiment:
Positive

AI confidence:
92%
```

---

# 10.56 Turn-level data

Store important turns:

| Turn | Speaker | Intent | Topic | Sentiment | Extraction |
|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Agent | Opening | Callback | Neutral | — |
| 2 | Customer | Language | Hindi | Positive | language |
| 5 | Customer | Need | Physio | Neutral | primary need |
| 9 | Customer | Preference | Evening | Positive | timing |
| 14 | Customer | Objection | Price | Negative | dislike |
| 18 | Customer | Other need | Mother | Neutral | secondary opportunity |
| 25 | Customer | Booking | Appointment | Positive | conversion |

This creates exceptional Voice-of-Customer analytics.

---

# 10.57 Conversation quality scoring

Score each call across:

```text
Opening
Disclosure
Understanding
Language quality
Need discovery
Relevance
Accuracy
Grounding
Listening
Barge-in
Empathy
Objection handling
Tool correctness
Booking accuracy
Policy compliance
Closing
```

Example:

```text
Conversation Quality = 91/100
```

But critical failures override composite score.

Example:

```text
DNC violation = CRITICAL FAIL
```

even if overall score would otherwise be 95.

---

# 10.58 Automated QA evaluator

After each call:

```text
Transcript
+
Call Events
+
Tool Trace
+
Policy Decisions
      ↓
QualityAI
      ↓
Scores + Failures
```

Never evaluate only transcript text.

Tool traces reveal whether the system actually performed the correct action.

---

# 10.59 Golden conversation dataset

Create at least:

```text
500 conversations for MVP
2,000+ before serious scale
5,000+ as platform matures
```

Categories:

happy path  
multilingual  
pricing  
objection  
competitor  
booking  
reschedule  
DNC  
wrong person  
angry customer  
clinical question  
technical failure  
noise  
silence  
barge-in.

---

# 10.60 Example test-data categories

### Customer styles

Friendly  
rushed  
confused  
angry  
skeptical  
talkative  
quiet.

### Speech

fast  
slow  
accented  
code-switched  
poor connection.

### Business

new lead  
existing customer  
family member  
corporate buyer.

### Intent

booking  
pricing  
availability  
information  
complaint  
DNC.

---

# 10.61 Conversation test example

Input:

> “Your price is too high. XYZ charges $60.”

Expected:

```text
intent = PRICE_OBJECTION
competitor = XYZ
competitor_price = 60
customer_sentiment = negative
```

Agent must:

acknowledge  
not attack competitor  
retrieve valid pricing/options  
not invent discount.

---

# 10.62 Edge case — several needs in one sentence

Customer:

> “I want yoga for myself, something gentle for my mother, and maybe a corporate program for our office.”

Expected:

```text
Need 1 = yoga/self
Need 2 = senior program/family
Need 3 = corporate wellness/company
```

Don't collapse into one generic "yoga" need.

---

# 10.63 Edge case — customer changes mind

Customer:

> “Book Tuesday.”

then:

> “Actually Thursday.”

Only final confirmed value should reach booking.

Maintain:

```text
candidate_slot
confirmed_slot
```

---

# 10.64 Edge case — customer gives ambiguous date

> “Next Friday.”

Date interpretation can be ambiguous.

Agent should confirm absolute date:

> “Do you mean Friday, August 28?”

This reduces booking errors.

---

# 10.65 Edge case — spelling

Customer:

> “My email is p-r-a-v-e-e-n…”

Use specialized entity-capture mode.

Repeat back:

> “I have praveen@example.com. Is that correct?”

---

# 10.66 Edge case — phone numbers

Do not read or repeat large numbers as one uninterrupted string.

Chunk naturally:

> “403, 555, 1234.”

Confirm.

---

# 10.67 Edge case — customer keeps correcting agent

Track:

```text
correction_count
```

If repeated:

```text
quality_risk = HIGH
```

Potential action:

human transfer.

---

# 10.68 Edge case — STT confidence low on critical field

Example:

```text
time_confidence = 0.51
```

Do not proceed.

Ask:

> “Was that six-thirty or seven-thirty?”

---

# 10.69 Edge case — RAG conflict

Two knowledge documents give different pricing.

Do not choose arbitrarily.

Pricing should come from authoritative structured API.

For other conflicting information:

abstain/escalate and flag content quality issue.

---

# 10.70 Edge case — tool success but spoken confirmation wrong

Booking API:

```text
Tuesday 18:30
```

Agent says:

> “You're booked Wednesday at 6:30.”

This is a serious voice-layer defect.

QA must compare:

```text
tool output
vs
spoken response
```

---

# 10.71 Edge case — caller disconnects after booking

Booking may have succeeded before disconnect.

Workflow must:

confirm backend status  
send authorized confirmation  
record outcome.

Don't automatically rebook.

---

# 10.72 Edge case — agent repeats personal data

Minimize unnecessary repetition of:

full phone  
email  
sensitive information.

Use partial confirmation where appropriate.

---

# 10.73 Prompt architecture

Use multiple prompt layers:

```text
GLOBAL PLATFORM POLICY
        ↓
TENANT POLICY
        ↓
AGENT ROLE
        ↓
USE-CASE INSTRUCTIONS
        ↓
STATE INSTRUCTIONS
        ↓
CUSTOMER CONTEXT
        ↓
TOOL RESULTS
```

Higher layers override lower ones.

---

# 10.74 Prompt variables

Use structured variables:

```text
{{brand_name}}
{{customer_first_name}}
{{service_interest}}
{{preferred_language}}
{{campaign_reason}}
{{approved_service_information}}
```

Do not maintain hundreds of copy-pasted prompts.

---

# 10.75 Prompt versioning

Store:

```text
prompt_id
version
language
agent_profile
owner
approval
QA_score
production_status
```

Deploy:

```text
DEV
→ TEST
→ STAGING
→ CANARY
→ PROD
```

---

# 10.76 Script A/B testing

Test:

Opening A vs B.

Discovery short vs detailed.

Price explanation A vs B.

Measure:

connect  
engagement  
booking  
complaints  
call duration  
DNC.

Don't optimize solely for conversion.

---

# 10.77 Tools

Conversation/orchestration options:

LiveKit Agents  
provider-native engines  
LangGraph/custom state machine.

Backend:

Python/FastAPI.

State:

Redis + PostgreSQL.

RAG:

pgvector/Qdrant/OpenSearch depending scale.

Evaluation:

Langfuse/LangSmith + custom evaluators.

Tracing:

OpenTelemetry.

---

# 10.78 Recommended state engine

For serious production, I would implement the **business conversation state machine outside the provider prompt**.

Concept:

```text
Conversation Orchestrator
        ↓
State
        ↓
Prompt fragment
        ↓
LLM
        ↓
Structured action
        ↓
Validator
        ↓
Next state
```

That makes provider switching much easier.

---

# 10.79 Structured LLM response

Internally ask the model to produce something conceptually like:

```json
{
  "reply": "I can check evening appointments.",
  "intent": "CHECK_AVAILABILITY",
  "state": "S18_BOOKING",
  "entities": {
    "time_preference": "evening"
  },
  "tool_request": "get_availability"
}
```

Then validate before execution.

---

# 10.80 Conversation guardrails

Check every response for:

unsupported claims  
forbidden advice  
privacy issues  
unsafe content  
invalid discounts  
unavailable service  
tool misuse.

Use deterministic controls wherever possible.
