## 22.57 Drift-driven governance review

If:

Hindi quality falls below threshold,

automatically create:

```text
GOVERNANCE_REVIEW_REQUIRED
```

Possible:

reduce traffic  
suspend language  
change provider.

Governance should react to runtime evidence.

## 22.58 Incident-driven reapproval

Serious incident:

```text
Wrong appointment
```

Agent may be:

```text
SUSPENDED
```

until:

fix  
regression test  
risk reassessment  
reapproval.

## 22.59 Provider-change governance

If RouteAI adds a new voice provider:

require:

security review  
privacy review  
quality benchmark  
language benchmark  
cost review  
failover tests.

Then approve by use case/region.

## 22.60 Prompt-change governance

Even small prompt wording can materially alter behavior.

Classify changes:

### Minor

Grammar/text clarification.

### Significant

Conversation logic.

### Critical

Safety/policy/tool behavior.

Testing/approval burden increases accordingly.

## 22.61 Knowledge-change governance

Example:

clinic updates pricing.

Do not require full AI architecture review.

But require:

content approval  
version update  
RAG refresh  
pricing consistency test.

Risk-based governance keeps the process practical.

## 22.62 Governance SLA

Define:

low-risk change review target  
high-risk review target  
critical incident reapproval.

Otherwise governance becomes a bottleneck.

## 22.63 Governance automation

Automate evidence collection:

test results  
security scans  
quality metrics  
risk scores  
provider health.

Human reviewers should review decisions, not manually copy screenshots into spreadsheets.

## 22.64 Evidence expiration

An evaluation from 18 months ago may no longer prove a new model is safe.

Store:

```text
evidence_valid_until
```

Re-run when:

model/provider changes  
major prompt changes  
new language  
new use case.

## 22.65 Periodic review

Each production asset gets:

```text
review_frequency
next_review
```

Risk-based.

Example:

High-risk agent: quarterly.

Low-risk FAQ agent: annually.

Actual cadence follows policy.

## 22.66 Ownership change

If employee/team changes:

ownership must transfer.

Detect:

```text
ORPHANED_ASSET
```

A production model with no owner is a governance defect.

## 22.67 Technical debt governance

Track:

deprecated SDK  
old model  
unsupported prompt architecture  
expiring contract.

Create:

```text
TECHNICAL_GOVERNANCE_DEBT
```

with deadline.

## 22.68 Compliance mappings

GovernAI can map controls to applicable frameworks/organizational requirements.

Examples may include:

privacy/security standards  
AI governance standards  
internal policies.

Avoid assuming a particular framework automatically applies to every deployment; map per tenant/jurisdiction.

## 22.69 Control mapping

Example:

```text
CTRL-002 Critical booking confirmation
```

maps to:

Risk: incorrect transaction.

Tests:

TC-BOOK-101  
TC-BOOK-145.

Assets:

all booking agents.

This creates full traceability.

## 22.70 Requirements traceability

Ideal chain:

```text
Business Requirement
        ↓
Risk
        ↓
Control
        ↓
Architecture
        ↓
Implementation
        ↓
Test
        ↓
Evidence
        ↓
Approval
        ↓
Production Monitoring
```

This is what enterprise governance should look like.

## 22.71 Exception test

Scenario:

Exception permits Provider B until September 30.

On October 1:

RouteAI attempts Provider B.

Expected:

```text
BLOCK
EXCEPTION_EXPIRED
```

Automate this.

## 22.72 Edge case — model provider silently updates behavior

Even if model name unchanged, quality drift may trigger:

```text
MODEL_BEHAVIOR_CHANGE
```

GovernAI can require revalidation.

Version what you can; monitor what you cannot control.

## 22.73 Edge case — hotfix bypass

Developer manually modifies production prompt.

Detect configuration drift.

GovernAI compares:

approved configuration

vs:

runtime configuration.

Any mismatch:

```text
UNAUTHORIZED_CONFIG_DRIFT
```

and alert/block depending severity.

## 22.74 Configuration attestation

Regularly hash:

agent config  
prompt  
tool list  
policy references.

Compare to approved deployment manifest.

This is powerful governance.

## 22.75 Edge case — retired knowledge still retrieved

Run automated tests against deprecated facts.

Expected:

not retrievable.

Otherwise governance metadata and actual runtime are inconsistent.

## 22.76 Edge case — agent uses unapproved tool

Runtime Tool Gateway checks registry.

Even if prompt requests it:

```text
AGENT_TOOL_NOT_APPROVED
```

Block.

## 22.77 Edge case — expired model approval

If model review expired:

decide based on policy:

warning  
new deployment blocked  
production suspended for high-risk case.

Do not silently ignore overdue review.

## 22.78 Edge case — owner leaves organization

Asset ownership service finds inactive identity.

Trigger:

```text
OWNER_REASSIGNMENT_REQUIRED
```

## 22.79 Testing GovernAI

Test:

asset creation  
approval  
rejection  
conditional approval  
expiry  
rollback  
retirement  
orphan ownership  
configuration drift  
dependency impact.

## 22.80 Governance security testing

Critical:

unauthorized approval  
self-approval bypass  
audit modification  
exception abuse  
role escalation  
cross-tenant governance access.

## 22.81 Golden governance scenarios

Examples:

```text
Unapproved prompt → deploy attempt → BLOCK

Expired exception → provider use → BLOCK

Critical test fails → release → BLOCK

Agent has no owner → production promotion → BLOCK

Rollback version missing → high-risk release → BLOCK

All gates satisfied → APPROVE
```

## 22.82 Governance KPIs

Track:

```text
Production assets
Assets without owner
Overdue reviews
Open exceptions
Expired exceptions
Unapproved runtime assets
Critical test failures
Open high risks
Average approval cycle
Rollback events
```

## 22.83 Governance maturity

### Level 1

Spreadsheets/manual approvals.

### Level 2

Central registry + versioning.

### Level 3

Automated test/evidence integration.

### Level 4

Runtime policy enforcement.

### Level 5

Continuous governance driven by telemetry/risk.

For your architecture, target Level 3–4 initially and grow toward Level 5.

## 22.84 Recommended technology

Core:

PostgreSQL + FastAPI/Spring Boot.

Workflow:

Temporal.

Policy:

OPA/custom PolicyAI.

Model artifacts:

MLflow.

LLM tracing/evals:

Langfuse/LangSmith-style tooling.

Source control:

GitHub/GitLab.

Dashboards:

Grafana/Metabase.

Data lineage at scale:

OpenLineage/DataHub-style tools.

Keep GovernAI as the central orchestration/control layer rather than duplicating every underlying capability.

# Phase 23 — ReportAI + Executive / Operations / AI / Compliance / FinOps Reporting

This phase turns all platform data into **decision-grade reporting**. The goal is not simply to build dashboards. It is to create one governed reporting layer where every KPI has a definition, source, owner, calculation logic, refresh cadence, and drill-down path.

> **ReportAI should answer what happened, why it happened, what changed, what is at risk, and what action should be taken next.**

## 23.1 Reporting architecture

```text
Forms / Leads / CRM
CampaignAI
Voice / Telephony
ConversationAI
NeedAI
ScoreAI
RecommendAI
NextAI
ToolAI
QualityAI
PolicyAI
RiskAI
ResAI
GovernAI
FinOps
      ↓
Canonical Events
      ↓
Operational DB / Event Bus
      ↓
ELT / Transformation
      ↓
Analytics Warehouse
      ↓
Semantic / Metric Layer
      ↓
ReportAI
      ↓
┌────────────┬────────────┬────────────┬────────────┐
Executive    Marketing    Sales/Ops    AI/QA
Compliance   Risk         FinOps       Market/VOC
```

## 23.2 Reporting domains

| Domain | Primary questions |
|---|---|
| Executive | Is the platform creating business value? |
| Acquisition | Which channels create quality leads? |
| Campaign | Which campaigns perform best? |
| Sales | Which leads/customers should be worked next? |
| Voice Operations | Are calls connecting and completing reliably? |
| Conversation | Where are calls succeeding/failing? |
| Customer | What do customers need, like, dislike? |
| AI | Are models/agents performing correctly? |
| Quality | Where are defects and regressions? |
| Compliance | Are consent/DNC/policy controls working? |
| Risk | Which risks are increasing? |
| Governance | Are assets approved and reviewed? |
| Provider | Which platform/provider performs best? |
| FinOps | What does each outcome cost? |
| Market Intelligence | What new demand and competitor signals exist? |

```text
      ↓

      ↓

      ↓

```

# 23.71 Explainable reports

Every chart should let staff inspect:

metric definition  
source  
last refresh  
filters  
owner.

filters

Track:

report created  
report viewed  
sensitive export  
metric definition changed

---

# 23.75 Alert thresholds

Examples:

```text
Booking ↓ >20%
DNC ↑ >2× baseline
Critical QA failure >0
Provider error > threshold
Cost/booking ↑ >25%
```

Tune using actual baselines.

---

# 23.76 ReportAI edge case — Simpson's paradox

Overall conversion rises, but important subsegments deteriorate.

Always support dimensional breakdowns before concluding improvement.

---

# 23.77 Edge case — tiny sample

Agent B:

booking = 100%

but only two calls.

Display sample size and confidence.

Don't rank providers/models from trivial samples.

---

# 23.78 Edge case — seasonality

Monday morning vs Christmas week should not be interpreted identically.

Use appropriate historical baselines.

---

# 23.79 Edge case — denominator changes

If eligibility rules change, connect rate can appear to improve because fewer low-quality leads were called.

Report:

both numerator and denominator changes.

---

# 23.80 Edge case — attribution overclaim

Customer saw:

Instagram  
Google  
email  
AI call.

Do not claim AI call alone caused conversion without experimental evidence.

Report:

attributed/assisted conversion.

---

# 23.81 Edge case — missing provider cost

Do not silently calculate:

$0.

Mark:

```text
COST_INCOMPLETE
```

and exclude or estimate only with clear labeling.

---

# 23.82 Edge case — dashboard hides critical failure

If overall Quality = 95

but:

one DNC bypass occurred,

dashboard should surface:

```text
CRITICAL CONTROL FAILURE
```

separately.

Averages must never hide severe incidents.

---

```text
 │ Pricing Intelligence               │
 │ Service-Gap Detection              │
 │ Geographic Demand                  │
 │ Language Demand                    │
 │ Objection Intelligence             │
 │ Customer Question Mining           │
 │ Emerging Trend Detection           │
 │ Opportunity Scoring                │
 └────────────────────────────────────┘
                    ↓
                MarketAI
                    ↓
 Product / Pricing / Marketing / Sales / Strategy
```

## 24.2 Market signal taxonomy

Capture separate signal types.

| Signal | Example |
|---|---|
| Service demand | “Do you offer home physio?” |
| Scheduling demand | “I need weekends.” |
| Price expectation | “I expected around $80.” |
| Price objection | “$120 is too expensive.” |
| Competitor mention | “XYZ charges $75.” |
| Competitor like | “Their location is convenient.” |
| Competitor dislike | “They never have evening appointments.” |
| Service gap | Punjabi support unavailable |
| Geographic gap | Demand in NW but no capacity |
| Channel preference | “Text me instead.” |
| Language demand | Punjabi calls increasing |
| Trust concern | “How experienced are your therapists?” |
| Feature request | Home visit / online booking |
| Emerging need | Corporate stress-management program |

---

# 24.3 Market signal record

```text
MARKET_SIGNAL

signal_id
tenant_id
customer_id
interaction_id

signal_type
category
subcategory

raw_evidence_ref
normalized_value

service_id
location
language

explicit_or_inferred
spontaneous_or_prompted

strength
confidence

timestamp
taxonomy_version
```

This lets you distinguish genuine spontaneous demand from something the agent suggested first.

---

# 24.4 Spontaneous demand matters more

Customer spontaneously asks:

> “Do you offer home visits?”

Strong market signal.

Agent asks:

> “Would you be interested in home visits?”

Customer:

> “Maybe.”

Much weaker signal.

Store:

```text
SPONTANEOUS = HIGH_WEIGHT
AGENT_PROMPTED = LOW_WEIGHT
```

Otherwise your own scripts will artificially create “market demand.”

---

# 24.5 Demand intelligence

Measure:

```text
request_frequency
unique_customers
repeat_mentions
intent_strength
urgency
conversion_if_available
trend
service_coverage
```

Example:

```text
Weekend Physio

Requests              430/month
Unique customers      391
High-intent requests  72%
Trend                  +31%
Current coverage       LOW
```

---

# 24.6 Demand Strength Score

Conceptually:

```text
Demand Strength =
Frequency
× Explicitness
× Spontaneity
× Intent
× Urgency
× Growth
```

Normalize to 0–100.

Do not use one factor alone.

---

# 24.7 Market opportunity score

A more complete opportunity score:

```text
Opportunity =
Demand Strength
+
Growth
+
Unmet-Service Gap
+
Conversion Potential
+
Strategic Fit
+
Capacity Feasibility
+
Economics
-
Operational Complexity
-
Risk
```

Example:

```text
Weekend Physio      91
Home Physio         87
Punjabi Support     81
Corporate Wellness  74
```

These numbers should support prioritization, not replace business judgment.

---

# 24.8 Unmet-demand analysis

Compare:

```text
Customer Need
      ↓
Current Service Catalog
      ↓
MATCH
PARTIAL_MATCH
NO_MATCH
```

Then calculate:

```text
Unmet Demand %
```

Example:

```text
Home physiotherapy

Requests: 275
Matched: 0
Unmet: 100%
```

Very different from a service customers frequently request but can already access.

---

# 24.9 Gap taxonomy

Common gaps:

```text
SERVICE_NOT_OFFERED
NO_CAPACITY
NO_LANGUAGE_SUPPORT
NO_LOCATION
NO_WEEKEND
NO_EVENING
PRICE_MISMATCH
DELIVERY_MODE_GAP
INSURANCE_ADMIN_GAP
HUMAN_SUPPORT_GAP
```

This lets management distinguish product gaps from operations gaps.

---

# 24.10 Capacity gap vs service gap

Example:

Customers ask for evening physiotherapy.

You already provide it.

But all slots are full.

That's:

```text
CAPACITY_GAP
```

not:

```text
SERVICE_NOT_OFFERED
```

Business response is different.

---

# 24.11 Geographic intelligence

Aggregate by legitimate geographic fields such as:

city  
service area  
clinic catchment.

Example:

```text
Calgary

NW:
Physio demand          HIGH
Evening demand         VERY HIGH

NE:
Massage demand         HIGH

SW:
Corporate wellness     GROWING
```

Avoid inappropriate demographic inference from neighborhood.

---

# 24.12 Geographic demand map

Useful outputs:

```text
Requests per postal/service zone
Appointment availability
No-match rate
Competitor mentions
Average travel objection
```

This can support:

new clinic locations  
mobile/home service  
staff allocation.

---

# 24.13 Language-demand intelligence

Track:

```text
preferred_language
actual_call_language
code_switching
quality
service demand
booking
```

Example:

| Language | Demand | Growth | Current Quality | Gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| English | High | +4% | 96 | Low |
| Hindi | High | +18% | 94 | Low |
| Punjabi | Medium | +31% | 86 | High |
| French | Low | +8% | 92 | Medium |

This helps prioritize language investment.

---

# 24.14 Language quality vs demand

High demand + low quality is a priority.

Example:

```text
Punjabi demand = growing 31%
Punjabi booking accuracy = 86%
```

Action:

improve STT/TTS/agent quality before aggressively scaling campaign volume.

---

# 24.15 Competitor intelligence

Capture:

```text
competitor_name
service
price_mentioned
location
customer_like
customer_dislike
switching_reason
switching_intent
```

Always label as:

**customer-reported competitor information**

unless independently verified.

---

# 24.16 Competitor dashboard

Example:

| Competitor | Mentions | Main Like | Main Dislike | Switching Interest |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|
| Clinic A | 1,230 | Price | Availability | 32% |
| Clinic B | 840 | Quality | Price | 21% |
| Clinic C | 520 | Location | Wait time | 39% |

This gives marketing and strategy meaningful direction.

---

# 24.17 Competitor switching analysis

Classify:

```text
LOYAL
SATISFIED
NEUTRAL
UNSATISFIED
ACTIVELY_SWITCHING
```

Only when enough evidence exists.

Example:

> “They are fine, I’m just checking prices.”

Different from:

> “I want to leave because I can never get an appointment.”

---

# 24.18 Switching-reason taxonomy

```text
PRICE
AVAILABILITY
WAIT_TIME
QUALITY
LOCATION
CUSTOMER_SERVICE
LANGUAGE
CONVENIENCE
SERVICE_RANGE
OTHER
```

Then report:

> What actually causes competitor customers to consider switching?

---

# 24.19 Price Intelligence

Capture separately:

```text
our_price
customer_expected_price
competitor_price_mentioned
price_objection
discount_request
accepted_price
```

Don't collapse all into “price sensitive.”

---

# 24.20 Price expectation distribution

Example:

```text
Expected price

<$60       12%
$60–79     28%
$80–99     34%
$100–119   17%
$120+       9%
```

Segment by:

service  
location  
customer intent.

This helps pricing research.

---

# 24.21 Price objection curve

Example:

| Price band | Objection rate | Booking rate |
|---|---:|---:|
| <$75 | 9% | 43% |
| $75–99 | 18% | 38% |
| $100–124 | 31% | 27% |
| $125+ | 48% | 17% |

Do not automatically infer causality; other service/package factors may differ.

---

# 24.22 Willingness-to-pay

Only use explicit conversational evidence.

Customer:

> “I could pay up to around $100.”

Store.

Do not infer income or financial status from voice, name, neighborhood, or language.

---

# 24.23 Price elasticity experiments

For mature deployments, use carefully controlled pricing experiments where appropriate.

Track:

```text
price
conversion
retention
complaint
service utilization
```

Pricing experiments require business/legal review depending context.

---

# 24.24 Customer psychology signals

Keep this business-grounded rather than trying to infer personality.

Useful categories:

```text
TRUST_CONCERN
PRICE_CONCERN
CONVENIENCE_PRIORITY
QUALITY_PRIORITY
TIME_PRESSURE
INFORMATION_SEEKING
HUMAN_PREFERENCE
DECISION_DELAY
```

These are observable buying concerns, not personality diagnoses.

---

# 24.25 Buying-friction model

Aggregate:

```text
Price
Trust
Availability
Location
Language
Complex booking
No human support
Insufficient information
Competitor lock-in
```

Then report:

```text
Top reasons qualified leads fail to convert
```

---

# 24.26 Friction funnel

Example:

```text
1,000 qualified
      ↓
290 price objection
      ↓
210 availability issue
      ↓
120 trust concern
      ↓
95 location issue
```

Customers can have multiple frictions, so report both incidence and primary drop-off reason.

---

# 24.27 Question mining

Aggregate every customer question.

Examples:

```text
Do you have evening appointments?
How much does it cost?
Do you take insurance?
Do you have Punjabi-speaking staff?
Can someone come to my home?
```

Measure:

frequency  
answer availability  
answer confidence  
conversion following answer.

---

# 24.28 Question → content strategy

High-frequency unanswered question:

```text
"Do you offer home visits?"
```

could trigger:

service review.

High-frequency answered but poorly understood question:

pricing policy might require clearer communication.

---

# 24.29 Knowledge-gap intelligence

Track:

```text
question_frequency
RAG_no_answer_rate
human_transfer_rate
```

Example:

Insurance questions:

```text
820 questions
18% unresolved
```

Action:

improve approved knowledge or workflow.

---

# 24.30 Emerging-trend detection

Monitor weekly/monthly changes.

Example:

```text
"Home visits"

Jan  32
Feb  42
Mar  71
Apr 128
```

Trend engine flags significant growth.

---

# 24.31 Trend detection method

Start simple:

moving average  
growth rate  
z-score.

Later:

seasonal decomposition  
change-point detection.

Avoid complex ML before you have enough data.

---

# 24.32 Seasonality

Example:

Massage requests may vary around holidays.

Corporate wellness may spike during annual benefits/planning cycles.

Compare trends against expected seasonality before calling them new demand.

---

# 24.33 Trend score

Conceptually:

```text
Trend Score =
Recent Growth
× Persistence
× Volume
× Statistical Confidence
```

A 300% increase from 1 to 4 requests should not outrank a steady increase from 200 to 350.

---

# 24.34 Emerging opportunity

Example:

```text
CORPORATE STRESS PROGRAM

Current requests: 182/month
3-month growth: +46%
High-intent: 58%
Current service coverage: partial
Main source: LinkedIn/B2B
Opportunity score: 86
```

This is actionable.

---

# 24.35 Segment-market analysis

Break demand by:

segment  
service  
location  
language  
source  
campaign.

Example:

```text
HIGH_INTENT + HINDI + PHYSIO
```

may have different objections than:

```text
RESEARCHER + ENGLISH + PHYSIO
```

Scripts/offers can adapt accordingly.

---

# 24.36 Acquisition-source intelligence

Ask:

> What kinds of customers does each channel produce?

Example:

Google:

higher intent.

Instagram:

higher volume, more researchers.

Referral:

highest trust/conversion.

This helps channel investment.

---

# 24.37 Source → need matrix

Example:

| Source | Top Need | Top Friction |
|---|---|---|
| Google | Appointment | Availability |
| Instagram | General info | Price |
| Referral | Booking | Timing |
| LinkedIn | Corporate wellness | ROI |

Very useful for campaign design.

---

# 24.38 Campaign message intelligence

Analyze which customer problems each campaign actually attracts.

Campaign intended for:

Stress-management yoga.

But conversations reveal:

70% ask about weight loss.

Possible issue:

creative/message mismatch.

---

# 24.39 Ad-to-call consistency

Track:

```text
Ad promise
→ Landing page
→ Customer expectation
→ Voice conversation
```

Large mismatch causes distrust and complaints.

MarketAI can identify it.

---

# 24.40 Campaign expectation-gap score

Measure mismatch between:

campaign offer/topic

and:

customer-requested topic.

Example:

```text
Campaign: Free Physio Consultation
Actual calls:
42% expect completely free ongoing treatment
```

Marketing copy may need correction.

---

# 24.41 Service-performance intelligence

For each service track:

demand  
availability  
recommendations  
acceptance  
bookings  
cancellations  
complaints  
revenue.

A high-demand service can still be unattractive if operational performance is poor.

---

# 24.42 Lost-revenue analysis

Estimate categories:

```text
No availability
Price objection
No language support
No service offered
No human callback
Technical failure
```

Then:

```text
potential lost opportunities
```

Use assumptions transparently.

---

# 24.43 Opportunity economic model

Potential inputs:

```text
monthly demand
expected conversion
average revenue
margin
implementation cost
capacity cost
risk
```

Then approximate:

```text
Opportunity Value
```

This supports prioritization.

---

# 24.44 Example opportunity ranking

| Opportunity | Demand | Growth | Gap | Economics | Score |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Weekend Physio | High | 31% | High | Strong | 92 |
| Punjabi Support | Med | 38% | High | Strong | 88 |
| Home Visits | Med | 47% | Very High | Medium | 84 |
| Corporate Yoga | Med | 22% | Medium | Strong | 78 |

---

# 24.45 Recommendation to management

MarketAI output should include:

```text
Observation
Evidence
Opportunity
Risk
Recommended next experiment
```

Example:

```text
Observation:
Weekend physio demand increased 31%.

Evidence:
430 unique requests in 30 days.

Gap:
72% could not find preferred weekend slot.

Recommendation:
Pilot Saturday capacity at NW clinic.

Measure:
Booking, utilization, margin, CSAT.
```

This is stronger than simply showing a chart.

---

# 24.46 Experiment generation

MarketAI can suggest experiments, not autonomously launch them.

Examples:

extend evening hours  
pilot weekend service  
add Punjabi agent  
test new price package  
new FAQ content.

Governance approves experiments.

---

# 24.47 Market research from outbound calls

Outbound agents can ask lightweight, permission-aware questions such as:

> “What matters most when choosing a clinic—timing, location, price, or something else?”

But avoid turning every sales call into a research survey.

Use targeted sampling.

---

# 24.48 Research sample design

For formal research:

define:

population  
sample  
questionnaire  
sampling bias  
response bias.

Do not assume Voice AI conversation data is representative of the entire market.

It represents people who entered your funnel.

---

# 24.49 Funnel bias

Example:

Your Instagram campaign attracts younger users.

MarketAI sees high demand for evening appointments.

That may not represent the overall Calgary market.

Label:

```text
FUNNEL-BASED MARKET SIGNAL
```

rather than general-population fact.

---

# 24.50 External market data integration

MarketAI can later combine internal VOC with:

public trends  
competitor websites/pricing where lawfully collected  
industry reports  
search trends  
survey results  
CRM sales data.

Keep external-source provenance.

---

# 24.51 Internal vs external evidence

Example:

```text
Internal VOC:
430 weekend requests

External survey:
37% prefer weekend

Search trend:
weekend physio searches growing
```

Triangulated evidence is stronger.

---

# 24.52 Competitor-data verification

Customer says:

> “XYZ costs $50.”

Store as:

```text
customer_reported_price = 50
```

If externally verified later:

```text
verified_competitor_price
```

Keep them separate.

---

# 24.53 Market intelligence confidence

Every insight should have:

```text
sample_size
signal_strength
source_diversity
data_recency
confidence
```

Example:

```text
Weekend Physio Demand

Confidence: HIGH
Sample: 430 unique customers
Sources: Voice, form, website
Period: last 30 days
```

---

# 24.54 Small-sample guardrail

Do not produce:

> “Punjabi customers prefer X”

from six calls.

Use minimum sample thresholds and cautious language.

---

# 24.55 Insight record

```text
MARKET_INSIGHT

insight_id
tenant_id

type
title
summary

supporting_metrics[]
signal_ids[]

segment
service
location
language

sample_size
confidence

trend

business_impact
recommended_action

generated_at
expires_at
```

```text
DETECTED
 ↓
VALIDATED
 ↓
REVIEWED
 ↓
ACTIONED
 ↓
MEASURED
 ↓
CLOSED
```

Otherwise insights become dashboard clutter.

Flow:

```text
 ↓

 ↓

 ↓
```

Closed-loop innovation.

# 24.58 MarketAI + PricingAI

Price objections increase.

MarketAI identifies:

service  
segment  
location.

Pricing team can test:

new package  
trial  
bundling.

Then measure downstream outcome.

# 24.59 MarketAI + CampaignAI

Insight:

Hindi-speaking high-intent leads respond better to evening callbacks.

CampaignAI can adjust eligible campaigns—but only through approved experimentation/governance.

# 24.60 MarketAI + RouteAI

If Punjabi demand grows rapidly:

business case exists for better Punjabi STT/TTS/provider investment.

Routing strategy should be based on quality evidence.

---

# 24.61 MarketAI + Workforce planning

Demand by:

day/hour  
location  
language  
service.

Can forecast:

human reception staffing  
clinician capacity  
language-support capacity.

---

# 24.62 Demand forecasting

Later use:

time-series forecasting.

Possible:

ARIMA/Prophet-style methods  
gradient boosting  
hierarchical forecasting.

Forecast:

calls  
appointments  
service demand.

Start only after enough history.

---

# 24.63 Forecast dimensions

Forecast:

```text
Service × Location × Week
```

Avoid extremely granular sparse forecasts.

Use hierarchy:

company  
service  
location.

---

# 24.64 Capacity forecasting

Compare:

```text
Forecast Demand
vs
Available Capacity
```

Example:

```text
Weekend physio demand = 150
available slots = 70

capacity gap = 80
```

Very actionable.

---

# 24.65 Competitive-loss analysis

For leads that do not convert:

extract:

competitor selected  
reason  
price  
availability  
trust.

Report:

```text
Lost to competitor because:
Price        38%
Availability 27%
Location     18%
Other        17%
```

Only where the customer actually provides this information.

# 24.66 Win analysis

Why customers chose you:

location  
availability  
language  
price  
quality perception  
referral trust.

This helps brand positioning.

# 24.67 Win/Loss dashboard

```text
Won because:
Evening availability

No weekend
```

# 24.68 Brand trust signals

Track conversational questions:

> “Are you established?”

> “Who are the therapists?”

These indicate trust friction.

Marketing may need:

stronger testimonials  
credentials

Use verified claims only.

Measure:

# 24.70 Customer effort score

```text
repeated_questions
```

# 24.75 Data pipeline

```text
Conversation Complete
 ↓
NeedAI
 ↓
Market Signals
 ↓
Aggregation
 ↓
Trend Engine
 ↓
Opportunity Scoring
 ↓
Market Insight
```

Run near-real-time for operational signals and daily/weekly aggregation for strategy.

---

# 24.76 Data quality

Market insights fail if upstream extraction is bad.

Monitor:

unknown need rate  
competitor extraction precision  
price extraction accuracy  
duplicate customers  
source bias.

MarketAI should inherit confidence from upstream extraction.

---

# 24.77 Testing

Test:

trend calculation  
unique-customer counts  
duplicate signal suppression  
prompted vs spontaneous weighting  
service-gap detection  
competitor normalization  
price extraction.

---

# 24.78 Competitor normalization

Customer may say:

```text
XYZ
XYZ Clinic
XYZ Physiotherapy
```

Map to one competitor entity where confidence is sufficient.

Keep unknown aliases for review.

---

# 24.79 Price normalization

Handle:

```text
$80
80 dollars
eighty bucks
$80/session
$400 for five
```

Store:

amount  
currency  
unit basis.

Avoid comparing package price directly with per-session price without normalization.

---

# 24.80 Edge case — customer exaggeration

Customer:

> “They charge like a thousand dollars.”

Low-confidence competitor price.

Do not put $1,000 into verified competitor-price dashboard as fact.

---

# 24.81 Edge case — same customer repeats request

One customer mentions home visits in five calls.

Demand count should distinguish:

mentions

from:

unique customers.

Both are useful.

---

# 24.82 Edge case — agent repeatedly suggests same service

This can artificially inflate demand.

Use spontaneous/prompted distinction.

---

# 24.83 Edge case — marketing campaign creates trend

New ad specifically promotes massage.

Massage inquiries jump.

Trend is real within funnel, but not necessarily organic market demand.

Annotate campaign effects.

---

# 24.84 Edge case — new service launch

Requests spike because customers now know the service exists.

Distinguish:

awareness-driven demand

from:

previously unmet spontaneous demand.

---

# 24.85 Edge case — availability failure creates repeated calls

Customers may repeatedly ask for evening slots because booking system failed.

MarketAI could falsely interpret repeated calls as increasing market demand.

Use unique customers + transaction context.

---

# 24.86 Edge case — competitor name misheard

STT may turn:

“Lifemark”

into another word.

Require confidence/entity normalization before competitor aggregation.

---

# 24.87 Privacy

Market reporting should generally operate on aggregated/de-identified data.

Do not expose individual customer transcripts for ordinary market analysis.

---

# 24.88 Sensitive profiling guardrail

Do not segment market demand based on inferred race, religion, health status, or other sensitive personal attributes for marketing.

Use legitimate factors such as:

service need  
language preference  
location/service area  
timing  
channel  
customer-stated priorities.

---

# 24.89 Explainability

Each market insight should show:

```text
why detected
sample size
period
sources
trend
confidence
```

Example:

```text
INSIGHT
Weekend physiotherapy demand rising

Evidence:
430 unique customers
+31% vs prior 30 days
3 acquisition channels
confidence HIGH
```

---

# 24.90 Market insight QA

Human analyst samples supporting records before major investment decision.

Especially for:

new service launches  
pricing changes  
location expansion.

AI should accelerate research, not eliminate validation.

---

# 24.91 Opportunity experiment loop

```text
Insight
 ↓
Hypothesis
 ↓
Pilot
 ↓
Campaign
 ↓
Measure
 ↓
Compare
 ↓
Scale / Modify / Stop
```

Example:

Hypothesis:

Saturday physio capacity increases conversion.

Pilot:

two Saturdays.

Measure:

utilization  
booking  
margin  
CSAT.

---

# 24.92 Market intelligence maturity

### Level 1

Manual reports.

### Level 2

Automated VOC classification.

### Level 3

Trend and service-gap detection.

### Level 4

Opportunity scoring + forecasting.

### Level 5

Closed-loop experimentation and strategy recommendations.

Target Level 2–3 for MVP; grow based on data volume.

---

```text
MARKET OPPORTUNITY

DEMAND
430 unique requests / month

+31% vs previous 30 days

HIGH-INTENT
72%

CURRENT CAPACITY
Insufficient

PRIMARY CUSTOMER PAIN
No suitable weekend/evening availability

MAIN OBJECTION
Schedule, not price

LANGUAGE MIX
English / Hindi / Punjabi

COMPETITOR SIGNAL
Two competitors frequently mentioned for weekend availability

SERVICE GAP
CAPACITY_GAP

OPPORTUNITY SCORE
92/100

CONFIDENCE
HIGH

RECOMMENDED EXPERIMENT
Pilot additional Saturday slots for four weeks

MEASURE
Utilization
Booking conversion
Margin
CSAT
Cancellation rate
```

The next phase is **Phase 25 — FinAI / FinOps + Unit Economics**, where we build call-level cost accounting, telephony/STT/TTS/LLM/provider costs, budget controls, route economics, CAC, cost per booking/customer, gross margin, ROI, forecast, anomaly detection, scenario modeling, cost optimization, and provider/model trade-off analysis.

# Phase 25 — FinAI / FinOps + Unit Economics + Budget & Cost Optimization

This phase turns the voice-agent platform into a financially controlled system. The objective is not merely to know the monthly cloud bill. It is to understand the economics of every call, campaign, provider route, service, customer journey, booking, and conversion.

> **FinAI answers: What did this action cost, what outcome did it produce, was the spend justified, and how should the platform optimize quality versus cost?**

## 25.1 Target architecture

```text
Telephony
STT
TTS
LLM
Voice Platform
RAG
Workflow
CRM/API
Storage
Observability
SMS/Email
Human Support
     ↓
Cost Events
     ↓
FinAI Cost Ledger
     ↓
Call-Level Cost
     ↓
Journey / Campaign Cost
     ↓
Customer Acquisition Cost
     ↓
Revenue / Margin
     ↓
Unit Economics
     ↓
BudgetAI
     ↓
Cost Anomaly + Forecast
     ↓
RouteAI / CampaignAI / Management
```

## 25.2 Cost categories

Track costs separately instead of storing one generic `call_cost`.

| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| Telephony | carrier minutes, phone numbers, SIP |
| Voice platform | Retell/Vapi/Bolna/etc. |
| STT | speech recognition |
| TTS | speech synthesis |
| LLM | input/output tokens |
| Realtime model | audio/token usage |
| RAG | embeddings/vector/search |
| Tools | paid APIs |
| Workflow | Temporal/cloud/n8n infrastructure |
| Storage | audio/transcripts/logs |
| Messaging | SMS, WhatsApp, email |
| Observability | logs/traces/metrics |
| Human | escalations/manual review |
| Cloud | CPU/GPU/database/network |
| Support | operational overhead |

## 25.3 Cost event model

Every chargeable operation produces a canonical event:

```text
COST_EVENT

cost_event_id
tenant_id
customer_id
call_id
campaign_id
journey_id

component
provider

usage_quantity
usage_unit

unit_rate
currency

estimated_cost
actual_cost

pricing_version
timestamp
```

Examples:

```text
STT
82 seconds
$X/min

LLM
3,412 input tokens
527 output tokens

SMS
1 message

Telephony
4.6 minutes
```

## 25.4 Call-level cost ledger

For every call:

```text
CALL_COST

telephony
voice_platform
STT
LLM
TTS
RAG
tool_API
recording
storage
monitoring

TOTAL
```

Example:

```text
CALL-90182

Telephony          $0.09
Voice platform     $0.26
STT                $0.07
LLM                $0.05
TTS                $0.08
Tools              $0.01
Observability      $0.02
--------------------------------
TOTAL              $0.58
```

The exact rates come from provider pricing contracts.

## 25.5 Cost attribution hierarchy

You should be able to aggregate:

```text
Cost Event
  ↓
Turn
  ↓
Call
  ↓
Customer
  ↓
Journey
  ↓
Campaign
  ↓
Service
  ↓
Tenant
```

Then answer:

> Which campaigns are expensive?

> Which services require the longest calls?

> Which provider combination gives the best cost per booking?

## 25.6 Cost per call is not enough

Important KPIs:

```text
Cost / Dial Attempt
Cost / Connected Call
Cost / Qualified Lead
Cost / Recommendation
Cost / Booking
Cost / Attended Appointment
Cost / Converted Customer
```

A cheap call can be commercially expensive if it rarely succeeds.

## 25.7 Unit economics funnel

Example:

```text
1,000 Leads
 ↓
850 Callable
 ↓
650 Dialed
 ↓
420 Connected
 ↓
280 Qualified
 ↓
140 Booked
 ↓
115 Attended
 ↓
90 Converted Customers
```

Suppose total acquisition + voice spend:

```text
$4,500
```

Then:

```text
Cost / Lead       = $4.50
Cost / Connect    = $10.71
Cost / Booking    = $32.14
CAC               = $50.00
```

These are far more useful than API cost/minute alone.

## 25.8 Revenue model

Track:

```text
gross_revenue
discount
refund
net_revenue
```

Then connect customer conversion to revenue.

For service businesses also track:

appointment value  
package value  
repeat revenue.

## 25.9 Contribution margin

Conceptually:

```text
Contribution Margin =
Revenue
- Variable Service Cost
- Acquisition Cost
- Voice AI Cost
- Messaging Cost
```

Do not call revenue “profit.”

## 25.10 Gross margin by acquisition channel

Example:

| Channel | CAC | Avg Revenue | Contribution |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Referral | $28 | $380 | Strong |
| Google | $52 | $350 | Strong |
| Instagram | $78 | $290 | Moderate |
| Cold outbound | $105 | $280 | Weak |

This can materially change marketing strategy.

## 25.11 Campaign ROI

Conceptually:

```text
ROI =
Attributed Contribution - Campaign Cost
---------------------------------------
Campaign Cost
```

Clearly identify whether revenue attribution is:

last-touch  
assisted  
experimental/causal.

## 25.12 Cost per provider route

Route object:

```text
Voice Platform
+
Telephony
+
STT
+
LLM
+
TTS
```

Track whole-route economics.

Example:

| Route | Cost/min | Booking % | Cost/Booking |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | $0.10 | 26% | $22 |
| B | $0.14 | 42% | $16 |
| C | $0.07 | 17% | $27 |

Route B is more expensive per minute but cheaper per booking.

## 25.13 Quality-adjusted economics

Don't optimize only cost.

Create:

```text
Quality Adjusted Route Score =
Business Outcome
× Voice Quality
× Reliability
× Compliance
÷ Cost
```

A route with poor critical-entity accuracy should not win merely because it saves $0.03/minute.

## 25.14 Risk-adjusted economics

Extend further:

```text
Risk-Adjusted Value =
Expected Contribution
- Expected Failure Cost
- Expected Complaint Cost
- Risk Penalty
```

This integrates FinAI with RiskAI.

## 25.15 Cost of quality failure

Measure financial impact of:

wrong appointment  
duplicate booking  
failed transfer  
customer complaint  
provider outage.

Example:

```text
20 incorrect bookings
× estimated recovery cost
+
lost revenue
+
manual support
```

Quality problems have economic consequences.

## 25.16 Cost of human escalation

Human transfers are not free.

Track:

```text
transfer_count
average_human_minutes
human_cost/min
```

Then:

```text
human_escalation_cost
```

This helps identify which AI deficiencies generate manual workload.

## 25.17 Automation savings

Compare:

```text
Human-only baseline
vs
AI-assisted
```

Metrics:

human hours avoided  
cost avoided  
response-time improvement  
incremental bookings.

Do not claim “AI saved X” without a baseline.

## 25.18 Budget hierarchy

Support budgets at:

```text
Platform
Tenant
Brand
Campaign
Channel
Provider
Agent
Day
Month
```

Example:

```text
Tenant daily budget      $1,000
Campaign budget            $300
Voice-provider limit       $500
```

## 25.19 Budget service

Before expensive actions:

```text
CampaignAI
 ↓
BudgetAI
 ↓
ALLOW / WARN / HOLD / BLOCK
```

Response:

```text
remaining_budget
estimated_action_cost
budget_status
```

## 25.20 Cost reservation

For high concurrency, budget should be reserved before calls start.

```text
Call estimated = $0.60

100 simultaneous calls
→ reserve $60
```

After call:

```text
actual cost = $53
release $7
```

Otherwise concurrency can overspend before actual invoices arrive.

## 25.21 Budget thresholds

Example:

```text
70% → informational
85% → warning
95% → restrict lower-priority campaigns
100% → stop new discretionary calls
```

Transactional/customer-requested calls can follow separate policy.

## 25.22 Do not block critical service blindly

Budget controls should distinguish:

general marketing

from:

customer-requested callbacks  
appointment-related workflows.

Business policy determines priority.

## 25.23 Provider spend caps

Set:

```text
provider_daily_cap
provider_monthly_cap
```

Useful if a routing bug suddenly sends 100% traffic to an expensive provider.

## 25.24 Model-cost controls

LLM selection can have cost tiers:

```text
FAST_LOW_COST
STANDARD
PREMIUM
```

Route simple FAQ turns to cheaper approved models where quality permits.

Use premium models for genuinely difficult cases.

## 25.25 Dynamic model routing

Example:

```text
Simple:
"What are your hours?"
→ cheaper model / deterministic retrieval

Complex:
Customer has multiple needs and constraints
→ stronger model
```

This can reduce cost without degrading quality.

## 25.26 RAG cost optimization

Avoid embedding/retrieving unnecessarily.

For structured facts:

price  
availability  
appointments

use APIs.

RAG for:

approved informational knowledge.

This improves accuracy and cost.

## 25.27 Conversation-length economics

Track:

```text
average duration
duration by outcome
duration by agent
duration by language
```

Example:

Agent V18:

4.2 min average.

Agent V19:

6.8 min.

If conversion unchanged, V19 may be economically worse.

## 25.28 Long-call anomaly

Detect calls far above expected duration.

Potential causes:

conversation loop  
STT misunderstanding  
customer needs human  
tool timeout.

FinAI sends signal to ObserveAI/QualityAI.

## 25.29 Token monitoring

Per call:

```text
input_tokens
output_tokens
cached_tokens
tool-related tokens
```

Break down by state:

greeting  
discovery  
RAG  
booking.

This helps optimize prompt size.

## 25.30 Prompt cost

A massive system prompt repeated on every turn can become expensive.

Track:

```text
static_prompt_tokens
dynamic_context_tokens
conversation_history_tokens
```

Optimize with:

structured state  
summary memory  
context minimization.

## 25.31 Context cost control

Do not send entire transcript every turn.

Use:

```text
recent turns
+
structured state
+
relevant memory
```

This reduces both cost and distraction.

## 25.32 Cache economics

Use model/provider caching where available and appropriate.

Track:

```text
cache_hit_rate
cost_saved
latency_saved
```

But never cache customer-specific responses across customers incorrectly.

## 25.33 Storage cost

Recordings can become expensive at scale.

Track:

```text
recording GB
transcript GB
trace GB
log GB
```

Forecast:

30 days  
90 days  
1 year.

Retention policy is both privacy and FinOps.

## 25.34 Observability cost

Voice AI creates enormous telemetry.

Track:

logs  
traces  
metrics cardinality.

Use:

sampling  
retention tiers  
aggregation.

Do not spend more on observability than on the AI itself without intentional reason.

## 25.35 Phone-number cost

Track:

number rental  
number registration  
unused numbers.

Remove or reassign unused inventory.

## 25.36 SMS/email economics

Track:

cost per message  
delivery rate  
response  
conversion.

Example:

SMS may cost more than email but produce far more conversions.

Optimize by outcome.

## 25.37 Cost anomaly detection

Monitor:

```text
cost/min
cost/call
daily spend
provider spend
LLM tokens
call duration
```

Compare with rolling baseline.

Example:

```text
Normal cost/call = $0.62
Today = $1.08
```

Trigger investigation.

## 25.38 Cost anomaly RCA

Possible causes:

provider pricing change  
routing bug  
premium model usage  
longer conversations  
retry storm  
duplicate calls  
telephony fraud.

Correlate with deployment/config changes.

## 25.39 FinOps alerts

Examples:

```text
Daily spend > forecast × 1.25
Cost/booking > target
Provider spend > cap
LLM tokens/call > baseline × 2
Average call duration > threshold
```

## 25.40 Forecasting

Forecast:

call volume  
telephony minutes  
LLM tokens  
SMS volume  
storage  
monthly spend.

Start with historical averages/seasonality.

Later use time-series forecasting.

## 25.41 Monthly cost forecast

```text
Expected leads
× contact rate
× attempts
× average call duration
× route cost
+
messaging
+
storage
+
infrastructure
```

Make assumptions explicit.

## 25.42 Scenario planner

Support:

```text
10k calls/month
50k
100k
500k
1M
```

For each calculate:

provider cost  
infrastructure  
human escalations  
storage.

This is essential before scaling.

## 25.43 Scenario — provider change

Example:

```text
Provider A:
$0.11/min
quality 94

Provider B:
$0.07/min
quality 86
```

Scenario model should estimate:

cost savings

versus:

possible lower conversion and higher correction/support cost.

## 25.44 Break-even analysis

If better-quality provider costs an extra:

```text
$0.05/call
```

but increases booking enough to generate:

```text
+$1.20 expected contribution/call
```

it's clearly economically better.

## 25.45 Sensitivity analysis

Vary:

conversion  
call duration  
provider rate  
revenue/customer.

Show how unit economics change.

This is more useful than relying on one forecast.

## 25.46 CAC

Define carefully:

```text
CAC =
Marketing + Sales + Voice AI attributable acquisition cost
-----------------------------------------------------------
New customers
```

Decide whether fixed payroll/platform costs are included.

Use consistent definition.

## 25.47 LTV

For repeat-service business:

```text
LTV =
Expected customer contribution over relationship
```

Not merely first appointment revenue.

Avoid overly optimistic long-term assumptions.

## 25.48 LTV:CAC

Useful high-level metric:

```text
LTV / CAC
```

But calculate from real retention data once available.

## 25.49 Payback period

Measure how long customer contribution takes to recover CAC.

Important for cash planning.

## 25.50 Cohort economics

Analyze customers acquired:

January  
February  
March.

Track:

revenue  
repeat bookings  
retention  
profitability.

Avoid using only initial conversion.

## 25.51 Service-level economics

Some services may have:

high conversion  
low margin.

Others:

lower volume  
higher margin.

Report both demand and contribution.

## 25.52 Customer-segment economics

Analyze:

high-intent  
researcher  
reactivation  
corporate.

Metrics:

CAC  
conversion  
revenue  
human effort.

Do not use economics to unfairly restrict legitimate service access.

## 25.53 Campaign profitability

Campaign:

```text
Spend
+
Voice
+
Messaging
+
Human support
```

versus:

attributed contribution.

Output:

```text
PROFITABLE
MARGINAL
LOSS-MAKING
```

with confidence/attribution assumptions.

## 25.54 Stop-loss control

CampaignAI can automatically pause discretionary campaign if:

```text
cost/booking exceeds ceiling
AND
minimum sample size reached
```

Avoid stopping after only three calls.

## 25.55 Minimum sample requirement

A new route:

1 booking from 2 calls

looks amazing.

Do not optimize from tiny samples.

Require:

minimum calls/outcomes/confidence.

## 25.56 Experiment economics

A/B test:

Script A vs B.

Compare:

conversion  
duration  
cost  
complaints.

Winner should maximize **risk-adjusted contribution**, not conversion alone.

## 25.57 Quality-cost frontier

Visualize routes:

```text
Quality ↑

    B
       C
 A

──────────── Cost →
```

Choose Pareto-efficient routes rather than one simplistic winner.

## 25.58 Cost allocation

Shared infrastructure:

Kubernetes  
database  
observability.

Allocate by:

calls  
tokens  
tenant usage  
storage.

Use transparent methodology.

## 25.59 Tenant billing

For SaaS:

calculate:

```text
base fee
+
usage
+
premium features
+
human support
```

Keep internal cost separate from customer-facing pricing.

## 25.60 Billing metering

Create immutable usage events:

```text
USAGE_EVENT

tenant
service
quantity
unit
timestamp
```

Examples:

voice minutes  
AI calls  
SMS  
storage.

Useful for invoicing and margin analysis.

## 25.61 Usage reconciliation

Compare:

your metering

with:

provider invoice.

Detect billing discrepancies.

## 25.62 Provider invoice reconciliation

Process:

```text
Internal usage
      ↓
Provider invoice
      ↓
Match
      ↓
Variance
```

Flag:

unexpected charges  
duplicate billing  
rate change.

## 25.63 Contract rate management

Store provider pricing versions:

```text
provider
effective_date
unit_rate
volume_discount
```

Do not hardcode current pricing throughout applications.

## 25.64 Volume discounts

At scale:

provider A may become cheaper after 100k minutes.

Scenario planner should account for tiered pricing.

## 25.65 Currency handling

If providers bill USD but customers/reports use CAD:

store:

original currency  
FX rate used  
converted amount.

Keep rate/date provenance.

## 25.66 Tax handling

Separate:

provider tax  
customer-facing tax  
net cost.

Avoid mixing tax-inclusive and tax-exclusive metrics.

## 25.67 Cost API

Recommended:

```text
POST /cost/events

GET /calls/{id}/cost
GET /campaigns/{id}/economics

GET /finops/provider-costs
GET /finops/unit-economics

POST /finops/forecast
POST /finops/scenario
```

```text
POST /budget/check
POST /budget/reserve
```

Publish:

```text
cost.recorded

cost.anomaly_detected
forecast.updated
```

Main panels:

**Forecast**

**Cost by provider**

## 25.71 Provider economics dashboard

Example:

| Route | Spend | Calls | Quality | Booking | Cost/Booking |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A | $6,000 | 50k | 94 | 35% | $17 |
| B | $4,500 | 50k | 86 | 22% | $20 |

This is far more useful than vendor price sheets.

## 25.72 Executive financial dashboard

```text
Monthly AI/Voice Spend
Customer Acquisition Spend
Appointments
Customers
Revenue
Contribution Margin
CAC
Cost/Booking
LTV:CAC
ROI
```

## 25.73 Data quality

If provider billing data is delayed:

mark:

```text
COST_STATUS = ESTIMATED
```

When final:

```text
ACTUAL
```

Do not present estimates as settled actual costs.

## 25.74 Estimated vs actual

Store:

```text
estimated_cost
actual_cost
variance
```

Use actual for final financial reporting.

## 25.75 Testing

Test:

usage calculations  
rounding  
currency  
budget reservation  
concurrent spend  
provider rate versioning  
invoice reconciliation.

## 25.76 Concurrency edge case

Two hundred workers all see:

```text
budget remaining = $50
```

and each starts a $1 call.

You overspend.

Fix with transactional reservation/atomic budget counters.

## 25.77 Edge case — provider API timeout

Uncertain whether charge occurred.

Cost ledger should reconcile later rather than immediately duplicating charge estimates.

## 25.78 Edge case — duplicate call

If duplicate call accidentally happens:

record real cost.

FinAI shouldn't hide it.

QualityAI separately flags operational defect.

## 25.79 Edge case — free trial credits

Track:

gross vendor usage cost

and:

net invoiced cost after credits.

This prevents unrealistic economics once credits disappear.

## 25.80 Edge case — annual contract

Monthly cash invoice may differ from per-call economic cost.

Maintain:

cash accounting view

and:

usage/unit-economic view.

## 25.81 Edge case — human cost missing

If calls frequently transfer to humans but labor isn't included, AI economics look artificially good.

Include manual effort where material.

## 25.82 Edge case — high conversion but cancellation

Do not calculate only:

cost/booked appointment.

Also calculate:

cost/attended appointment  
cost/real customer.

## 25.83 Edge case — one expensive outlier call

Use:

average  
median  
P95.

One 40-minute call can distort averages.

## 25.84 Edge case — cost saving harms quality

New route saves 20%

but:

booking mismatch doubles.

RiskAI + QualityAI should block optimization.

## 25.85 FinAI optimization hierarchy

Optimize in this order:

```text
Safety / Policy
      ↓
Task Correctness
      ↓
Customer Experience
      ↓
Reliability
      ↓
Business Outcome
      ↓
Cost
```

Cost is important, but never first.

## 25.86 Cost optimization backlog

Examples:

reduce prompt tokens  
use deterministic APIs  
shorter responses  
cache static information  
route simple turns to cheaper models  
reduce unnecessary recording  
optimize trace retention  
provider negotiation.

Each optimization should measure quality impact.

## 25.87 FinAI + RouteAI

RouteAI receives:

```text
quality
health
risk
cost
capacity
```

and chooses best approved route.

FinAI supplies the economic component.

## 25.88 FinAI + CampaignAI

CampaignAI can prioritize campaigns using:

expected contribution  
budget  
capacity.

But consent/policy always overrides financial optimization.

## 25.89 FinAI + MarketAI

Market opportunity:

high demand

but:

service margin poor.

MarketAI + FinAI together provide a more realistic opportunity score.

## 25.90 FinAI + GovernAI

Cost model changes can be governed artifacts:

pricing tables  
budget policies  
provider rate cards.

Track versions and approvals.

# Phase 26 — MLOps + LLMOps + VoiceOps Release Engineering

This phase operationalizes **models, prompts, agents, voice routes, tools, policies, datasets, and evaluations** as versioned production artifacts.

The goal is:

> **Every AI/voice change must be reproducible, testable, promotable, observable, reversible, and traceable from source code to production behavior.**

## 26.1 Target release architecture

```text
Developer / AI Engineer
        ↓
Git Repository
        ↓
CI Pipeline
        ↓
Unit + Integration + Security Tests
        ↓
AI Evaluation Suite
        ↓
Voice / Audio Regression
        ↓
Policy + ResponsibleAI Gates
        ↓
Artifact Registry
        ↓
DEV
        ↓
QA
        ↓
STAGING
        ↓
CANARY
        ↓
PRODUCTION
        ↓
ObserveAI / QualityAI / RiskAI
        ↓
Continue / Rollback / Suspend
```

---

## 26.2 Assets that need release management

Treat all of these as deployable/versioned assets:

| Asset | Example |
|---|---|
| Application code | Voice orchestration service |
| Agent | PHYSIO-HINDI-v6 |
| Prompt | PHYSIO-DISCOVERY-v18 |
| LLM config | GPT/Claude/Gemini model profile |
| STT config | Hindi speech profile |
| TTS voice | Hindi conversational voice |
| RAG pipeline | Retriever/reranker configuration |
| Knowledge base | Clinic KB v13 |
| Score model | Conversion-XGB-v4 |
| Recommendation model | Ranker-v3 |
| NextAI rules | NBA-rules-v7 |
| Policy | CALL-POLICY-v5 |
| Tools | BOOK_APPOINTMENT-v4 |
| Workflow | CALLBACK-FLOW-v8 |
| Route policy | VOICE-ROUTE-v5 |
| Test dataset | Golden Calls v12 |

A change in any of these can affect production behavior.

---

# 26.3 Repository structure

A clean monorepo could look like:

```text
/platform
    /services
        /campaign
        /policy
        /voice-gateway
        /conversation
        /tool-gateway
        /reporting

    /agents
        /physio
        /dental
        /massage

    /prompts
        /global
        /languages
        /states

    /policies
    /workflows

    /evals
        /conversation
        /voice
        /rag
        /policy
        /security

    /datasets
        /manifests

    /infra
        /terraform
        /k8s

    /governance
        /model-cards
        /agent-cards
        /risk
```

Keep production artifacts source-controlled where practical.

---

# 26.4 Branch strategy

For an early team:

```text
main
feature/*
hotfix/*
```

Avoid excessively complex branching.

Production deployments should originate from reviewed, protected branches/tags.

---

# 26.5 Pull-request gates

Every PR should run relevant checks:

```text
Lint
Type check
Unit tests
Integration tests
Security scan
Secret scan
Dependency scan
Prompt/eval tests
Policy tests
```

Then require code review.

---

# 26.6 Prompt changes are code changes

Example:

```text
PHYSIO_PROMPT_v17
        ↓
sentence changed
        ↓
v18
```

Do not edit the production prompt directly in a provider console.

Change:

```text
Git
→ PR
→ evaluations
→ approval
→ deployment
```

Provider console should be synchronized from your release pipeline where possible.

---

# 26.7 Agent package

Create a canonical agent package:

```text
agent.yaml

agent_id
version
purpose

prompt_version
model_profile

languages[]

toolset[]

knowledge_version
policy_profile

voice_profile
route_profile

quality_thresholds
```

This package becomes the deployable business definition.

---

# 26.8 Example agent manifest

```yaml
agent_id: PHYSIO-HINDI
version: 6

prompt: PHYSIO-DISCOVERY-v18

languages:
  - hi
  - en

tools:
  - AVAILABILITY-v4
  - BOOKING-v4
  - SMS-v2

policy: HEALTHCARE-VOICE-v5
knowledge: PHYSIO-KB-v13
route: HINDI-HEALTHCARE-v4
```

Avoid manual configuration scattered across vendor consoles.

---

# 26.9 Environment separation

Maintain:

```text
DEV
QA
STAGING
PRODUCTION
```

Separate:

credentials  
databases  
phone numbers  
webhooks  
provider accounts/agents where possible.

Never accidentally run automated staging campaigns against real customers.

---

# 26.10 Configuration management

Separate:

```text
CODE
CONFIGURATION
SECRETS
```

Code:

Git.

Config:

versioned configuration system.

Secrets:

Vault / cloud secret manager.

Do not bake credentials into agent manifests.

---

# 26.11 Artifact registry

Store immutable release artifacts.

Examples:

```text
Docker images
Model binaries
Prompt bundles
Agent manifests
Evaluation reports
SBOMs
```

Possible:

GitHub Container Registry  
AWS ECR  
Azure ACR  
GCP Artifact Registry.

---

# 26.12 Semantic versioning

For services:

```text
2.4.1
```

For agent assets, use clear version numbers.

Example:

```text
PHYSIO-HINDI-v18
```

Never use:

```text
physio-final-final2
```

---

# 26.13 Build reproducibility

Given:

```text
Git commit
Artifact version
Configuration version
```

you should be able to reconstruct the deployed system.

Store:

```text
git_sha
build_id
container_digest
dependency_lock
```

---

# 26.14 Dependency pinning

Pin:

Python packages  
Node packages  
voice SDKs  
LLM SDKs.

Use lock files.

An unplanned SDK upgrade can change production behavior.

---

# 26.15 SBOM

Generate Software Bill of Materials.

Track:

libraries  
versions  
licenses.

Useful for supply-chain security and incident response.

Tools:

Syft  
CycloneDX.

---

# 26.16 CI pipeline

Typical:

```text
Checkout
 ↓
Install dependencies
 ↓
Lint
 ↓
Unit
 ↓
Static analysis
 ↓
Security
 ↓
Build
 ↓
Package
 ↓
Component tests
 ↓
Publish artifact
```

---

# 26.17 AI evaluation pipeline

After normal CI:

```text
Agent Artifact
     ↓
Golden Conversations
     ↓
RAG Tests
     ↓
Tool Tests
     ↓
DNC/Policy
     ↓
ResponsibleAI
     ↓
Multilingual
     ↓
Voice Benchmark
```

Output:

```text
PASS / FAIL
```

---

# 26.18 Evaluation thresholds

Example:

```text
DNC critical cases         100%
Booking integrity          100%
Tool-selection accuracy    >= target
Hindi critical entities    >= target
Hallucination rate         <= limit
P95 latency                <= SLO
```

Exact values should be established from business/risk requirements.

---

# 26.19 Severity-aware gates

A single cosmetic wording failure may not block release.

A single:

```text
wrong booking
DNC failure
cross-tenant leakage
unsafe clinical claim
```

should.

Use severity-aware gating.

---

# 26.20 Environment promotion

Do not rebuild artifact for every environment.

Better:

```text
Build once
 ↓
DEV
 ↓
QA
 ↓
STAGING
 ↓
PRODUCTION
```

Promote the **same immutable artifact**.

Only environment configuration changes.

---

# 26.21 Development deployment

DEV can allow:

mock services  
synthetic customers  
verbose logging.

Useful for rapid iteration.

---

# 26.22 QA deployment

QA uses:

synthetic data  
provider sandbox  
test telephony.

Automated scenario bank runs continuously.

---

# 26.23 Staging

Staging should resemble production:

same architecture  
similar scaling/configuration  
isolated data.

Run:

end-to-end calls  
load tests  
chaos tests  
security tests.

---

# 26.24 Production canary

Never push major Voice AI change immediately to 100%.

Example:

```text
1%
→ 5%
→ 20%
→ 50%
→ 100%
```

Each stage evaluates:

quality  
latency  
booking  
complaints  
DNC  
cost.

---

# 26.25 Canary traffic segmentation

Better than random-only canary:

start with:

internal/synthetic traffic  
low-risk use cases  
one tenant  
one language.

Then expand.

---

# 26.26 Blue/green deployment

Maintain:

```text
BLUE = current
GREEN = candidate
```

Traffic switching allows rapid rollback.

Very useful for orchestration services.

---

# 26.27 Agent-level blue/green

Example:

```text
PHYSIO-HINDI-v17
PHYSIO-HINDI-v18
```

Route 5% to v18.

Compare outcomes.

No infrastructure redeployment necessarily required.

---

# 26.28 Shadow deployment

Candidate model/NextAI can evaluate live traffic without controlling actions.

```text
Production Decision
      ↓
Champion
      ↓
Action

same context
      ↓
Challenger
      ↓
Shadow prediction only
```

Compare before promotion.

---

# 26.29 Champion / challenger

Useful for:

ScoreAI  
RecommendAI  
RouteAI  
NextAI.

Example:

```text
Champion:
Logistic Regression v4

Challenger:
XGBoost v2
```

Compare actual downstream metrics.

---

# 26.30 Model registry

Use MLflow or equivalent.

Track:

```text
model
version
training dataset
features
hyperparameters
metrics
status
```

Stages:

```text
EXPERIMENTAL
VALIDATED
STAGING
PRODUCTION
ARCHIVED
```

---

# 26.31 Experiment tracking

Track every training run:

```text
dataset version
code version
parameters
metrics
artifacts
```

This prevents “which model produced this?” problems.

---

# 26.32 Feature registry

For ScoreAI:

```text
feature_name
definition
source
version
owner
```

Example:

```text
days_since_last_contact_v2
```

Feature changes can materially change model behavior.

---

# 26.33 Point-in-time correctness

When training conversion models:

features must reflect what was known **at decision time**.

Avoid leakage from future events.

Build feature snapshots.

---

# 26.34 Data versioning

Track:

```text
dataset_id
snapshot_date
query/version
schema_version
```

Possible tools:

DVC  
lakehouse time travel  
Delta/Iceberg versioning.

---

# 26.35 Training pipeline

Example:

```text
Data validation
 ↓
Feature generation
 ↓
Train
 ↓
Evaluate
 ↓
Bias/fairness
 ↓
Calibration
 ↓
Model card
 ↓
Registry
```

Never promote directly from notebook to production.

---

# 26.36 Retraining trigger

Possible triggers:

scheduled  
new data volume  
performance degradation  
drift  
business change.

Don't retrain merely because the calendar says so if data/model hasn't materially changed.

---

# 26.37 Drift-triggered workflow

```text
ObserveAI
 ↓
Performance Drift
 ↓
Model Review
 ↓
Retraining
 ↓
Offline Evaluation
 ↓
Shadow
 ↓
Canary
 ↓
Production
```

Never automatically retrain + deploy without gates for higher-risk use cases.

---

# 26.38 PromptOps

Prompts need their own pipeline.

Track:

```text
prompt
version
model compatibility
language
evaluation
```

Prompt V20 might work with Model A but degrade with Model B.

Test combinations.

---

# 26.39 Prompt regression suite

Test:

opening  
need discovery  
price  
booking  
DNC  
human request  
language switch  
competitor question  
clinical question.

Every prompt release reruns them.

---

# 26.40 VoiceOps

Voice layer needs release management for:

STT  
TTS  
VAD  
turn-taking  
barge-in  
provider routing.

A small VAD change can dramatically affect UX.

---

# 26.41 Voice profile version

Example:

```text
HINDI-VOICE-v8
```

contains:

```text
TTS provider
voice ID
speed
pitch where supported
pronunciation dictionary
```

Benchmark before promotion.

---

# 26.42 Pronunciation dictionary versioning

Names/services may need corrections.

Store:

```text
PRONUNCIATION-HI-v12
```

Test:

clinic names  
staff names  
addresses  
medical/service vocabulary.

---

# 26.43 STT routing update

New STT provider may perform better in Hindi.

Route change:

```text
HINDI-STT-v6 → v7
```

must trigger:

audio benchmark  
entity tests  
latency  
cost evaluation.

---

# 26.44 Provider release dependency

Vendors may release updates outside your control.

Create:

```text
VENDOR_CHANGE_EVENT
```

when you detect:

model version update  
SDK change  
quality drift.

Rerun critical benchmark.

---

# 26.45 External model version pinning

Where APIs permit, pin explicit model versions.

Avoid ambiguous:

```text
latest
```

for critical workloads.

If pinning unavailable, runtime monitoring becomes even more important.

---

# 26.46 LLM fallback matrix

Define approved fallbacks.

```text
Primary Model A
 ↓ failure
Model B
 ↓ failure
Model C
```

But fallback model must have:

approved prompt compatibility  
quality threshold  
data policy.

---

# 26.47 Fallback testing

Test:

model timeout  
rate limit  
provider outage.

Verify:

conversation state preserved  
tools still work  
customer does not receive contradictory answers.

---

# 26.48 Rollback triggers

Automatic or human rollback if:

```text
critical booking error
DNC violation
hallucination spike
P95 latency regression
complaint spike
tool failure increase
```

Use minimum sample logic for noncritical statistical regressions.

---

# 26.49 Rollback scope

Rollback can target:

```text
Agent
Prompt
Model
Tool
Provider
Voice profile
Policy
Application
```

Avoid full-platform rollback when one asset is broken.

---

# 26.50 Rollback verification

After rollback:

run synthetic tests.

Verify:

old version actually receiving traffic.

Do not assume deployment command means recovery succeeded.

---

# 26.51 Configuration drift

Continuously compare:

```text
Approved manifest
vs
Runtime configuration
```

Detect:

manual provider-console edits  
unauthorized prompt changes  
tool changes.

Alert GovernAI.

---

# 26.52 Infrastructure as Code

Use Terraform/OpenTofu.

Manage:

network  
Kubernetes  
databases  
queues  
secrets references  
monitoring.

Avoid critical production infrastructure created manually.

---

# 26.53 Kubernetes deployment

If using K8s:

```text
Deployment
Service
HPA
PDB
NetworkPolicy
ConfigMap
Secret references
```

Configure resource limits.

---

# 26.54 Autoscaling

Scale based on:

CPU  
queue depth  
active calls  
workflow backlog.

For voice:

active sessions/concurrency may be more useful than CPU alone.

---

# 26.55 Backpressure

If demand exceeds provider/platform capacity:

```text
queue
throttle
reschedule
```

Don't overload upstream/downstream systems.

---

# 26.56 Capacity release tests

Before large campaign:

simulate expected concurrency.

Example:

```text
Normal = 100 calls
Campaign = 1,000 concurrent
```

Validate:

telephony  
voice provider  
backend  
booking APIs.

---

# 26.57 Performance regression

Compare candidate:

```text
P50
P95
P99
```

with production baseline.

Do not approve if performance materially worsens without justification.

---

# 26.58 Deployment observability

Annotate dashboards with:

```text
deployment_id
agent_version
prompt_version
model_version
```

Then correlate quality shifts with release.

---

# 26.59 Release manifest

Every release:

```text
release_id
git_sha

service_versions
agent_versions
prompt_versions
model_versions
policy_versions
tool_versions

deployment_time
approver
```

This becomes the full production snapshot.

---

# 26.60 Release evidence package

Attach:

test results  
security scans  
AI eval  
risk evaluation  
ResponsibleAI status  
performance results  
rollback plan.

GovernAI uses this.

---

# 26.61 Automated release gate

Concept:

```text
if critical_tests_pass
and security_pass
and quality_pass
and governance_approved
and risk_acceptable:
    deploy
else:
    block
```

This should be executable policy, not an email checklist.

---

# 26.62 Hotfix process

For P0/P1:

```text
Issue
 ↓
Hotfix branch
 ↓
Focused tests
 ↓
Critical regression
 ↓
Emergency approval
 ↓
Canary
 ↓
Production
 ↓
Post-incident review
```

Don't skip safety tests completely.

---

# 26.63 Database migration

Use versioned migrations:

Alembic  
Flyway  
Liquibase.

Need:

forward migration  
backward compatibility where possible  
rollback/repair plan.

---

# 26.64 Expand/contract pattern

For zero/low downtime schema changes:

```text
Add new field
 ↓
deploy compatible code
 ↓
migrate data
 ↓
switch reads
 ↓
remove old field later
```

Avoid breaking live call workflows.

---

# 26.65 API versioning

Tool APIs need compatibility:

```text
/v1/book
/v2/book
```

or schema-version strategy.

Agents shouldn't suddenly fail when tool contract changes.

---

# 26.66 Contract-test gate

Before Tool v4 deployment:

every dependent agent contract is tested.

Pact/OpenAPI tests can help.

---

# 26.67 Event-schema versioning

Events:

```text
call.completed.v1
```

may evolve.

Use backward-compatible changes where possible.

Schema registry if Kafka scale warrants it.

---

# 26.68 Feature flagging

Use feature flags for:

new agent behavior  
new provider  
new NextAI rule  
new UI feature.

Enable by:

tenant  
campaign  
percentage.

Useful for controlled rollout.

---

# 26.69 Kill switch vs feature flag

Feature flag:

planned rollout control.

Kill switch:

emergency shutdown.

Do not confuse the two.

---

# 26.70 Deployment permissions

Roles:

```text
Developer
Reviewer
Release Manager
Governance Approver
Platform Operator
```

High-risk production deployments should not be unrestricted.

---

# 26.71 CI/CD secrets

Use workload identity where possible.

Do not store production secrets as plain repository CI variables if safer alternatives exist.

---

# 26.72 Supply-chain controls

Check:

signed commits/releases where appropriate  
signed container images  
artifact provenance.

Cosign/Sigstore can help.

---

# 26.73 Dependency vulnerability release gate

Critical exploitable dependency:

block release.

Low-risk informational CVE:

tracked remediation.

Use risk-based approach.

---

# 26.74 Environment promotion tests

Before each promotion run:

```text
smoke tests
dependency health
configuration validation
```

Staging → production additionally:

governance authorization.

---

# 26.75 Smoke test after production

Automatically verify:

health endpoint  
policy check  
synthetic call  
availability tool  
safe test transaction where possible.

If critical smoke test fails:

rollback/pause.

---

# 26.76 Synthetic production test

Use dedicated test numbers/customers.

Never accidentally perform booking against real customers.

---

# 26.77 Release scorecard

Example:

```text
RELEASE
PHYSIO-HINDI-v18

Functional       100%
Policy           100%
Booking          100%
Security         PASS
ResponsibleAI    PASS

Hindi Quality    95
Tool Accuracy    99.8
P95 Latency      1.1s

Open P0          0
Open P1          0

STATUS
CANARY APPROVED
```

---

# 26.78 Post-release verification

For initial production traffic compare:

candidate vs baseline:

quality  
booking  
DNC  
latency  
cost.

Continue only if within guardrails.

---

# 26.79 Release burn-in

First:

100 calls.

Then:

500.

Then:

5,000.

Progressive validation based on call volume can complement percentage rollout.

---

# 26.80 Model performance rollback

Suppose ScoreAI calibration deteriorates.

Could rollback only scoring model while keeping Voice Agent version unchanged.

Design components independently deployable.

---

# 26.81 Edge case — prompt rollback with changed tool schema

Old prompt may expect tool v3, current runtime uses v4.

Rollback manifests must preserve compatible dependency sets.

Do not rollback one artifact blindly.

---

# 26.82 Edge case — model removed by vendor

Fallback to preapproved alternative.

Trigger:

governance review  
benchmark  
migration.

Avoid discovering dependency only during outage.

---

# 26.83 Edge case — silent vendor behavior change

ObserveAI sees:

customer correction rate doubled.

No internal deployment.

Correlate with:

provider/model metadata.

Trigger vendor-change investigation.

---

# 26.84 Edge case — failed migration during active calls

Deploy schema changes using backward-compatible approach.

Never require all live calls to finish unless unavoidable.

---

# 26.85 Edge case — rollback after transactions executed

Rolling back software does not undo:

appointments  
SMS  
payments.

Reconciliation is separate from software rollback.

---

# 26.86 Edge case — CI green but voice quality bad

Text/unit tests can all pass while TTS/VAD feels terrible.

Therefore VoiceOps audio benchmark is mandatory for voice-affecting changes.

---

# 26.87 Edge case — offline model better, production worse

Possible causes:

data drift  
latency  
integration  
customer distribution.

Use shadow/canary before promotion.

---

# 26.88 Edge case — new version improves conversion but increases DNC

Release should fail guardrail even if business KPI improves.

Quality/Risk/ResponsibleAI take precedence.

---

# 26.89 MLOps dashboard

Show:

production models  
versions  
training dates  
metrics  
drift  
retraining status.

---

# 26.90 LLMOps dashboard

Show:

models  
prompt versions  
tokens  
quality  
hallucinations  
cost  
fallback rate.

---

# 26.91 VoiceOps dashboard

Show:

STT/TTS versions  
voice profiles  
latency  
critical entity accuracy  
barge-in  
provider health.

---

# 26.92 Release dashboard

```text
Releases today
Canaries active
Rollback events
Failed gates
Deployment success rate
Mean time to restore
```

---

# 26.93 DORA-style metrics

Track:

deployment frequency  
lead time for changes  
change failure rate  
mean time to restore.

But contextualize for regulated/high-risk AI features.

---

# 26.94 AI-specific release metrics

Add:

AI regression rate  
prompt rollback rate  
model rollback rate  
critical evaluation failure rate  
production hallucination regression.

---

# 26.95 Continuous evaluation

Production samples continuously feed:

QualityAI.

Not necessarily model training.

Flow:

```text
Production
 ↓
Evaluation
 ↓
Drift/Defect
 ↓
Backlog
 ↓
Fix
 ↓
Regression
```

---

# 26.96 Continuous training vs continuous evaluation

For this platform:

**continuous evaluation is strongly recommended.**

**continuous automatic training/deployment is usually not.**

Higher-risk voice/healthcare workflows need deliberate promotion gates.

---

# 26.97 Reproducibility test

Pick historical call:

```text
CALL-90182
```

System should identify:

agent  
prompt  
model  
knowledge  
tool  
policy  
route.

That is release reproducibility.

---

# 26.98 Release audit

Store:

who changed  
who reviewed  
who approved  
what was tested  
when deployed  
what traffic received it.

This integrates with GovernAI.

---
