# Phase 27 — ResilienceAI + SRE + Business Continuity / Disaster Recovery

This phase ensures the Voice AI platform continues to operate safely when providers, clouds, databases, telephony, models, workflows, or integrations fail.

The objective is:

> **Failures should degrade service gracefully, not create duplicate calls, lost bookings, unsafe actions, or unrecoverable customer journeys.**

## 27.1 Resilience architecture

```text
Customers / Campaigns
        ↓
Global Traffic / API Gateway
        ↓
Primary Region
   ├── Voice Gateway
   ├── PolicyAI
   ├── ConversationAI
   ├── Tool Gateway
   ├── Workflow Engine
   └── Database
        │
        ├──────── Replication ────────┐
        ↓                            ↓
Secondary Region                Backup / DR
        ↓                            ↓
Approved Backup Providers      Restore Environment

External Dependencies
 ├── Voice Platform A/B/C
 ├── Telephony A/B
 ├── STT/TTS/LLM A/B
 ├── CRM
 ├── Scheduler
 └── Messaging
```

## 27.2 Failure domains

Treat these independently:

| Failure domain | Example |
|---|---|
| Application | Conversation service crashes |
| Database | PostgreSQL unavailable |
| Cache | Redis failure |
| Workflow | Temporal worker unavailable |
| Queue | Kafka/Redis backlog |
| Voice platform | Retell/Vapi/etc. outage |
| Telephony | Twilio/Telnyx outage |
| STT | Transcription service down |
| TTS | Voice generation failure |
| LLM | Model timeout/rate limit |
| RAG | Vector store unavailable |
| Tool | Booking API unavailable |
| CRM | Salesforce/HubSpot outage |
| Messaging | SMS provider failure |
| Cloud region | Entire region unavailable |
| Network | Connectivity/partition |
| Security | Credentials revoked/compromised |
| Configuration | Bad prompt/policy rollout |

---

# 27.3 Service criticality tiers

Classify services.

### Tier 0 — Safety/authorization

```text
PolicyAI
DNC/Consent
Identity
Security controls
```

If unavailable, new outbound activity generally fails closed.

### Tier 1 — Transaction critical

```text
Booking
Customer confirmation
Workflow state
```

Must protect consistency.

### Tier 2 — Customer-experience critical

```text
Voice
STT
LLM
TTS
```

Can sometimes fail over.

### Tier 3 — Async/noncritical

```text
Analytics
CRM activity logging
Reporting
```

Can queue and recover later.

---

# 27.4 Availability targets

Do not assign 99.999% to every component.

Define appropriate SLOs based on business need.

Example structure:

```text
Policy service       Very high
Voice Gateway        High
Booking transaction  High
Analytics            Moderate
Reporting            Moderate
```

Availability targets should map to business impact and cost.

---

# 27.5 RTO and RPO

Define per system.

**RTO — Recovery Time Objective**

How quickly service must recover.

**RPO — Recovery Point Objective**

How much data loss is tolerable.

Example:

```text
Booking transaction
RTO = minutes
RPO ≈ near-zero

Analytics warehouse
RTO = hours
RPO = potentially several minutes/hours
```

Do not use one RTO/RPO for the whole platform.

---

# 27.6 Resilience matrix

| Component | RTO | RPO | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| PolicyAI | Very low | Near zero | Fail closed |
| Customer DB | Low | Very low | DB failover |
| Booking | Low | Near zero | Retry/reconcile |
| Voice provider | Seconds/minutes | N/A | Route failover |
| CRM | Hours possible | Event queue | Async recovery |
| Reporting | Hours | Batch replay | Restore later |

---

# 27.7 High availability

Run stateless services with multiple instances.

```text
Voice Gateway
 ├── Instance A
 ├── Instance B
 └── Instance C
```

Use:

load balancer  
health probes  
pod anti-affinity  
multiple availability zones.

Avoid one-server architecture.

---

# 27.8 Stateless service principle

Keep call/session state outside ephemeral containers where possible.

Use:

workflow state  
database  
Redis where appropriate.

If pod dies:

another worker continues.

---

# 27.9 Stateful service HA

For PostgreSQL:

managed HA or replication.

Possible approaches:

cloud-managed PostgreSQL  
Patroni  
Aurora-like systems.

Need:

automatic failover  
backup  
point-in-time recovery.

---

# 27.10 Redis resilience

If Redis is used for:

cache only

failure can degrade performance.

If used for:

critical state

configure replication/persistence appropriately.

Better rule:

critical durable workflow state should not depend solely on volatile cache.

---

# 27.11 Temporal durability

Temporal is useful because workflow state survives worker crashes.

Example:

```text
Schedule callback
 ↓
Worker crashes
 ↓
Worker restarts elsewhere
 ↓
Workflow resumes
```

No lost callback timer.

---

# 27.12 Queue durability

For events/jobs:

```text
producer
 ↓
durable queue
 ↓
consumer
```

Need:

acknowledgment  
retry  
DLQ  
deduplication.

Do not lose a booking confirmation because a worker restarts.

---

# 27.13 Backpressure

If downstream capacity falls:

```text
incoming calls/tasks
        ↓
queue
        ↓
rate limiter
```

Do not overload:

scheduler  
CRM  
voice provider.

Graceful slowdown is better than cascading failure.

---

# 27.14 Bulkheads

Separate worker pools:

```text
Booking workers
CRM workers
SMS workers
Analytics workers
```

If CRM hangs, it should not exhaust all threads needed for booking.

---

# 27.15 Circuit breakers

Each dependency:

```text
CLOSED
 ↓ failures
OPEN
 ↓ cooldown
HALF_OPEN
 ↓ test
CLOSED
```

Example:

scheduler API failing.

Open circuit.

Agent stops repeatedly hitting it and offers callback/human alternative.

---

# 27.16 Retry strategy

Retry only transient failures.

Use:

exponential backoff  
jitter  
maximum attempts.

Avoid synchronized retry storms.

---

# 27.17 Retry budget

Do not permit unlimited retries.

Example:

```text
Provider call initiation retries = 2
Booking API retries = policy-defined
CRM async retries = longer
```

Customer-contact retries are separate from technical retries.

---

# 27.18 Idempotency everywhere

Critical for:

outbound call creation  
booking  
SMS confirmation  
CRM lead creation  
payment links.

Every retry-safe command should carry:

```text
idempotency_key
```

---

# 27.19 Unknown transaction state

One of the most important resilience scenarios.

```text
BOOK request
 ↓
network timeout
```

Outcome unknown.

Do not immediately retry.

Use:

```text
UNKNOWN
 ↓
reconciliation
 ↓
SUCCESS / NOT_CREATED / CONFLICT
```

---

# 27.20 Reconciliation engine

Run continuously for:

unknown bookings  
unknown calls  
message delivery uncertainty  
CRM sync inconsistencies.

Dashboard:

```text
Unknown transactions: 12
Oldest: 4 min
Critical: 1
```

---

# 27.21 Voice provider failover

Configure:

```text
Primary
Secondary
Tertiary
```

RouteAI uses health + policy + quality.

If Provider A fails **before call creation**:

try B.

If call state is uncertain:

reconcile first.

---

# 27.22 Telephony failover

Keep telephony abstraction separate where possible.

Example:

```text
Voice orchestration healthy
Twilio down
 ↓
Telnyx/SIP alternative
```

subject to approved integration and number strategy.

---

# 27.23 STT failure

Possible degraded modes:

```text
Primary STT
 ↓ failure
Secondary approved STT
```

If no safe STT:

human transfer/callback.

Do not continue pretending to understand.

---

# 27.24 TTS failure

Fallback:

approved secondary TTS/voice.

If unavailable:

human transfer  
callback.

Avoid abruptly replacing voice with an unvalidated language/voice in sensitive workflows.

---

# 27.25 LLM failover

Fallback matrix:

```text
Model A
 ↓
Model B
 ↓
Model C
```

Only pre-tested, policy-approved alternatives.

Need compatible:

tools  
prompt  
context format.

---

# 27.26 RAG outage

For structured business facts:

APIs may still work.

For FAQ:

agent can say:

> “I’m unable to access that information right now. I can connect you with the clinic.”

Do not hallucinate from memory.

---

# 27.27 Booking-system outage

Conversation can continue for general information.

But booking action becomes:

```text
BOOKING_UNAVAILABLE
```

NextAI:

create callback/human task.

Do not claim successful booking.

---

# 27.28 CRM outage

Prefer:

```text
business transaction
 ↓
event persisted
 ↓
CRM sync later
```

Appointment shouldn't fail solely because CRM activity logging is unavailable.

---

# 27.29 Messaging outage

Booking can remain successful.

Queue confirmation.

If message cannot be delivered within acceptable window:

create operational exception/human task.

---

# 27.30 Degraded modes

Define explicit states:

```text
NORMAL
DEGRADED_VOICE
DEGRADED_BOOKING
DEGRADED_CRM
READ_ONLY
HUMAN_ONLY
OUTBOUND_PAUSED
```

The platform should know which mode it is in.

---

# 27.31 Graceful degradation matrix

| Failure | Continue? | Fallback |
|---|---|---|
| Reporting down | Yes | queue data |
| CRM down | Usually yes | async sync |
| RAG down | Limited | abstain/general tools |
| Booking down | Limited | callback |
| LLM down | Maybe | approved fallback |
| Policy down | No new outbound | fail closed |
| DNC store unavailable | No marketing dial | fail closed |

---

# 27.32 Dependency health model

For each dependency:

```text
HEALTHY
DEGRADED
UNAVAILABLE
UNKNOWN
```

Use real transaction health, not only `/health`.

---

# 27.33 Synthetic dependency monitoring

Regularly test:

telephony initiation  
STT  
TTS  
LLM  
booking  
CRM  
SMS.

This catches partial failures before customers do.

---

# 27.34 Multi-AZ architecture

Primary region should ideally span multiple availability zones for:

API services  
Kubernetes workers  
database replication.

This handles localized infrastructure failure without full DR.

---

# 27.35 Multi-region strategy

Possible patterns:

### Active-passive

Primary handles traffic.

Secondary waits.

Simpler and cheaper.

### Active-active

Both handle traffic.

More complex.

For early-stage healthcare voice SaaS:

active-passive or selectively active-active may be more practical.

---

# 27.36 Region failover

Flow:

```text
Primary region unhealthy
       ↓
Failover decision
       ↓
Secondary region
       ↓
Validate DB / policy / secrets
       ↓
Resume safe traffic
```

Must ensure data state is sufficiently current.

---

# 27.37 DNS/global routing

Use:

cloud global load balancer  
DNS failover  
traffic manager.

Do not depend on manual DNS editing during emergency.

---

# 27.38 Data replication

Replication strategy depends on data type.

Transactional DB:

synchronous or near-synchronous where practical.

Analytics:

async replication acceptable.

Object storage:

cross-region replication where needed.

---

# 27.39 Split-brain risk

Active-active DB designs can create conflicting state.

For bookings/consent:

prioritize strong consistency.

Do not create two independently writable customer states without conflict strategy.

---

# 27.40 DR backups

Backup:

PostgreSQL  
object storage metadata  
configuration  
workflow data  
governance records  
audit data.

Backups must be:

encrypted  
tested  
versioned  
access controlled.

---

# 27.41 Point-in-time recovery

Enable where supported.

Useful for:

accidental deletion  
bad migration  
logical corruption.

Test restoration regularly.

---

# 27.42 Backup is not DR

A backup that has never been restored is only an assumption.

Run:

```text
backup
 ↓
restore into isolated environment
 ↓
integrity tests
```

---

# 27.43 DR test schedule

Examples:

quarterly tabletop  
semiannual technical restore  
annual full failover.

Higher-risk deployments may need more frequent testing.

---

# 27.44 DR exercise

Scenario:

Primary Canadian region unavailable.

Validate:

traffic shift  
database recovery  
secrets  
provider access  
PolicyAI  
voice calls  
booking  
monitoring.

Record actual RTO/RPO.

---

# 27.45 Disaster scenario library

Test:

```text
Cloud region loss
Database corruption
Credential compromise
Telephony outage
Voice provider outage
LLM outage
Scheduler outage
DNS failure
Ransomware scenario
Bad deployment
Data deletion
```

---

# 27.46 Tabletop exercises

Before technical drills, walk teams through:

Who declares incident?

Who can stop campaigns?

Who communicates with clinics?

Who approves failover?

What happens to active calls?

This catches process gaps cheaply.

---

# 27.47 Active-call behavior during outage

Define per failure.

If monitoring fails:

call continues.

If CRM fails:

call continues.

If policy authorization becomes unavailable before a new high-impact action:

restrict/block that action.

If voice provider dies mid-call:

offer recovery path where technically possible.

---

# 27.48 Mid-call disconnect recovery

If call drops:

do not blindly redial.

Check:

call outcome  
customer preference  
campaign policy.

Possible:

callback task  
SMS if independently eligible.

---

# 27.49 Session recovery

Persist enough state to reconstruct:

customer  
current state  
completed tool actions  
last confirmed values.

But avoid unsafe resume if customer identity/context cannot be re-established.

---

# 27.50 Transaction checkpointing

After critical steps:

```text
customer confirmed slot
 ↓
checkpoint
 ↓
booking requested
 ↓
checkpoint
 ↓
booking confirmed
```

This improves recovery.

---

# 27.51 Call job durability

Each outbound job:

```text
PENDING
DISPATCHING
CALL_CREATED
CONNECTED
COMPLETED
```

Persistent transitions prevent duplicate dispatch after worker crash.

---

# 27.52 Exactly-once illusion

Distributed systems rarely give true exactly-once across vendors.

Design for:

at-least-once delivery

+

idempotent consumers.

This is much safer.

---

# 27.53 Event replay

Retain events long enough to rebuild derived state.

Example:

CRM sync service loses database.

Replay customer events to reconstruct.

Govern retention appropriately.

---

# 27.54 Dead-letter queue operations

DLQ entries need:

owner  
age  
severity  
retryability.

Do not let DLQ become a graveyard.

---

# 27.55 DLQ SLA

Example:

critical booking event DLQ → immediate response.

analytics DLQ → lower priority.

Severity-aware processing.

---

# 27.56 SRE error budgets

Use availability SLOs to guide release velocity.

If Voice Gateway error budget is nearly exhausted:

pause risky releases.

This connects reliability and engineering planning.

---

# 27.57 Capacity planning

Forecast:

concurrent calls  
API requests  
DB QPS  
LLM throughput  
STT sessions  
worker count.

Plan for:

normal  
peak  
campaign spike.

---

# 27.58 Headroom

Do not operate continuously at 100% capacity.

Maintain appropriate headroom for:

traffic spikes  
provider failover.

If all providers run at 90% capacity, failover may not actually work.

---

# 27.59 Provider failover capacity

If Provider A handles 70% and dies:

can B/C absorb it?

Track:

```text
available_fallback_capacity
```

A fallback that cannot handle load is not a real resilience strategy.

---

# 27.60 Load shedding

When overloaded, prioritize:

```text
Customer-requested callbacks
Appointment-related calls
High-priority transactional work
```

over:

low-priority marketing.

Do this according to business/policy rules.

---

# 27.61 Queue prioritization

Use:

```text
P0
P1
P2
P3
```

with starvation controls.

Low-priority campaigns can wait.

---

# 27.62 Autoscaling

Scale on:

active calls  
queue depth  
CPU  
workflow backlog.

Test scaling speed.

Voice workloads may spike faster than CPU-based autoscaling reacts.

---

# 27.63 Cold-start risk

Serverless/scale-to-zero services can create latency.

Do not scale critical realtime voice services to zero unless cold-start is proven acceptable.

---

# 27.64 Database capacity

Monitor:

connections  
locks  
query latency  
replication lag  
disk growth.

Booking/customer state should not fail because analytics query consumed the database.

---

# 27.65 Read replicas

Use for:

analytics/read-heavy workloads.

Do not serve stale consent/DNC decisions from lagging replica if freshness is critical.

---

# 27.66 Data-consistency tiers

### Strong

DNC  
consent  
booking  
payments.

### Eventual

analytics  
CRM activity  
reports.

Document explicitly.

---

# 27.67 Chaos engineering

Inject:

pod death  
database failover  
provider outage  
latency  
packet loss  
queue backlog.

Observe:

customer impact  
automatic recovery  
alerts.

Start in staging before controlled production exercises.

---

# 27.68 Chaos experiment example

```text
Experiment:
Kill 50% of ConversationAI pods

Expected:
No active state lost
New calls redistributed
P95 latency within threshold
No duplicate calls
```

---

# 27.69 Provider chaos

Simulate:

Provider A unavailable.

Expected:

circuit breaker opens  
RouteAI selects B  
no duplicate calls  
quality within threshold.

---

# 27.70 Booking chaos

Inject:

5-second scheduler latency.

Expected:

agent communicates delay  
timeout strategy activates  
no duplicate bookings  
fallback/callback offered.

---

# 27.71 Database chaos

Force primary DB failover.

Measure:

workflow pause  
transaction retry  
actual recovery time.

Check no corrupt state.

---

# 27.72 Network partition

Test service-to-service connectivity loss.

Avoid cascading retry storms.

Circuit breaker + timeout + backoff are critical.

---

# 27.73 Security-driven resilience

If credential compromised:

revoke quickly.

But service should support rotation/fallback credentials without hours of downtime.

---

# 27.74 Secret-manager outage

Applications should not continuously retrieve every secret per API call.

Use secure short-lived caching where appropriate.

But avoid stale credentials after revocation.

Balance resilience and security.

---

# 27.75 Dependency contract fallback

If vendor API introduces incompatible change:

adapter should fail safely.

Contract tests + schema validation prevent malformed data from propagating.

---

# 27.76 Business continuity plan

Technical DR is only part.

BCP should address:

clinic operations  
human fallback  
customer communication  
campaign suspension.

Example:

Voice AI unavailable → route critical inbound calls to humans where possible.

---

# 27.77 Manual fallback

Design manual procedures before outage.

Examples:

CSV callback queue  
clinic receptionist handoff  
manual appointment processing.

Do not invent these during incident.

---

# 27.78 Human capacity for fallback

If 10,000 AI calls/day fail over to 3 receptionists, manual fallback is unrealistic.

Document capacity limits.

Prioritize essential customer flows.

---

# 27.79 Customer communication

For material outages:

provide approved messaging.

Example:

> “Our scheduling system is temporarily unavailable. We can arrange a callback.”

Don't expose technical details unnecessarily.

---

# 27.80 Clinic/client communication

Operational dashboard can show:

service affected  
start time  
current mitigation  
estimated business impact.

Avoid unsupported restoration estimates if uncertain.

---

# 27.81 Incident command

For severe incidents define roles:

Incident Commander  
Operations Lead  
Technical Lead  
Communications  
Security/Privacy if relevant  
Business owner.

One clear command structure.

---

# 27.82 Incident severity

### SEV0

Safety/privacy/systemwide severe event.

### SEV1

Major customer/business outage.

### SEV2

Partial degradation.

### SEV3

Minor issue.

Severity determines response process.

---

# 27.83 Failover authorization

Automate routine failover.

For major region/failover events:

define authorized roles and conditions.

Avoid waiting for six approvals during an outage.

---

# 27.84 Recovery order

Example:

```text
Security / IAM
 ↓
Policy / Consent
 ↓
Customer DB
 ↓
Voice Gateway
 ↓
Booking
 ↓
Campaign
 ↓
CRM
 ↓
Analytics
```

Restore based on business criticality.

---

# 27.85 Data validation after recovery

Before full traffic:

check:

DB consistency  
policy availability  
DNC state  
workflow queue  
provider credentials.

Then synthetic test.

---

# 27.86 Re-enable traffic gradually

After outage:

```text
5%
20%
50%
100%
```

Monitor.

Avoid stampeding a barely recovered dependency.

---

# 27.87 Backlog recovery

After downtime:

10,000 queued calls may exist.

Do not immediately dial all.

Re-evaluate:

eligibility  
time window  
DNC  
appointment status  
campaign expiry.

Many jobs may now be obsolete.

---

# 27.88 Stale-job suppression

Example:

customer booked while outage ongoing.

Queued sales call becomes invalid.

Pre-dispatch revalidation removes it.

---

# 27.89 Retry storm prevention

After provider recovery:

use jittered worker ramp-up.

Avoid all queued jobs retrying simultaneously.

---

# 27.90 Reconciliation after outage

Check:

calls with uncertain status  
bookings  
CRM sync  
messages.

Produce outage reconciliation report.

---

# 27.91 Post-incident review

For serious incident capture:

timeline  
impact  
root cause  
what worked  
what failed  
corrective action  
preventive action.

Blameless technical analysis, but with clear ownership.

---

# 27.92 Incident → regression

Every confirmed failure becomes:

new test  
new alert if appropriate  
new control.

This connects SRE with QualityAI.

---

# 27.93 Incident → architecture

Example:

Single telephony provider outage caused complete failure.

Action:

prioritize telephony abstraction/failover.

Reliability findings should drive architecture decisions.

---

# 27.94 Resilience metrics

Track:

```text
Availability
MTTD
MTTA
MTTR
Failover time
Recovery success
Retry success
Reconciliation backlog
DLQ size
Callback SLA
```

---

# 27.95 MTBF

Mean Time Between Failures.

Useful for provider/component reliability trending.

---

# 27.96 Failure rate by provider

Example:

| Provider | Failure | Failover Success | MTTR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 1.2% | 98% | 4 min |
| B | 2.1% | 95% | 7 min |

RouteAI can consume reliability signals.

---

# 27.97 DR dashboard

Show:

last backup  
last successful restore  
replication lag  
DR readiness  
last failover test  
RTO/RPO performance.

---

# 27.98 Resilience scorecard

Per service:

```text
HA                   PASS
Backup               PASS
Restore              PASS
Failover             PASS
Chaos Test           PASS
Runbook              PASS
Capacity             PASS
```

Critical missing items become risk register entries.

---

# 27.99 Recommended tools

| Capability | Possible tool |
|---|---|
| Durable workflows | Temporal |
| Kubernetes HA | Kubernetes |
| Metrics | Prometheus |
| Alerts | Grafana/Alertmanager |
| Tracing | OpenTelemetry |
| Chaos | Chaos Mesh/Litmus |
| DB backup | Managed DB/PITR |
| IaC | Terraform/OpenTofu |
| Incident | PagerDuty/Opsgenie-equivalent |
| Runbooks | Git/Confluence/operational docs |

You can start with simpler tooling and mature as scale grows.

---

## 🤖 Assistant — msg #91

# Phase 28 — HumanOps + Agent Assist + Supervisor Console

This phase designs the human side of the platform: receptionists, sales staff, supervisors, QA reviewers, technical support, and managers who need to monitor, intervene, take over, review, and improve AI conversations.

The principle is:

> **AI should reduce human workload, not remove human control. When AI confidence, safety, customer preference, or operational conditions demand it, humans need immediate context and authority.**

## 28.1 Target architecture

```text
Voice AI / CampaignAI / NextAI
          ↓
Conversation Context
          ↓
HumanOps Orchestrator
          ↓
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Live Supervisor Console                     │
│ Agent Assist                                │
│ Human Transfer                              │
│ Takeover                                    │
│ Callback Queue                              │
│ Task Queue                                  │
│ QA Review                                   │
│ Escalation                                  │
│ Staffing / Skills / Language Routing        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ↓
Human Agent
          ↓
CRM / Booking / Messaging / Resolution
          ↓
Outcome + Override + Feedback
          ↓
QualityAI / NextAI / LearnAI
```

## 28.2 Human roles

| Role | Main function |
|---|---|
| Receptionist | Scheduling, general clinic support |
| Sales Agent | Lead qualification/conversion |
| Service Specialist | Detailed product/service support |
| Billing Agent | Billing/admin questions |
| Clinical Staff | Restricted healthcare questions where appropriate |
| Supervisor | Live escalation and operations |
| QA Analyst | Conversation review |
| AI Operations | Agent/model troubleshooting |
| Compliance/Risk | High-risk incident review |
| Manager | Capacity/performance management |

## 28.3 Human handoff triggers

A transfer should be triggered by explicit rules and AI signals.

Common triggers:

```text
Customer asks for human
Low AI confidence
Repeated misunderstanding
Customer frustration
Complaint
Restricted clinical question
Booking failure
Pricing exception
Unauthorized discount request
Unsupported language
Complex B2B opportunity
Sensitive privacy concern
AI/tool failure
```

Do not keep a caller inside the AI flow simply because conversion optimization prefers it.

## 28.4 Transfer decision

NextAI outputs:

```text
TRANSFER_HUMAN
```

with:

```text
reason
required_skill
preferred_language
priority
context
```

Example:

```text
reason = INSURANCE_QUESTION
skill = CLINIC_ADMIN
language = HINDI
priority = HIGH
```

## 28.5 Skills-based routing

Human queues need more than one generic receptionist pool.

Skills could include:

```text
Dental
Physiotherapy
Chiropractic
ENT
Massage

Booking
Billing
Insurance/Admin
Complaint
Corporate Sales

English
Hindi
Punjabi
French
```

Route:

```text
Issue
+
Language
+
Priority
+
Availability
→ Best human queue
```

## 28.6 Human queue model

Store:

```text
queue_id
name

supported_skills[]
supported_languages[]

business_hours

agents_online
agents_available

estimated_wait
priority_rules
overflow_queue
```

## 28.7 Agent profile

```text
HUMAN_AGENT

agent_id
tenant_id
name

skills[]
languages[]

status

AVAILABLE
BUSY
AWAY
OFFLINE

active_sessions
max_sessions
```

## 28.8 Transfer pre-check

Before telling a caller:

> “I’ll connect you now.”

Check:

```text
queue open?
eligible agent available?
expected wait acceptable?
telephony transfer healthy?
```

If not:

offer callback.

## 28.9 Warm transfer

Preferred for complex calls.

```text
AI
 ↓
Human accepts transfer
 ↓
Human receives summary
 ↓
AI/customer connected to human
```

Human already knows context before speaking.

This is much better than blindly forwarding the caller.

## 28.10 Cold transfer

Sometimes simpler:

```text
AI
→ Queue
```

Use only when appropriate.

Warm transfer is preferable for complaints, complex needs, and sensitive situations.

## 28.11 Context package

Before transfer, give the human a compact summary.

Example:

```text
Customer:
Raj

Language:
Hindi / English

Reason:
Physiotherapy inquiry

Need:
Evening appointment

Preference:
NW clinic

Main concern:
Price

Actions completed:
Availability checked

Current issue:
Insurance question outside AI scope

Appointment:
Not yet booked

Customer sentiment:
Neutral

Requested:
Human assistance
```

The receptionist should not ask the caller to repeat the entire conversation.

## 28.12 Context package structure

```text
TRANSFER_CONTEXT

customer_id
call_id

summary

primary_need
secondary_needs[]

language

important_preferences[]

objections[]

recommendation

completed_actions[]
pending_actions[]

risk_flags[]

transfer_reason
```

## 28.13 Live transcript

Supervisor/human can view:

```text
Customer speech
Agent response
Intent
Current state
Tool activity
```

with appropriate privacy and access control.

Sensitive data should be masked by role.

## 28.14 Live call timeline

Example console:

```text
14:01:07 CALL CONNECTED
14:01:11 AI disclosure
14:01:36 Need = Physiotherapy
14:02:15 Price objection
14:02:52 Availability tool
14:03:14 Insurance question
14:03:15 HUMAN_TRANSFER_REQUIRED
```

This is invaluable for supervisors.

## 28.15 Live supervisor dashboard

Supervisor should see:

```text
Active AI calls
Calls waiting for human
Transfers in progress
High-risk calls
Complaints
Long calls
Low-confidence calls
Stuck calls
Provider degradation
```

Avoid making them watch every call manually.

## 28.16 Priority queue

Possible priority:

```text
P0 Safety/privacy incident
P1 Customer requested human / complaint
P2 Transaction issue
P3 High-value sales opportunity
P4 General support
```

Actual business rules can differ.

## 28.17 Queue SLA

Track:

```text
time_to_accept
time_to_connect
abandonment
```

Example targets are business-configurable.

Do not claim you provide human escalation if customers wait indefinitely.

## 28.18 Queue overflow

If preferred queue is full:

```text
Primary queue
 ↓
overflow skill group
 ↓
callback
```

Do not transfer randomly to an unqualified person.

## 28.19 Language overflow

If Hindi-speaking staff unavailable:

options:

English human if customer accepts  
scheduled Hindi callback  
AI continues only for permitted low-risk tasks.

Customer preference matters.

## 28.20 AI Agent Assist

Once a human joins, AI can change roles.

Instead of speaking directly to customer, AI becomes:

```text
Agent Assist
```

providing:

customer summary  
suggested questions  
service information  
pricing lookup  
availability  
next-best action.

Human remains in control.

## 28.21 Agent Assist panel

Possible panels:

```text
Customer profile
Need summary
Current call transcript
Recommended response
Knowledge search
Available appointments
Next best action
CRM actions
```

Keep suggestions concise.

## 28.22 Suggested response

Human sees:

> Suggested: “The NW clinic has Tuesday 6:30 PM and Thursday 7 PM available.”

Human can:

accept  
edit  
ignore.

Never auto-send unless configured for low-risk workflows.

## 28.23 Recommendation confidence

Display:

```text
Suggested action:
Offer Thursday 7 PM

Confidence:
92%

Reason:
Matches evening + NW preferences
```

Low-confidence suggestion should be visually obvious.

## 28.24 AI should not distract humans

Do not show 25 recommendations simultaneously.

Prioritize:

next question  
critical warning  
next action.

Agent Assist should reduce cognitive load.

## 28.25 Whisper/coaching mode

For live human-led calls, AI may privately suggest:

```text
Ask preferred day
Mention current approved offer
Confirm phone number
Customer asked about pricing
```

AI should not speak to the customer directly in whisper mode.

## 28.26 Real-time compliance coaching

Example:

Human begins to make unsupported claim.

Assist could flag:

```text
Pricing information should be retrieved from Pricing API.
```

Or:

```text
Customer requested no additional marketing.
```

Useful for both AI and human quality.

## 28.27 Real-time policy alerts

Supervisor sees:

```text
DNC detected
Sensitive question
Recording disabled
Unauthorized discount
Customer requested human
```

Warnings should be actionable and limited to important events.

## 28.28 Human takeover

Sometimes transfer is too slow.

Authorized supervisor may:

```text
TAKE_OVER
```

AI stops speaking.

Human immediately controls the call.

Use for:

complaint  
unsafe response  
AI loop  
technical malfunction.

## 28.29 Takeover state

```text
AI_ACTIVE
→ TAKEOVER_REQUESTED
→ HUMAN_ACTIVE
```

Do not allow AI to continue responding simultaneously.

## 28.30 AI resume

Potentially:

```text
HUMAN_ACTIVE
→ AI_RESUME
```

only if appropriate and explicitly triggered.

Useful if human resolves one exceptional question and returns routine booking to AI.

## 28.31 Takeover audit

Store:

```text
who
when
reason
call_state
AI_version
```

Repeated takeover of same issue becomes product-improvement evidence.

## 28.32 Human override

Human can override:

NextAI  
RecommendAI  
ScoreAI classifications  
customer preferences where corrected  
campaign status.

Require reason for material override.

## 28.33 Override reason taxonomy

```text
CUSTOMER_CORRECTION
AI_INCORRECT
BUSINESS_EXCEPTION
CUSTOMER_REQUEST
POLICY_EXCEPTION
NEW_INFORMATION
OTHER
```

## 28.34 Override learning

Aggregate:

```text
AI Recommendation
vs
Human Decision
```

Example:

AI says:

`NURTURE`

Human repeatedly chooses:

`CALLBACK`.

Investigate whether NextAI rules need improvement.

## 28.35 Do not blindly train on overrides

Human overrides can also be wrong.

Use outcomes + QA review before turning them into labels.

## 28.36 Callback queue

When live transfer impossible:

```text
CALLBACK_TASK
```

Fields:

```text
customer_id
reason
requested_time
timezone
language
required_skill
priority
due_at
```

## 28.37 Callback SLA

Track:

```text
scheduled time
assigned time
actual call time
```

Measure:

```text
on_time_callback_rate
```

Customer-requested callbacks should be prioritized.

## 28.38 Callback reassignment

If assigned employee goes offline:

task must return to queue.

Do not let callbacks disappear in personal task lists.

## 28.39 Task management

Besides calls, humans may receive:

```text
Review complaint
Resolve booking discrepancy
Answer insurance question
Approve discount
Review low-confidence extraction
```

Create:

```text
HUMAN_TASK
```

with SLA and owner.

## 28.40 Task states

```text
NEW
ASSIGNED
IN_PROGRESS
WAITING_CUSTOMER
WAITING_SYSTEM
RESOLVED
CLOSED
```

## 28.41 Task escalation

Example:

High-priority complaint unresolved for 30 minutes.

Escalate to supervisor.

Use SLA rules.

## 28.42 Supervisor staffing dashboard

Show:

```text
Agents online
Available
Busy
Queue length
Wait time
Abandon rate
Language capacity
```

This allows active staffing management.

## 28.43 Skill capacity

Example:

```text
English support: 8 available
Hindi: 2
Punjabi: 0
Insurance/admin: 1
```

NextAI can avoid offering immediate Punjabi human transfer if no capacity exists.

## 28.44 Workforce forecasting

Use historical:

calls by hour  
transfer rate  
language  
average handling time.

Forecast:

```text
human agents required
```

for next day/week.

## 28.45 Erlang-style planning

For call-center scale, conventional queueing/workforce models can estimate required staff based on:

arrival rate  
average handling time  
target service level.

AI does not replace proven workforce mathematics.

## 28.46 Human handling time

Track:

```text
AHT
```

but don't optimize only for shortest calls.

Also measure:

resolution  
customer satisfaction  
repeat calls.

## 28.47 First Contact Resolution

Important KPI:

```text
FCR
```

Did the customer's problem get resolved without another call/task?

High FCR usually indicates better operational design.

## 28.48 Transfer containment

Measure:

```text
AI-only resolution
AI→human resolution
human→second-human transfer
```

Repeated transfers indicate routing/design problems.

## 28.49 Human escalation rate

Per AI agent:

```text
human_transfer_rate
```

Break down by reason.

High rate can mean:

correct cautious behavior

or:

weak automation.

Analyze root causes.

## 28.50 Avoid minimizing escalation blindly

A lower transfer rate is not always good.

If AI improperly answers restricted healthcare questions rather than transferring, transfer rate falls while safety worsens.

Use quality-adjusted metrics.

## 28.51 Human quality score

Human interactions can also be scored:

```text
Accuracy
Policy compliance
Customer experience
Task completion
```

ResponsibleAI/governance applies to human-assisted workflows as well.

## 28.52 AI-assisted QA

After human call:

AI can suggest:

summary  
disposition  
needs  
objections.

Human confirms/edit.

This reduces after-call work.

## 28.53 After-call work

Typical ACW:

```text
CRM notes
Disposition
Follow-up
Appointment
Task creation
```

AI can prefill structured fields.

Human validates important items.

## 28.54 Automatic call summary

Example:

```text
Customer asked about physiotherapy evening availability.
Prefers NW location.
Price concern noted.
Insurance question required receptionist.
No appointment booked.
Follow-up requested Tuesday evening.
```

Keep summary factual.

## 28.55 Summary consistency

QA should compare:

transcript  
tool activity  
summary.

Do not allow:

“appointment booked”

when tool failed.

## 28.56 CRM write-back

Human-approved summary can update:

CRM activity  
lead stage  
next action.

Use ToolAI rather than unrestricted direct updates.

## 28.57 Disposition codes

Standardize:

```text
BOOKED
QUALIFIED
CALLBACK
INFO_SENT
HUMAN_RESOLVED
NOT_INTERESTED
DNC
COMPLAINT
UNRESOLVED
```

Humans shouldn't invent free-text dispositions for reporting-critical outcomes.

## 28.58 Human notes

Allow free text, but separate from structured fields.

Do not use staff opinion as authoritative customer fact.

Example bad:

```text
customer difficult
```

Better structured observation:

```text
customer requested shorter conversation
```

## 28.59 QA review console

```text
Audio
Transcript
AI/human transitions
Tool calls
Policy events
Customer outcome
Automated QA score
```

Then add manual review.

## 28.60 QA sampling

Queue calls based on:

random sample  
low automated quality  
complaints  
high-risk transaction  
new agent version  
new language  
human override.

## 28.61 QA rubric

For AI and human portions:

```text
Disclosure
Understanding
Accuracy
Policy
Need discovery
Empathy
Tool correctness
Resolution
Closing
```

## 28.62 Calibration sessions

QA reviewers need periodic calibration.

Same call → multiple reviewers.

Compare scoring.

This reduces evaluator drift.

## 28.63 Supervisor coaching

Aggregate per human:

common missed steps  
policy failures  
unresolved objections  
high transfer rate.

Use for coaching, not simplistic punitive scoring.

## 28.64 AI coaching feedback loop

```text
Frequent insurance transfer
```

If:

## 28.85 Transfer failure taxonomy

```text
NO_AGENT_AVAILABLE
```

## 28.86 Edge case — human accepts after customer disconnects

Cancel transfer and create appropriate callback/task.

Do not connect staff to dead session.

## 28.87 Edge case — two humans accept

Use atomic assignment.

Only one owns the call.

## 28.88 Edge case — supervisor takes over during transfer

State machine must resolve ownership.

Example:

```text
AI
→ transfer pending
→ supervisor takeover
```

Cancel pending queue assignment.

## 28.89 Edge case — human asks AI to perform unauthorized action

Human says:

> “Just refund it.”

Tool Gateway still applies permissions.

HumanOps does not bypass PolicyAI/SecureAI.

## 28.90 Edge case — human enters incorrect information

Tool validation and transaction confirmation still apply.

Human is not an unrestricted trusted root process.

## 28.91 Edge case — human manually changes DNC

Removal of DNC should require appropriate restricted process.

Do not let ordinary sales user reverse suppression.

## 28.92 Edge case — customer asks AI back after human takeover

Human decides whether to resume AI.

Do not automatically switch based solely on customer's ambiguous phrasing.

## 28.93 Edge case — AI summary wrong

Human should edit before relying on it.

Capture correction and feed QualityAI.

## 28.94 Edge case — queue overload

If queue wait exceeds threshold:

stop promising immediate transfer.

Offer callback.

CampaignAI may reduce lower-priority volume.

## 28.95 Edge case — all language specialists unavailable

Do not misrepresent.

Offer:

other accepted language  
scheduled specialist callback.

SSO

audit.

Sensitive customer information creates a significant insider-risk surface.

Record:

data changes.

## 28.98 Human privacy

Avoid unnecessary employee surveillance metrics.

Use operational/quality metrics proportionately and transparently.

## 🤖 Assistant — msg #93

# Phase 29 — FraudAI + Abuse Prevention + Lead Authenticity

This phase protects the acquisition and outbound-call system from **fake leads, bots, spam submissions, duplicate identities, premium-number abuse, call farming, credential misuse, SMS abuse, promo abuse, and malicious automation**.

The goal is:

> **Decide whether a lead, customer, campaign, phone number, or action is trustworthy enough to proceed — without blocking legitimate customers unnecessarily.**

## 29.1 Target architecture

```text
Form / API / Import / CRM / Campaign
            ↓
      Fraud Screening
            ↓
 ┌───────────────────────────────┐
 │ Phone Validation              │
 │ Email Validation              │
 │ Duplicate Detection           │
 │ Device / IP Signals           │
 │ Velocity Checks               │
 │ Bot Detection                 │
 │ Reputation Signals            │
 │ Identity Consistency          │
 │ Campaign Abuse Detection      │
 │ Telephony Fraud Detection     │
 │ Promotion Abuse Detection     │
 └───────────────────────────────┘
            ↓
        Fraud Score
            ↓
 ┌──────────┼──────────┬──────────┐
 ↓          ↓          ↓          ↓
ALLOW     VERIFY      REVIEW      BLOCK
            ↓
       Customer/Lead
            ↓
     Campaign / Call
```

FraudAI should usually provide a **risk signal**, while PolicyAI makes the final executable decision.

---

## 29.2 Fraud domains

| Domain | Example |
|---|---|
| Form Fraud | Automated fake submissions |
| Lead Fraud | Fabricated customer details |
| Duplicate Fraud | Same person submitted repeatedly |
| Contact Fraud | Invalid/disposable phone/email |
| Bot Abuse | Scripted form submissions |
| Campaign Abuse | Artificial lead generation |
| Telephony Fraud | Premium-rate or international call abuse |
| Call Farming | Artificially extending calls for financial gain |
| Account Abuse | Stolen credentials |
| Promotion Abuse | Repeated free-trial usage |
| Referral Abuse | Fake referral chains |
| Tool Abuse | Unauthorized booking/cancellation attempts |
| Vendor Abuse | Unexpected provider API activity |

---

# 29.3 Fraud signal record

Create:

```text
FRAUD_SIGNAL

signal_id
tenant_id

subject_type
subject_id

signal_type

value
severity
confidence

source

detected_at
expires_at
```

Example:

```text
signal_type = HIGH_FORM_VELOCITY
value = 27 submissions / 5 min
severity = HIGH
```

---

# 29.4 Fraud decision

Use:

```text
ALLOW
ALLOW_WITH_VERIFICATION
MANUAL_REVIEW
BLOCK
```

Do not use only:

```text
fraud = true/false
```

because most real-world fraud decisions are uncertain.

---

# 29.5 Fraud score

Conceptually:

```text
Fraud Risk =
Identity Risk
+
Contact Risk
+
Velocity Risk
+
Device Risk
+
Behavior Risk
+
Telephony Risk
+
Historical Abuse Risk
```

Normalize:

```text
0–100
```

Example operational bands:

```text
0–30     LOW
31–60    MEDIUM
61–80    HIGH
81–100   VERY HIGH
```

But hard rules may override numeric scores.

---

# 29.6 Form-level fraud checks

At form submission:

```text
Validate schema
↓
CAPTCHA / bot signal
↓
IP velocity
↓
Device/session velocity
↓
Email validation
↓
Phone validation
↓
Duplicate detection
↓
Fraud score
```

Do this before automatically launching costly outbound calls.

---

# 29.7 CAPTCHA strategy

For public forms, support:

CAPTCHA / invisible bot assessment

where justified.

But CAPTCHA alone is insufficient.

Bots can bypass or outsource it.

Combine with behavioral and velocity signals.

---

# 29.8 Honeypot fields

Low-cost technique:

hidden field normal users should never fill.

Bot populates it:

```text
BOT_SIGNAL
```

Useful as one signal, not absolute proof.

---

# 29.9 Form completion timing

Example:

20-field form completed in:

```text
0.4 seconds
```

Suspicious.

Track:

```text
form_duration_ms
```

But autofill can also be fast, so use as weighted signal.

---

# 29.10 IP velocity

Example:

```text
1 IP
→ 300 leads
→ 10 minutes
```

Possible:

bot  
partner import  
shared corporate network.

Do not block blindly without context.

---

# 29.11 Device velocity

Track a privacy-conscious device/session identifier where appropriate.

Signals:

many names  
many numbers  
many campaigns

from same device/session.

---

# 29.12 IP reputation

Possible signals:

data-center/VPN/proxy indicator  
known abuse reputation  
geographic mismatch.

Treat these carefully.

VPN use alone does not mean fraud.

---

# 29.13 Phone validation

Normalize to:

```text
E.164
```

Then check:

valid numbering format  
country  
line type where available  
carrier  
reachable status where permitted.

Classify:

```text
VALID
INVALID
SUSPECT
UNKNOWN
```

---

# 29.14 Premium-number protection

Critical for outbound systems.

Before dialing:

```text
destination country
number range
rate class
```

Check against allow/block policy.

Block:

premium-rate numbers  
known high-cost destinations

unless explicitly approved.

---

# 29.15 International calling policy

Example:

```text
Canada / US → allowed
UK → approved campaign only
Other international → manual approval
Premium ranges → blocked
```

Actual policy depends on business.

This prevents expensive credential abuse.

---

# 29.16 Phone velocity

One phone appears in:

```text
40 different form submissions
```

under different names.

Signal:

```text
PHONE_REUSE_HIGH
```

Possible:

shared family phone  
business receptionist  
fraud.

Send to identity-resolution logic rather than automatically concluding malicious behavior.

---

# 29.17 Email validation

Check:

syntax  
domain validity  
MX records through appropriate services  
disposable-domain signals  
bounce history.

Classify:

```text
VALID
DISPOSABLE
INVALID
RISKY
UNKNOWN
```

---

# 29.18 Disposable email

Disposable email may reduce trust score but isn't automatically fraud.

Some legitimate customers use privacy-focused aliases.

Use proportional controls.

---

# 29.19 Email reuse

Example:

same email

+ 15 different names.

Possible:

family/shared office  
test account  
abuse.

Combine with other evidence.

---

# 29.20 Identity consistency

Compare:

```text
name
phone
email
CRM identity
form history
```

Example:

customer claims:

```text
Raj Sharma
```

but contact is already confidently associated with another record.

Trigger:

```text
IDENTITY_CONFLICT
```

Do not merge automatically.

---

# 29.21 Duplicate lead detection

Duplicates can arise legitimately.

Use:

exact match  
normalized match  
fuzzy match  
phone/email match.

Classify:

```text
EXACT_DUPLICATE
LIKELY_DUPLICATE
RELATED
NEW
```

---

# 29.22 Duplicate-call prevention

If customer fills the form three times in 5 minutes:

Do not start three simultaneous AI calls.

Create:

```text
active_contact_workflow
```

and deduplicate/merge eligible requests.

---

# 29.23 Lead freshness + duplicate logic

Example:

Form 1:

Physio.

Five minutes later:

Form 2:

Dental.

Do not necessarily dedupe the second as duplicate because service intent differs.

Use semantic/business dedupe.

---

# 29.24 Bot-lead pattern

Common bot pattern:

```text
random names
same IP
same phone prefix
disposable email
rapid submissions
```

Combined signals produce high confidence.

---

# 29.25 Lead authenticity score

Separate from fraud score.

Example:

```text
AUTHENTICITY_SCORE
```

Inputs:

verified phone  
verified email  
customer interaction  
CRM match  
human response.

A lead may be:

not fraudulent

but:

low authenticity/unreachable.

---

# 29.26 Engagement confirmation

One of strongest signals:

customer actually answers.

Then:

```text
contactability ↑
authenticity ↑
```

If correct person confirms request:

strong positive evidence.

---

# 29.27 Fake lead attacks

Competitor or attacker may submit other people's numbers.

Then your system starts unwanted outbound calls.

Mitigation:

form-rate controls  
confirmation mechanisms where appropriate  
initial conservative contact logic  
easy opt-out.

Monitor complaints:

> “I never requested this.”

This is an important fraud signal.

---

# 29.28 “Never requested” event

Store:

```text
UNSOLICITED_LEAD_REPORTED
```

Then investigate:

lead source  
IP/device  
campaign  
form session.

If repeated from same source:

auto-pause source/campaign.

---

# 29.29 Campaign-source fraud

Suppose partner sends:

10,000 leads

but:

80% invalid numbers  
70% “never requested” complaints.

FraudAI should score:

```text
SOURCE_RISK
```

not just individual leads.

---

# 29.30 Lead-source health

Metrics:

```text
valid_phone_rate
connect_rate
wrong_number_rate
complaint_rate
never_requested_rate
duplicate_rate
conversion
```

Calculate:

```text
SOURCE_TRUST_SCORE
```

---

# 29.31 Affiliate fraud

If affiliates are paid per lead:

risks increase dramatically.

Potential:

fake forms  
self-generated leads  
duplicate identities  
bot traffic.

Require:

source attribution  
quality thresholds  
delayed payout/validation.

---

# 29.32 Referral abuse

Example:

same customer creates many referral identities to collect rewards.

Signals:

shared phone  
shared device  
shared payment/booking context  
unusual referral graph.

Use graph-based detection later.

---

# 29.33 Promotion abuse

Example:

“First session free.”

Same customer creates new emails repeatedly.

Signals:

phone normalization  
customer identity  
device/session  
appointment history.

Do not use sensitive biometric identity casually.

---

# 29.34 Telephony fraud

Monitor:

```text
unusual destination
unusual call duration
international spike
high failure
premium-number calls
unexpected night calling
```

---

# 29.35 Call farming

A malicious destination or operator may keep calls active artificially.

Signals:

unusually long duration  
minimal meaningful conversation  
repetitive audio  
no business progression.

FinAI + FraudAI can detect.

---

# 29.36 Call-duration anomaly

Example:

Normal:

4 minutes.

Suddenly:

60–90 minute calls to same destination range.

Action:

```text
PAUSE_DESTINATION
```

and investigate.

---

# 29.37 Telephony velocity

Track:

```text
calls/min
calls/hour
cost/hour
```

per:

tenant  
campaign  
API credential  
destination prefix.

---

# 29.38 Credential abuse

If API key stolen:

attacker may start thousands of calls.

Controls:

short-lived credentials  
rate limits  
country restrictions  
budget limits  
behavior anomaly detection.

---

# 29.39 API request anomaly

Example:

Normal:

50 call-creation requests/min.

Suddenly:

5,000/min.

RiskAI/FraudAI:

```text
CREDENTIAL_ABUSE_SUSPECTED
```

Then:

rate limit  
revoke token  
stop campaign.

---

# 29.40 Tool abuse

Voice-agent user might attempt:

> “Cancel every appointment.”

Tool Gateway already prevents broad tool execution.

FraudAI can still log:

```text
BULK_ACTION_ATTEMPT
```

for security investigation.

---

# 29.41 Booking abuse

Potential:

repeatedly reserve slots and cancel

to block clinic capacity.

Track:

```text
booking_count
cancellation_count
no_show_count
reservation_expiry_count
```

Use carefully—legitimate customers can also reschedule often.

---

# 29.42 Slot-hold abuse

If temporary slot holds exist:

limit:

holds/customer  
holds/session  
hold duration.

Prevent scripts from locking all appointments.

---

# 29.43 SMS abuse

Compromised system could send high-volume SMS.

Control:

```text
messages/min
tenant budget
destination policy
template restrictions
```

---

# 29.44 OTP abuse

Attackers may repeatedly request OTP to harass a person or increase cost.

Limit:

resends  
attempts  
per-number/per-IP volume.

---

# 29.45 Fraud rule engine

Start deterministic.

Example:

```text
IF
same_ip_submissions > 50
AND
disposable_email_rate > 80%

THEN
risk = HIGH
```

Another:

```text
IF
destination = premium_rate
THEN
BLOCK
```

---

# 29.46 ML fraud model

Later, with sufficient labels, train:

logistic regression  
XGBoost

on:

velocity  
contact quality  
duplicate patterns  
source history  
interaction outcomes.

Avoid complex deep learning early.

---

# 29.47 Graph FraudAI

At larger scale:

```text
Customer
 ↔ Phone
 ↔ Email
 ↔ Device
 ↔ IP
 ↔ Campaign
 ↔ Referral
```

Graph patterns can expose coordinated abuse.

Neo4j or graph analytics may help.

---

# 29.48 Fraud graph example

```text
Device D1
 ├── 40 emails
 ├── 38 names
 └── 2 phone numbers
```

Strong coordinated pattern.

But shared kiosks/shared corporate networks need context.

---

# 29.49 Fraud reason codes

Examples:

```text
HIGH_IP_VELOCITY
HIGH_DEVICE_VELOCITY
PHONE_REUSED
EMAIL_DISPOSABLE
IDENTITY_CONFLICT
BOT_PATTERN
PREMIUM_DESTINATION
CALL_DURATION_ANOMALY
SOURCE_LOW_TRUST
PROMOTION_REUSE
```

---

# 29.50 Explainable fraud

Staff should see:

```text
REVIEW

Reasons:
27 forms from same device
8 customer names
same phone reused
```

Not:

> “AI says fraud.”

---

# 29.51 Fraud review queue

High-risk uncertain leads go to:

```text
FRAUD_REVIEW
```

Reviewer sees:

lead  
source  
signals  
history  
recommended action.

Actions:

```text
APPROVE
VERIFY
BLOCK
MERGE
```

---

# 29.52 Step-up verification

For medium risk:

send verification link/OTP where appropriate.

Then:

```text
verification_passed
→ authenticity increases
```

Avoid unnecessary friction for low-risk leads.

---

# 29.53 Verification modes

Potential:

phone OTP  
email verification  
customer confirmation during call.

Choose based on action risk.

---

# 29.54 Risk-based verification

General FAQ request:

low verification.

High-value account modification:

stronger verification.

Do not impose high-friction verification everywhere.

---

# 29.55 Fraud false positives

A fraud system can damage acquisition by blocking legitimate customers.

Track:

```text
fraud_review_overturn_rate
false_positive_rate
```

Especially:

shared family phones  
corporate networks  
university/public Wi-Fi.

---

# 29.56 False-negative monitoring

Fraud detected after action:

mark historical decision.

Feed into model/rules.

Examples:

fake lead complaint  
charge abuse  
campaign bot attack.

---

# 29.57 Champion/challenger

For fraud model:

production model makes decision.

new model runs shadow.

Compare:

precision  
recall  
review workload  
customer friction.

---

# 29.58 Cost-sensitive fraud threshold

Fraud errors have different costs.

False positive:

lost legitimate customer.

False negative:

wasted call cost / harassment / fraud.

Optimize threshold using expected cost + risk.

---

# 29.59 FraudAI + PolicyAI

Architecture:

```text
FraudAI
  ↓
risk signal
  ↓
PolicyAI
  ↓
ALLOW / VERIFY / REVIEW / BLOCK
```

FraudAI should not bypass centralized policy.

---

# 29.60 FraudAI + CampaignAI

If campaign/source fraud spikes:

```text
pause source
reduce traffic
manual review
```

before consuming more voice spend.

---

# 29.61 FraudAI + RouteAI

High-risk destination:

RouteAI should not try another telephony provider to bypass a block.

Fraud/policy restrictions apply globally.

---

# 29.62 FraudAI + FinAI

FinAI detects:

cost spike.

FraudAI checks:

international calls  
call farming  
credential abuse.

Together:

faster RCA.

---

# 29.63 FraudAI + Security

Security incident signals:

stolen credential  
API abuse  
automation attack.

SecurityAI may revoke identity.

FraudAI provides behavioral evidence.

---

# 29.64 FraudAI + MDM

Identity resolution should distinguish:

duplicate

from:

same household/shared business number.

MDM supplies canonical customer entities.

---

# 29.65 Source reputation

Maintain:

```text
SOURCE_REPUTATION

source_id

valid_rate
complaint_rate
conversion_rate
fraud_rate
```

Dynamic.

One bad affiliate should not contaminate all acquisition sources.

---

# 29.66 Number reputation

Maintain destination reputation:

```text
phone_hash
wrong_person_rate
never_requested_rate
fraud_reports
```

Use carefully and allow corrections.

---

# 29.67 Device/IP retention

These identifiers can be privacy-sensitive.

Use:

purpose limitation  
retention limits  
hashed/pseudonymous representation where appropriate.

Do not retain indefinitely “just in case.”

---

# 29.68 Fraud data access

Limit detailed signals to:

fraud/security teams.

Ordinary sales agents may only need:

```text
VERIFIED
REVIEW
BLOCKED
```

not raw IP/device history.

---

# 29.69 Monitoring dashboard

Show:

```text
Submissions
Blocked bots
Invalid phones
Disposable emails
Duplicates
Review queue
Premium-call blocks
Source risk
Telephony anomalies
```

---

# 29.70 Source health dashboard

Example:

| Source | Leads | Invalid | Fraud Risk | Never Requested |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Google | 1,200 | 3% | Low | 0.5% |
| Affiliate A | 900 | 31% | High | 17% |
| Referral | 320 | 1% | Low | 0.2% |

Affiliate A needs investigation.

---

# 29.71 Fraud funnel

```text
10,000 submissions
     ↓
9,200 schema-valid
     ↓
8,900 bot-clean
     ↓
8,300 contact-valid
     ↓
7,900 unique
     ↓
7,700 low-risk
     ↓
7,500 campaign eligible
```

This shows how much spend you're protecting.

---

# 29.72 Fraud KPIs

Track:

```text
Fraud detection rate
Bot rate
Invalid contact rate
Duplicate rate
Manual review rate
Review approval rate
False-positive rate
Never-requested complaint rate
Premium-call blocks
Cost prevented
```

---

# 29.73 Cost prevented

Example:

10,000 fake leads blocked.

Average outbound handling cost:

$0.50.

Potential avoided cost:

$5,000.

Label this as estimated prevented cost.

---

# 29.74 Alerting

Alerts:

```text
form submissions > baseline × N
premium destination attempt
never-requested complaints spike
international call spend spike
OTP abuse
same credential launches huge volume
```

---

# 29.75 Automated response

Safe automatic actions:

rate-limit abusive source  
pause suspicious campaign  
block premium ranges  
revoke compromised credential.

For uncertain customer fraud:

prefer review/verification.

---

# 29.76 Fraud incident workflow

```text
DETECTED
→ CONTAIN
→ INVESTIGATE
→ VERIFY IMPACT
→ FIX
→ RECOVER
→ RCA
→ NEW CONTROL
```

---

# 29.77 Testing

Create synthetic attacks:

```text
1,000 forms / minute
Disposable emails
Same phone / 50 names
Same IP / 500 leads
Premium number
International fraud burst
Repeated OTP
Duplicate booking
Referral ring
```

Verify expected risk/response.

---

# 29.78 Load test fraud layer

Fraud screening itself must not become acquisition bottleneck.

Test:

1k  
10k  
100k submissions/hour

depending target scale.

Cache/reuse safe reputation results where appropriate.

---

# 29.79 Edge case — corporate office IP

100 legitimate employees submit through same corporate NAT.

High IP velocity alone should not block them.

Combine:

device  
email domains  
timing  
behavior.

---

# 29.80 Edge case — family shares phone

Parents/spouse use one number.

Do not collapse automatically into one identity without appropriate context.

---

# 29.81 Edge case — customer repeatedly submits form because nobody called

Looks like duplicate abuse.

Actually operational failure.

Check:

previous contact status.

Potential response:

priority callback

rather than block.

---

# 29.82 Edge case — disposable email + valid phone

Could still be legitimate.

Maybe:

ALLOW_WITH_VERIFICATION

rather than BLOCK.

---

# 29.83 Edge case — VPN

VPN alone is not fraud.

Treat as weak signal.

---

# 29.84 Edge case — traveling customer

IP country differs from phone/service location.

Do not assume malicious intent.

---

# 29.85 Edge case — shared clinic receptionist phone

One business phone may represent many employees.

B2B data needs different duplicate rules from B2C.

---

# 29.86 Edge case — source changes suddenly

Affiliate quality was good for months.

Suddenly fake-lead rate spikes.

Dynamic source trust should respond quickly.

---

# 29.87 Edge case — attacker tests limits slowly

Low-and-slow abuse may evade velocity rules.

Use longer windows:

hour  
day  
week.

---

# 29.88 Edge case — fraud model learns language proxy

Avoid using language or name as suspiciousness proxy unless there is a legitimate, defensible technical reason unrelated to protected identity.

Fairness review required.

---

# 29.89 Edge case — customers challenged by fraud decision

Support correction/review.

Fraud score is a risk signal, not a statement of character.

---

# 29.90 Privacy

Collect only fraud signals necessary for stated security/business purpose.

Document:

retention  
access  
use.

Fraud prevention does not justify unlimited surveillance.

---

# 29.91 Fraud model explainability

For XGBoost, use reason mapping/SHAP internally.

Example:

```text
Risk 76

Drivers:
High device velocity
Phone reused
Source reputation degraded

Reducing risk:
Valid carrier
Customer answered previous call
```

---

# 29.92 Golden fraud dataset

Create labeled cases:

legitimate  
duplicate  
bot  
source fraud  
premium number  
credential abuse  
promotion abuse.

Track:

precision  
recall  
F1  
PR-AUC.

Fraud datasets are often imbalanced, so plain accuracy is misleading.

---

# 29.93 Fraud model drift

Monitor:

signal distributions  
review approvals  
complaints  
fraud confirmation.

If manual reviewers start overturning many blocks:

threshold/model may have drifted.

---

# 29.94 Fraud rule versioning

Store:

```text
FRAUD-RULESET-v8
```

Each decision logs version.

A fraud-policy change can have major conversion impact.

---

# 29.95 Release gates

Before new fraud model/rules:

offline benchmark  
false-positive assessment  
source segmentation  
shadow mode  
canary.

Do not roll to 100% immediately.

---

# 29.96 Fraud audit

Store:

```text
decision
signals
reason codes
model/rule version
review
override
final outcome
```

Access restricted.

---
