## 🤖 Assistant — msg #131

# Phase 42D — Inbound Routing + Queue + HumanOps Architecture

This phase defines how an inbound call moves from **phone number → AI agent → correct department → correct human queue → specialist → callback/fallback**, without dropping context or forcing the caller to repeat everything.

> **Routing should optimize for correctness first, then wait time, language fit, skill fit, customer preference, and operational cost.**

## 42D.1 Routing objectives

The routing layer should answer:

```text
Which tenant?
Which clinic?
Which service?
Which language?
Which intent?
Which AI agent?
Which human queue?
Which human skill?
Transfer now or callback?
What happens if no one is available?
```

## 42D.2 End-to-end inbound routing architecture

```text
Incoming Call
    ↓
DID / SIP Number
    ↓
Telephony Gateway
    ↓
Tenant Resolution
    ↓
Clinic Resolution
    ↓
Business-Hours Check
    ↓
Inbound Agent Profile
    ↓
Caller Resolution
    ↓
Language
    ↓
Intent / NeedAI
    ↓
RouteAI
    ↓
┌────────────────────────────────┐
│ AI Self-Service                │
│ Reception Queue                │
│ Service Queue                  │
│ Billing/Admin Queue            │
│ Language Queue                 │
│ Complaint Queue                │
│ Supervisor Queue               │
│ Callback Queue                 │
└────────────────────────────────┘
    ↓
HumanOps
    ↓
Warm Transfer / Callback
    ↓
Outcome
    ↓
Tracking + SLA + QA
```

## 42D.3 Routing dimensions

Route based on multiple dimensions, not only intent.

| Dimension | Example |
|---|---|
| Tenant | Clinic Group A |
| Location | NW clinic |
| Intent | Reschedule |
| Service | Physiotherapy |
| Language | Hindi |
| Customer type | Existing |
| Priority | Complaint |
| Human skill | Insurance/admin |
| Queue state | Overloaded |
| Business hours | Closed |
| Risk | High |
| Customer preference | Human requested |

## 42D.4 DID-based routing

Different numbers may map to different starting contexts.

Example:

```text
Main Clinic DID
→ GENERAL_INBOUND

Physio DID
→ PHYSIO_INBOUND

Corporate DID
→ B2B_SALES

After-Hours DID
→ AFTER_HOURS_AGENT
```

This reduces unnecessary intent discovery.

## 42D.5 DID routing configuration

```text
DID_ROUTE

did_id
phone_number
tenant_id
clinic_id

default_agent
default_language

business_hours_profile
after_hours_route

fallback_route
active
```

## 42D.6 Routing hierarchy

A useful precedence model:

```text
Emergency/Safety
    ↓
Explicit Human Request
    ↓
Complaint/Escalation
    ↓
Existing Transaction
    ↓
Service/Intent
    ↓
Language
    ↓
Availability
    ↓
General Queue
```

Do not route a complaint into a generic sales queue just because the caller mentioned physiotherapy.

## 42D.7 AI vs human decision

Before entering a human queue, determine whether AI can resolve the task safely.

Example:

```text
Clinic hours
→ AI

General pricing
→ AI

Book appointment
→ AI if tools healthy

Complex insurance
→ Human

Customer explicitly requests human
→ Human
```

## 42D.8 Queue taxonomy

Recommended queues:

```text
RECEPTION
PHYSIO
DENTAL
CHIROPRACTIC
ENT
MASSAGE

BILLING
INSURANCE_ADMIN

COMPLAINT
SUPERVISOR

CORPORATE_SALES

HINDI_SUPPORT
PUNJABI_SUPPORT
FRENCH_SUPPORT

CALLBACK
```

Avoid creating hundreds of tiny queues unnecessarily.

## 42D.9 Skill-based routing

Human workers can have skills:

```text
Physio
Insurance
Billing
Hindi
Punjabi
Complaint handling
Corporate sales
```

Example:

```text
Call requires:
INSURANCE + HINDI
```

Preferred worker:

```text
Employee A
skills:
Insurance
Hindi
```

## 42D.10 Skill model

```text
AGENT_SKILL

human_agent_id
skill_id

proficiency
certification_status

effective_from
effective_to
```

Do not infer skills from job title alone.

## 42D.11 Required vs preferred skills

Example:

```text
REQUIRED
Insurance

PREFERRED
Hindi
```

If Hindi specialist unavailable:

offer customer:

English-speaking insurance agent

or:

Hindi callback.

Do not silently downgrade language.

## 42D.12 Routing score

After hard filters:

```text
Route Score =
Skill Match
+ Language Match
+ Queue Wait
+ Customer Preference
+ Continuity
+ Workload Balance
```

Compliance/safety restrictions remain hard constraints.

## 42D.13 Continuity routing

If the caller previously worked with the same receptionist/specialist:

continuity may improve experience.

But only use if:

```text
person available
appropriate skill
wait acceptable
```

Do not create excessive delay simply to preserve continuity.

## 42D.14 Queue priority

Example:

```text
P0 Safety/Critical
P1 Complaint
P1 Customer-requested human
P2 Existing appointment issue
P3 New booking
P4 General information
```

Priority should reflect operational urgency, not customer revenue value.

## 42D.15 Priority queue model

```text
QUEUE_ITEM

queue_item_id
call_id
customer_id

queue_id
priority

required_skills[]
preferred_skills[]

entered_at
sla_due_at

status
```

## 42D.16 Queue states

```text
WAITING
OFFERED
ACCEPTED
CONNECTED
CALLBACK_SELECTED
ABANDONED
EXPIRED
FAILED
```

## 42D.17 Call state through transfer

```text
AI_ACTIVE
↓
TRANSFER_REQUESTED
↓
QUEUE_WAIT
↓
HUMAN_OFFERED
↓
HUMAN_ACCEPTED
↓
HANDOFF
↓
HUMAN_ACTIVE
```

Failures:

```text
TRANSFER_FAILED
QUEUE_TIMEOUT
CALLER_ABANDONED
```

## 42D.18 Warm transfer

Preferred for context-heavy cases.

Flow:

```text
AI
↓
Prepare transfer summary
↓
Place caller appropriately
↓
Offer call to human
↓
Human sees context
↓
Human accepts
↓
AI exits
↓
Caller connected
```

## 42D.19 Transfer summary

Include:

```text
Customer
Language
Intent
Need
Appointment
Important preferences
What AI already did
Outstanding question
Reason for transfer
```

Exclude irrelevant sensitive information.

## 42D.20 Warm-transfer user experience

Caller hears something like:

> “I’m connecting you with our clinic team. I’ll pass along what we’ve already discussed.”

This sets expectation that they should not have to repeat everything.

## 42D.21 Cold transfer

Use only where warm transfer isn't necessary/possible.

Risk:

customer may repeat information.

Track cold vs warm transfers separately.

## 42D.22 Human accept screen

Human sees:

```text
INCOMING TRANSFER

Customer
Raj

Intent
Reschedule

Service
Physiotherapy

Language
Hindi

Wait
38 sec

AI Summary
...

[ACCEPT]
[DECLINE]
```

## 42D.23 Human decline

If an offered call is declined:

```text
return to routing pool
```

Do not send caller back to the AI greeting.

Track decline reason where useful.

## 42D.24 Offer timeout

Human receives call offer but does not respond.

After configured threshold:

```text
OFFER_TIMEOUT
```

Try next eligible human.

## 42D.25 Queue wait-time prediction

Estimate:

```text
Expected Wait =
queue depth
×
service time
/
active capacity
```

More advanced models can use historical patterns.

Show only reliable estimates to customers.

## 42D.26 Hold vs callback

If predicted wait exceeds threshold:

offer:

```text
Continue holding
or
Receive callback
```

This is a major customer-experience feature.

## 42D.27 Callback-from-queue flow

```text
Caller chooses callback
↓
Capture/confirm callback details
↓
Create high-priority callback
↓
Preserve queue context
↓
End current call
```

Callback should retain:

```text
intent
queue
language
priority
summary
```

## 42D.28 Virtual queue

Instead of holding:

```text
Caller position retained
↓
System calls customer back
↓
When human capacity available
```

Useful for high-volume clinics.

## 42D.29 Callback priority

Queue callback should retain equivalent priority.

Do not move customer to bottom simply because they chose callback.

## 42D.30 Queue SLA

Example SLIs:

```text
Time to human
Transfer completion
Callback timeliness
Queue abandonment
```

SLOs should vary by queue.

Example:

```text
Complaint
higher priority

General admin
lower priority
```

## 42D.31 SLA object

```text
QUEUE_SLA

queue_id
priority
target_answer_seconds
callback_target_minutes
escalation_policy
```

## 42D.32 SLA countdown

Supervisor UI:

```text
Customer A
WAIT 1:42
SLA 2:00
18 sec remaining
```

High-risk calls become visually prominent.

## 42D.33 SLA breach workflow

```text
SLA nearing breach
↓
Raise priority
↓
Notify supervisor
↓
Consider alternate queue
↓
Offer callback
```

Do not simply record breach afterward.

## 42D.34 Queue overflow

Example:

Physio admin queue overloaded.

Possible route:

```text
PHYSIO_ADMIN
↓
GENERAL_RECEPTION
↓
CALLBACK
```

Only use alternate queue if staff are qualified.

## 42D.35 Overflow configuration

```text
QUEUE_OVERFLOW

primary_queue
secondary_queue
max_wait
callback_enabled
```

## 42D.36 Language overflow

Hindi queue unavailable.

Options:

```text
Hindi callback
English human with customer agreement
AI continue if suitable
```

Never silently route to unsupported language.

## 42D.37 After-hours queue routing

```text
Human queues closed
↓
AI handles supported intents
↓
Human-required
↓
Next business day callback queue
```

Store SLA relative to business reopening.

## 42D.38 Department closed while clinic open

Example:

clinic open until 8 PM.

Billing closes at 5 PM.

Routing must understand department-level hours.

## 42D.39 Business-hour configuration hierarchy

```text
Clinic Hours
Department Hours
Queue Hours
Individual Shift
```

All matter.

## 42D.40 Human availability states

```text
AVAILABLE
BUSY
WRAP_UP
BREAK
OFFLINE
DO_NOT_DISTURB
```

Routing should use actual status.

## 42D.41 Wrap-up state

After call, human may need time for:

notes  
CRM updates.

Do not immediately assign next call unless configuration allows.

## 42D.42 Auto-ready

Optional:

after wrap-up timer, return user to AVAILABLE.

Allow manual extension.

## 42D.43 Workload balancing

Avoid always routing to fastest/strongest agent.

Possible algorithms:

```text
Round robin
Least occupied
Longest idle
Skill-weighted
Priority-based
```

For MVP:

skill filter + longest idle is often reasonable.

## 42D.44 Skill-weighted routing

Example:

Agent A:

Insurance 100
Hindi 90

Agent B:

Insurance 100
Hindi 40

Hindi insurance customer:

Agent A ranked higher.

Scores should reflect verified operational competence, not subjective profiling.

## 42D.45 Simultaneous calls per human

Typically:

```text
voice concurrency = 1
```

unless special role.

Messaging may support higher concurrency.

Do not overload humans with multiple voice calls.

## 42D.46 AI concurrency

AI can handle many calls.

But downstream resources have limits:

```text
telephony
STT
LLM
TTS
scheduler
```

Queue layer should understand overall capacity.

## 42D.47 Backpressure

If scheduler is severely degraded:

do not let 1,000 inbound booking calls create retry storms.

Possible:

```text
temporarily disable booking
→ capture callback
```

while FAQ remains active.

## 42D.48 Admission control

During major overload:

prioritize:

```text
existing customer issues
customer-requested callbacks
critical queues
```

before low-value optional workflows.

## 42D.49 Human queue capacity model

Track:

```text
active agents
effective capacity
AHT
queue depth
arrival rate
```

Use for real-time staffing alerts.

## 42D.50 Erlang-style workforce planning

For more mature operations, use contact-center queueing models such as Erlang C assumptions where appropriate.

Inputs:

```text
calls/hour
average handle time
target service level
shrinkage
```

Then estimate staffing.

Actual voice-AI environment may violate classical assumptions, so validate against real traffic.

## 42D.51 Skill-based workforce planning

Don't only ask:

“How many agents?”

Ask:

```text
How many Hindi-speaking staff?
How many billing staff?
How many complaint specialists?
```

Capacity must be skill-specific.

## 42D.52 Callback workload forecast

Callbacks consume future capacity.

Forecast:

```text
callbacks due/hour
+
expected inbound transfer workload
```

Otherwise queue may look fine now but fail later.

## 42D.53 HumanOps master record

```text
HUMAN_AGENT

agent_id
tenant_id

name
status

skills[]
languages[]

queues[]

shift
current_call

daily_calls
AHT
```

Keep performance data access appropriately controlled.

## 42D.54 Queue membership

An agent can belong to multiple queues:

```text
Reception
Hindi
Physio
```

Routing uses all applicable memberships.

## 42D.55 Dynamic queue membership

Supervisors can temporarily add/remove agents during spikes.

Example:

```text
Billing overload
→ supervisor adds general admin staff
```

Only if appropriately trained/authorized.

## 42D.56 Supervisor console

Show:

```text
Active calls
Waiting queues
Longest waits
Callbacks due
Agents available
Agents busy
SLA risks
Transfer failures
```

## 42D.57 Supervisor actions

```text
Take over call
Assign human
Reassign queue
Increase priority
Create callback
Pause queue
Activate overflow
```

All audited.

## 42D.58 Queue dashboard

Example:

| Queue | Waiting | Available | Avg Wait | Oldest | SLA |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Reception | 4 | 5 | 34s | 1:22 | Good |
| Billing | 9 | 2 | 4:12 | 7:01 | Risk |
| Hindi | 2 | 1 | 1:31 | 2:14 | Watch |

## 42D.59 Queue detail screen

Show waiting customers:

```text
Priority
Wait
Intent
Language
Customer
AI summary
SLA
```

Human can click caller for preview if permitted.

## 42D.60 Agent status dashboard

```text
AVAILABLE        12
ON CALL           8
WRAP UP            3
BREAK              2
OFFLINE            5
```

Break down by skill.

## 42D.61 Transfer dashboard

Track:

```text
transfer requested
transfer successful
transfer failed
callback chosen
queue abandoned
```

## 42D.62 Transfer success rate

```text
successful human connections
/
valid transfer requests
```

Do not confuse with total calls.

## 42D.63 Queue abandonment rate

```text
customers who leave queue
/
customers entering queue
```

Analyze against wait duration.

## 42D.64 Callback adoption

Measure:

```text
% callers choosing callback
when offered
```

Useful for queue design.

## 42D.65 Callback completion

```text
callbacks completed
/
callbacks promised
```

Critical customer trust metric.

## 42D.66 First Contact Resolution

If human resolves issue after AI transfer during same call:

still counts as FCR.

AI-only and human-assisted FCR should be reported separately.

## 42D.67 Transfer repetition

Bad experience:

```text
AI
→ Reception
→ Billing
→ Reception
→ Supervisor
```

Track:

```text
transfers_per_call
```

High repeat-transfer rate indicates routing failure.

## 42D.68 Transfer loop detection

If queue path repeats:

```text
Billing
→ Reception
→ Billing
```

detect and escalate to supervisor.

## 42D.69 Wrong-queue detection

Human marks:

```text
WRONG_QUEUE
```

with correct target.

This becomes training data for RouteAI.

## 42D.70 Human feedback to routing

After transfer:

```text
Was this routed correctly?
YES / NO
```

Optional quick control.

Avoid burdening every agent excessively; sample if needed.

## 42D.71 RouteAI learning

Training signals:

```text
Correct queue
Transfer success
Resolution
Re-transfer
Wait
Customer effort
```

Do not optimize only wait time.

## 42D.72 Routing model maturity

### Stage 1

Rules.

### Stage 2

Rules + scoring.

### Stage 3

Predictive routing.

### Stage 4

Capacity-aware optimization.

Start with Stage 1–2.

## 42D.73 Rule-based routing example

```text
IF intent = BILLING
→ Billing Queue

IF language = HINDI
AND intent = INSURANCE
→ Hindi Insurance Queue

IF customer_requests_human
AND no specialist need
→ Reception
```

## 42D.74 Route fallback

If target queue unavailable:

```text
preferred queue
↓
approved fallback
↓
callback
```

No arbitrary department selection.

## 42D.75 Customer choice

Sometimes customer should choose:

> “I can connect you with billing now, or arrange a callback from a Hindi-speaking team member.”

Explicit choice improves trust.

## 42D.76 Queue message design

Keep hold messages informative but minimal.

Possible:

```text
Your call is still in the queue.
```

If accurate:

```text
You can continue holding or request a callback.
```

Avoid repeating sales promotions during complaint queues.

## 42D.77 Queue music

If used:

ensure transitions between AI speech, hold audio, and human are clean.

No overlapping audio.

## 42D.78 Transfer context persistence

When call enters queue:

ConversationAI session should not lose state.

Human desktop receives structured summary.

If AI resumes after failed transfer:

same conversation context continues.

## 42D.79 Human-to-AI return

Optional advanced feature:

human handles difficult question

then returns call to AI for:

booking  
confirmation.

Use explicit handoff.

Avoid hidden switching.

## 42D.80 Supervisor takeover

Supervisor can join active AI call.

Modes could include:

```text
LISTEN
TAKEOVER
```

If whisper/coaching is implemented, design carefully so the customer experience and operational policies are clear.

## 42D.81 Live-call risk flag

Example:

```text
3 customer corrections
+
tool failure
+
high frustration
```

Supervisor UI:

```text
INTERVENTION RECOMMENDED
```

## 42D.82 Call prioritization during incident

Booking API down.

Thousands of booking-related calls.

Route:

```text
general FAQ remains AI
booking intent → callback queue
complaints → humans
```

This protects scarce staff.

## 42D.83 Queue-level kill switch

Example:

```text
PAUSE AUTOMATIC BILLING TRANSFERS
```

during an incident.

Calls can route:

reception/callback.

## 42D.84 Human-system outage

If workforce UI unavailable:

voice platform should have controlled fallback:

callback  
voicemail  
basic routing.

Do not leave customer in infinite queue.

## 42D.85 Telephony transfer failure

Retry safely if provider error is transient.

If transfer state uncertain:

reconcile before initiating second transfer.

## 42D.86 Duplicate transfer request

ConversationAI and NextAI both produce human request.

Idempotency should create one queue item.

## 42D.87 Call ends while waiting

Queue receives disconnect signal.

Remove item promptly.

Do not later connect human to dead call.

## 42D.88 Caller reconnects

Optionally associate recent abandoned/failed queue session.

But revalidate current intent.

## 42D.89 Callback duplicate prevention

If customer already has active callback:

update it rather than create another.

## 42D.90 Priority inversion

Low-priority call should not indefinitely occupy specialist capacity while high-priority complaint waits.

Use priority scheduling with starvation protection.

## 42D.91 Starvation prevention

Low-priority callers still need eventual service.

Possible:

aging factor.

```text
effective_priority =
base_priority
+
wait_age
```

Use carefully.

## 42D.92 Queue fairness

Do not prioritize based on:

customer wealth  
commercial value

for basic healthcare administrative support.

Use operational/service urgency and customer request.

## 42D.93 Multi-tenant fairness

Tenant A load shouldn't consume all shared human/voice resources.

Use:

```text
tenant quotas
weighted fair scheduling
```

where resources are shared.

## 42D.94 Queue isolation

Some queues should be tenant-specific.

Shared outsourced support queues may support multiple tenants but require strict context isolation.

## 42D.95 Shared-agent UI

If human supports multiple clinics:

display clinic branding/context prominently.

Prevent:

> “Thank you for calling Clinic B”

when caller belongs to Clinic A.

## 42D.96 Skill mismatch guard

Human should not receive tasks outside authorized skills.

Backend enforcement, not only UI filtering.

## 42D.97 Queue security

Ensure:

```text
tenant authorization
queue authorization
call authorization
```

before exposing live caller details.

## 42D.98 PII masking before accept

Queue preview can show only:

```text
Raj S.
***1234
Intent: billing
```

Full permitted details appear after accept if role allows.

## 42D.99 Audit

Track:

```text
who accepted
who declined
who transferred
who reprioritized
who took over
who changed queue
```

with timestamp/reason.

## 42D.100 Routing event model

Publish:

```text
routing.requested
routing.decision
queue.entered
queue.priority_changed
queue.callback_selected

transfer.offered
transfer.accepted
transfer.failed

human.connected
human.disconnected
```

Example:

```text
Intent:
INSURANCE

Language:
Hindi

Reception
Insurance
Hindi Insurance

Selected:
Hindi Insurance
```

```text
entered_at

accepted_at
```

Allows precise operational reporting.

## 42D.103 Human wrap-up code

At call end, human selects/validates:

```text
RESOLVED
CALLBACK
TRANSFERRED
UNRESOLVED
```

plus reason.

Avoid excessive manual coding if AI can prepopulate it accurately.

## 42D.104 AI-assisted disposition

AI proposes:

```text
RESOLVED — insurance question
```

Human:

```text
ACCEPT / EDIT
```

Good productivity feature.

## 42D.105 Queue forecasting

Forecast by:

```text
hour
weekday
clinic
intent
language
```

Example:

Monday 8–10 AM:

high reschedule volume.

Use historical event data.

Example:

```text
Expected calls     180
Expected transfers 42

Recommended:
Reception 5
Billing 2
Hindi 1
```

HumanOps can use this for planning.

## 42D.107 Real-time capacity anomaly

Example:

Billing:

arrival rate ↑ 80%.

System:

```text
QUEUE_SURGE
```

| Language | Waiting | Available | SLA Risk |
|---|---:|---:|---:|

Example:

```text
Insurance Hindi
demand = 84 calls/week

```

This becomes workforce planning evidence.

## 42D.112 Transfer reason report

Track:

```text
Human requested
Insurance

Unsupported task

```

High AI uncertainty → improve AI.

High insurance → perhaps build more self-service.

## 42D.113 Wrong-route report

Example:

```text
Insurance calls incorrectly sent to Reception
14%
```

## 42D.114 Re-transfer report

Track:

```text
calls requiring >1 human queue
```

Aim to reduce.

## 42D.115 Queue abandonment curve

Plot:

```text
abandonment probability
vs
wait seconds
```

Helps set callback-offer timing.

## 42D.116 Callback offer threshold

If data shows abandonment jumps after 120 sec:

offer callback before that.

ExperimentAI can validate.

## 42D.117 Operational experiment

Test:

callback offer at:

60 sec

vs:

120 sec.

Measure:

abandonment

CX.

Do not test critical safety queues casually.

## 42D.118 Quality metrics

For routing:

```text
Correct queue
First human resolves
Re-transfer
Customer repeats information
Wait
Callback fulfillment
```

These matter more than routing latency alone.

## 42D.119 Customer repeat-information metric

Human asks customer to repeat full story despite AI summary.

Capture via QA/human feedback.

Goal:

reduce.

Examples:

```text
Intent = Billing
Language = English
→ Billing

Intent = Insurance

→ Hindi Insurance

Intent = Human request
No specialist requirement
→ Reception

Intent = Complaint
→ Complaint/Supervisor
```

Include queue availability variants.

## 42D.121 Routing test — queue unavailable

Expected:

approved fallback.

Not:

random queue.

## 42D.122 Routing test — preferred language unavailable

Expected:

customer option/fallback.

## 42D.123 Routing test — explicit human request

Expected:

no unnecessary AI qualification.

## 42D.124 Routing test — complaint

Expected:

sales queue never selected.

## 42D.125 Routing test — shared tenant workforce

Verify Clinic A context doesn't leak to Clinic B.

## 42D.126 Concurrency test

1,000 simultaneous calls entering routing.

Ensure:

no duplicate queue items  
low routing latency  
correct priority.

## 42D.127 Load test

Test:

```text
100
500
1,000
5,000
```

concurrent waiting/active items depending target scale.

## 42D.128 Chaos test

Kill routing service instance.

Expected:

failover.

Kill queue datastore.

Expected:

controlled degraded mode.

## 42D.129 Telephony chaos test

Transfer provider unavailable.

Expected:

callback fallback.

## 42D.130 HumanOps chaos test

Agent-presence service unavailable.

Do not promise immediate human.

Offer callback/general fallback.

## 42D.131 Queue persistence

Waiting state must survive service restart.

Use durable state where required.

## 42D.132 Recommended implementation

Possible stack:

```text
Routing Service
Python/FastAPI or Java/Spring Boot

Events

Temporal

Realtime UI
```

## 42D.133 Avoid routing logic inside voice vendor

Even if Retell/Vapi/Bolna supports transfers, keep enterprise routing rules in your control plane where possible.

Voice platform can execute the transfer.

Your platform decides:

```text
where
why
when
```

This reduces vendor lock-in.

## 42D.134 Telephony abstraction

Use:

```text
TRANSFER_REQUEST

call_id
destination_route_id
mode = WARM
```

Then telephony adapter translates into provider-specific API.

The next inbound phase is **Phase 42E — Inbound Call State Machine + Conversation Flow Engine**, covering every state from **ringing → greeting → identification → intent → self-service → verification → tool execution → human queue → transfer → callback → close**, including allowed/forbidden state transitions, timeouts, retries, state recovery, call drops, multi-intent flows, and full state-level test coverage.

## 🤖 Assistant — msg #133

# Phase 42E — Inbound Call State Machine + Conversation Flow Engine

This phase makes the inbound voice agent predictable, testable, and recoverable by defining every valid call state and every permitted transition.

> **The LLM understands the caller and generates natural language. The state machine controls where the call is allowed to go.**

## 42E.1 Why this layer is necessary

Without an explicit state machine, the agent can:

- ask questions that were already answered,
- book before confirmation,
- continue selling after a human request,
- lose context during transfer,
- mishandle call drops,
- repeat tool actions,
- confuse reschedule with new booking,
- or return to the wrong part of the conversation after an FAQ.

The state engine prevents those failures.

## 42E.2 Master inbound state model

```text
CALL_CREATED
     ↓
RINGING
     ↓
CONNECTED
     ↓
INITIALIZING
     ↓
GREETING
     ↓
LANGUAGE_RESOLUTION
     ↓
CALLER_CONTEXT
     ↓
INTENT_DISCOVERY
     ↓
NEED_DISCOVERY
     ↓
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ FAQ / INFORMATION                       │
│ AVAILABILITY                            │
│ BOOKING                                 │
│ APPOINTMENT_LOOKUP                      │
│ RESCHEDULE                              │
│ CANCEL                                  │
│ BILLING / ADMIN                         │
│ COMPLAINT                               │
│ HUMAN_REQUEST                           │
│ CALLBACK                                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘
     ↓
ACTION / RESOLUTION
     ↓
CONFIRMATION
     ↓
FOLLOW_UP
     ↓
CLOSING
     ↓
COMPLETED
```

Global exits:

```text
ANY STATE
 ├── HUMAN_TRANSFER
 ├── CALLBACK
 ├── SAFETY_ESCALATION
 ├── CALL_DROPPED
 ├── CUSTOMER_HANGUP
 ├── TECHNICAL_FAILURE
 └── TERMINATED
```

## 42E.3 State object

```text
CALL_STATE

call_id
conversation_id
tenant_id

current_state
previous_state

state_entered_at
state_version

primary_intent
active_sub_intent

customer_id
caller_resolution_status

language
service

slots{}
constraints{}

pending_action
pending_tool

completed_actions[]

transfer_state
callback_state

policy_state
risk_state

retry_count
clarification_count
correction_count

last_turn_id
```

## 42E.4 State families

Organize states into families.

| Family | States |
|---|---|
| Telephony | CREATED, RINGING, CONNECTED |
| Initialization | CONFIG_LOAD, POLICY_INIT |
| Conversation | GREETING, LANGUAGE, INTENT |
| Discovery | NEED, CONSTRAINT, CLARIFICATION |
| Knowledge | FAQ, PRICE, HOURS, LOCATION |
| Transaction | AVAILABILITY, BOOK, RESCHEDULE, CANCEL |
| Verification | IDENTITY_CHECK, CONFIRMATION |
| HumanOps | QUEUE, TRANSFER, HUMAN_ACTIVE |
| Follow-up | CALLBACK, MESSAGE |
| Recovery | TOOL_FAILURE, RETRY, RECONCILE |
| Terminal | COMPLETED, HANGUP, FAILED |

## 42E.5 Telephony states

```text
CALL_CREATED
↓
RINGING
↓
CONNECTED
```

Possible outcomes:

```text
NO_CONNECT
REJECTED
PROVIDER_FAILURE
```

For inbound calls, `RINGING → CONNECTED` should usually happen quickly because AI can answer immediately.

## 42E.6 Initialization state

Immediately after connection:

```text
INITIALIZING
```

Load:

```text
tenant configuration
clinic
DID route
business hours
agent version
policy configuration
language hints
```

Do not begin complex conversation before critical runtime configuration is known.

## 42E.7 Initialization failure

If tenant configuration cannot be loaded:

```text
INITIALIZING
→ SAFE_FALLBACK
```

Potential response:

> “I’m unable to access the clinic system right now. I can connect you with the clinic team or take a callback request.”

Do not let the LLM improvise tenant information.

## 42E.8 Greeting state

```text
GREETING
```

Responsibilities:

```text
organization identification
AI disclosure where applicable
basic opening
```

Then transition to:

```text
LANGUAGE_RESOLUTION
```

or directly to intent if language is already established.

## 42E.9 Language-resolution state

Possible output:

```text
language = ENGLISH
confidence = 0.98
```

or customer explicitly requests:

```text
language = HINDI
source = CUSTOMER_EXPLICIT
```

Then:

```text
LANGUAGE_RESOLUTION
→ CALLER_CONTEXT
```

Language changes later are permitted without resetting business state.

## 42E.10 Caller-context state

Determine:

```text
KNOWN
UNKNOWN
MULTIPLE_MATCH
UNRESOLVED
```

This state should not block general FAQ access.

Example:

```text
UNKNOWN caller
+
asks clinic hours
```

→ no identity verification needed.

## 42E.11 Intent-discovery state

Caller:

> “I need to move my appointment.”

Extract:

```text
intent = RESCHEDULE
confidence = HIGH
```

Then transition:

```text
INTENT_DISCOVERY
→ APPOINTMENT_LOOKUP
```

not:

```text
INTENT_DISCOVERY
→ NEW_BOOKING
```

## 42E.12 Low-confidence intent

If:

```text
intent confidence < threshold
```

transition:

```text
INTENT_DISCOVERY
→ CLARIFY_INTENT
```

Possible question:

> “Are you trying to book a new appointment or change one you already have?”

## 42E.13 Intent transition table

| Intent | Next state |
|---|---|
| General information | FAQ |
| Price | PRICE |
| Availability | AVAILABILITY |
| Book | BOOKING_DISCOVERY |
| Reschedule | APPOINTMENT_LOOKUP |
| Cancel | APPOINTMENT_LOOKUP |
| Human | HUMAN_ROUTE |
| Complaint | COMPLAINT |
| Callback | CALLBACK_CAPTURE |
| Unknown | CLARIFY_INTENT |

## 42E.14 Multi-intent state

Caller:

> “I need to reschedule and I also want to know the cancellation fee.”

Maintain:

```text
ACTIVE_INTENT
RESCHEDULE

PENDING_INTENT
CANCELLATION_POLICY
```

Flow:

```text
RESCHEDULE
→ temporary PRICE/POLICY FAQ
→ return to RESCHEDULE
```

Use an intent stack.

## 42E.15 Intent stack

```text
INTENT_STACK

active_intent
pending_intents[]
completed_intents[]
```

This prevents the conversation from forgetting the original purpose.

## 42E.16 Need-discovery state

For new booking:

```text
BOOKING_DISCOVERY
```

Collect only missing required fields.

Example caller already says:

> “Physio Thursday after six at NW.”

State already contains:

```text
service = PHYSIO
day = THURSDAY
time > 18:00
location = NW
```

Then go directly to availability.

## 42E.17 Missing-slot engine

Each task defines required slots.

Example booking:

```text
service
date/time constraint
location when required
customer details before commit
```

Compute:

```text
MISSING_SLOTS[]
```

Then ask the highest-value missing question.

## 42E.18 Slot dependency

Some slots depend on others.

Example:

```text
provider
```

may depend on:

```text
service
location
```

Do not ask provider before service context exists if it adds no value.

## 42E.19 Clarification state

Use:

```text
CLARIFICATION
```

for ambiguous but recoverable information.

Examples:

```text
Tuesday or Thursday?
6 AM or 6 PM?
NW or NE?
```

After resolution:

return to previous state.

## 42E.20 Clarification stack

Store:

```text
return_state
clarification_field
```

Example:

```text
return_state = AVAILABILITY
field = time
```

This prevents losing task flow.

## 42E.21 FAQ state

```text
FAQ
```

Flow:

```text
question classification
↓
KnowledgeAI / structured source
↓
answer
↓
return to prior task
```

Example:

Booking task interrupted by:

> “How much is it?”

Answer price, then resume booking.

## 42E.22 FAQ return state

Always store:

```text
resume_state
```

Example:

```text
BOOKING_DISCOVERY
→ PRICE
→ BOOKING_DISCOVERY
```

This is critical for natural conversations.

## 42E.23 Availability state

Prerequisites:

```text
service known
sufficient timing/location constraints
scheduler accessible
```

Then:

```text
AVAILABILITY
→ TOOL_REQUEST
```

## 42E.24 Availability result states

Scheduler can return:

```text
SLOTS_FOUND
NO_MATCH
TOOL_FAILURE
```

Transitions:

```text
SLOTS_FOUND
→ PRESENT_OPTIONS

NO_MATCH
→ ALTERNATIVE_OPTIONS

TOOL_FAILURE
→ RECOVERY
```

## 42E.25 Present-options state

Store:

```text
presented_slots[]
```

Caller response should resolve against these options.

Example:

> “The first one.”

This should map to:

```text
presented_slots[0]
```

not require re-parsing arbitrary date/time.

## 42E.26 Slot-selection state

Possible:

```text
SELECTED
REJECTED
AMBIGUOUS
```

If ambiguous:

clarify.

If rejected:

ask preference or retrieve alternatives.

## 42E.27 Booking confirmation state

Before writing:

```text
BOOKING_CONFIRMATION
```

Show critical values:

```text
service
date
time
location
```

Example:

> “To confirm, physiotherapy at the NW clinic Thursday at 6:30 PM?”

## 42E.28 Explicit confirmation

Required:

```text
YES / CONFIRMED
```

before transition:

```text
BOOKING_CONFIRMATION
→ BOOK_TOOL
```

Ambiguous response:

> “Okay…”

may require context-sensitive confirmation depending confidence/risk.

## 42E.29 Booking tool state

```text
BOOK_TOOL
```

Tool result:

```text
SUCCESS
BUSINESS_CONFLICT
TECHNICAL_FAILURE
UNKNOWN
```

Each needs a different state.

## 42E.30 Booking success

```text
BOOK_TOOL
→ BOOKED
```

Store:

```text
appointment_id
confirmed date/time
source = scheduler
```

Only now can the agent say:

> “Your appointment is booked.”

## 42E.31 Booking conflict

Slot taken:

```text
BOOK_TOOL
→ SLOT_CONFLICT
→ AVAILABILITY
```

Retrieve alternatives.

Do not say:

> “Something went wrong.”

when you know the business reason.

## 42E.32 Unknown booking result

Timeout after request.

Transition:

```text
BOOK_TOOL
→ TRANSACTION_UNKNOWN
→ RECONCILIATION
```

Do not immediately retry.

## 42E.33 Reconciliation state

Lookup using:

```text
idempotency key
provider transaction ID
customer/time/service
```

Result:

```text
FOUND
NOT_FOUND
UNRESOLVED
```

Then continue safely.

## 42E.34 Appointment lookup state

For:

```text
RESCHEDULE
CANCEL
APPOINTMENT_INFO
```

Flow:

```text
APPOINTMENT_LOOKUP
↓
identity requirement?
↓
retrieve appointments
```

## 42E.35 Identity-check state

Possible:

```text
NOT_REQUIRED
REQUIRED
PASSED
FAILED
INCONCLUSIVE
```

Action-specific policy determines requirement.

## 42E.36 Identity failure

Do not expose appointment information.

Possible:

```text
IDENTITY_FAILED
→ HUMAN
```

or controlled retry if permitted.

## 42E.37 Multiple appointments

State:

```text
APPOINTMENT_SELECTION
```

Present minimal distinguishing information allowed.

Customer selects.

Then continue.

## 42E.38 Reschedule state

Flow:

```text
APPOINTMENT_SELECTED
↓
RESCHEDULE_DISCOVERY
↓
AVAILABILITY
↓
NEW_SLOT_SELECTED
↓
RESCHEDULE_CONFIRMATION
↓
RESCHEDULE_TOOL
```

## 42E.39 Reschedule transaction integrity

Do not remove old appointment until scheduler confirms new transaction semantics.

Depending scheduler API:

atomic reschedule

is preferable to:

cancel old → create new.

## 42E.40 Reschedule success

```text
RESCHEDULE_TOOL
→ RESCHEDULED
```

Then:

```text
cancel obsolete reminders
create new reminders
send confirmation
```

## 42E.41 Cancel state

Flow:

```text
APPOINTMENT_SELECTED
↓
CANCEL_CONFIRMATION
↓
CANCEL_TOOL
↓
CANCELLED
```

Explicit confirmation should be required.

## 42E.42 Cancellation ambiguity

Customer:

> “I might not make it.”

Do not transition to cancellation confirmation yet.

Possible state:

```text
CANCELLATION_DISCUSSION
```

Clarify actual intent.

## 42E.43 Human-request global transition

At nearly any conversation state:

```text
ANY
→ HUMAN_ROUTE
```

Examples:

```text
FAQ → HUMAN_ROUTE
BOOKING → HUMAN_ROUTE
PRICE → HUMAN_ROUTE
```

Do not force task completion before honoring human request.

## 42E.44 Human-route state

Determine:

```text
department
skill
language
priority
```

Then:

```text
HUMAN_ROUTE
→ HUMAN_QUEUE
```

## 42E.45 Human queue state

Possible events:

```text
HUMAN_ACCEPTED
CUSTOMER_CALLBACK_CHOSEN
QUEUE_TIMEOUT
CALLER_HANGUP
TRANSFER_FAILURE
```

Transitions accordingly.

## 42E.46 Warm-transfer state

```text
TRANSFER_PREP
↓
CONTEXT_SUMMARY
↓
TRANSFER_EXECUTE
↓
HUMAN_CONNECTED
```

Once human connected:

```text
AI_ACTIVE = FALSE
```

## 42E.47 Transfer failure recovery

```text
TRANSFER_FAILED
```

Then options:

```text
alternate queue
callback
resume AI
```

based on reason and customer preference.

Do not return to opening greeting.

## 42E.48 Callback-capture state

Collect:

```text
reason
preferred date
preferred time/window
language
contact point if required
```

Then confirmation.

## 42E.49 Callback confirmation state

Example:

> “I’ll arrange a callback tomorrow after 6 PM regarding physiotherapy.”

Customer confirms.

Then:

```text
CREATE_CALLBACK
```

## 42E.50 Callback success

Store:

```text
callback_id
scheduled_for
queue
```

Then close or continue other questions.

## 42E.51 Complaint state

When complaint identified:

```text
COMPLAINT
```

Behavior changes:

```text
disable upsell
capture issue
determine severity
offer appropriate human route
```

Complaint remains active context until resolved/handoff.

## 42E.52 Safety/restricted state

For clinic-approved restricted/urgent scenarios:

```text
RESTRICTED
```

Commercial state stack should be suspended.

Follow approved response/escalation.

Do not automatically return to sales flow unless appropriate.

## 42E.53 DNC/preference state

Inbound caller may say:

> “Don't call me again.”

Transition:

```text
ANY
→ CONTACT_PREFERENCE_UPDATE
```

Update appropriate preference/suppression.

Then return or close based on caller request.

## 42E.54 Information-only state

Caller:

> “Just answer my question, I don't want to book.”

Set:

```text
INFORMATION_ONLY = TRUE
```

Then NextAI should suppress unsolicited booking/up-sell CTAs during the current interaction.

## 42E.55 Closing state

Before ending:

```text
CLOSING
```

Generate outcome-accurate summary.

Examples:

Booked:

> “Your appointment is confirmed for Thursday at 6:30.”

Callback:

> “A callback is scheduled for tomorrow after six.”

FAQ-only:

> “I’m glad I could help.”

## 42E.56 Closing guard

Closing statements must use authoritative outcome state.

Never rely purely on generated transcript summary.

## 42E.57 Terminal states

Possible:

```text
COMPLETED
CUSTOMER_HANGUP
CALL_DROPPED
FAILED
TRANSFERRED
CALLBACK_CREATED
```

Business disposition remains separate.

## 42E.58 Telephony terminal vs business outcome

Example:

```text
Telephony:
COMPLETED

Business:
BOOKED
```

or:

```text
Telephony:
COMPLETED

Business:
FAQ_RESOLVED
```

Keep both fields.

## 42E.59 Call-drop state

If connection lost:

```text
CALL_DROPPED
```

Store:

```text
last stable state
pending transaction
current intent
```

FollowUpAI determines recovery.

## 42E.60 Call drop before transaction

Example:

customer selected slot

but had not confirmed.

Outcome:

```text
NOT_BOOKED
```

Do not infer booking.

## 42E.61 Call drop during transaction

Possible:

```text
TRANSACTION_UNKNOWN
```

Reconcile before callback or subsequent communication.

## 42E.62 Resume after reconnect

If customer immediately calls back:

retrieve recent interrupted session.

Possible response:

> “It looks like our previous call was disconnected.”

Resume only after validating transaction state.

## 42E.63 Session recovery

Persist state periodically/event-wise.

Minimum:

```text
active intent
critical slots
selected option
transaction state
```

Do not depend only on in-memory LLM context.

## 42E.64 Redis + durable state

Pattern:

```text
Redis
→ realtime conversation state

PostgreSQL/event store
→ durable important transitions
```

Critical transactional state should survive Redis loss.

## 42E.65 Event-sourced approach

Every state transition produces:

```text
STATE_CHANGED
```

Store:

```text
from
to
reason
turn
timestamp
```

Then current state can be reconstructed.

## 42E.66 Transition event

```text
CALL_STATE_EVENT

event_id
call_id

from_state
to_state

trigger
reason_code

turn_id
timestamp
```

## 42E.67 Allowed-transition matrix

Example:

| From | Event | To |
|---|---|---|
| GREETING | customer speaks | INTENT_DISCOVERY |
| INTENT | BOOK | BOOKING_DISCOVERY |
| BOOKING_DISCOVERY | fields complete | AVAILABILITY |
| AVAILABILITY | slots | PRESENT_OPTIONS |
| PRESENT_OPTIONS | slot selected | BOOK_CONFIRM |
| BOOK_CONFIRM | yes | BOOK_TOOL |
| BOOK_TOOL | success | BOOKED |
| ANY | human request | HUMAN_ROUTE |
| ANY | disconnect | CALL_DROPPED |

## 42E.68 Forbidden transition examples

These should never occur:

```text
GREETING
→ BOOK_TOOL
```

```text
DNC UPDATE
→ UPSELL
```

```text
BOOK_TOOL
→ BOOKED
```

without authoritative success.

```text
HUMAN_CONNECTED
→ AI_AUTO_SPEAK
```

unless explicitly handed back.

## 42E.69 Transition guards

Example:

```text
BOOK_CONFIRM
→ BOOK_TOOL
```

guard:

```text
customer_confirmed == true
service != null
slot_id != null
policy == ALLOW
```

If any false:

transition rejected.

## 42E.70 Guard failure

Return:

```text
STATE_GUARD_FAILED
```

with reason:

```text
MISSING_CONFIRMATION
```

NextAI determines corrective action.

## 42E.71 State timeout

Each state may have timeout.

Examples:

```text
TOOL_WAIT
TRANSFER_WAIT
CUSTOMER_SILENCE
```

Different states require different timeout behavior.

## 42E.72 Customer-silence timeout

Example:

```text
5 sec → wait
10 sec → gentle reprompt
20 sec → final check
30 sec → controlled close
```

Illustrative only; tune for actual voice UX.

## 42E.73 Tool timeout

Scheduler:

```text
2–3 sec target
```

If timeout:

transition to:

```text
TOOL_FAILURE
```

not endless spinner.

## 42E.74 Transfer timeout

If no human accepts within configured wait:

offer callback.

Avoid infinite queueing.

## 42E.75 Retry state

Technical transient error:

```text
TOOL_FAILURE
→ RETRY
```

Retry count controlled.

Then either:

```text
SUCCESS
```

or:

```text
FALLBACK
```

## 42E.76 Retry budget

Per operation define:

```text
max_attempts
backoff
timeout
```

Do not let state machine enter infinite retry loop.

## 42E.77 Conversation loop detection

Detect repeated cycle:

```text
ASK_LOCATION
→ CUSTOMER_ANSWER
→ ASK_LOCATION
→ CUSTOMER_ANSWER
```

After threshold:

```text
LOOP_DETECTED
→ CLARIFY/HUMAN
```

## 42E.78 State loop metrics

Track:

```text
repeated_state_count
state_cycle_count
```

ObserveAI alerts when agent version creates abnormal loops.

## 42E.79 Correction handling

Customer:

> “No, Thursday.”

Event:

```text
CUSTOMER_CORRECTION
```

State updater:

```text
day = Thursday
old day = superseded
```

Then resume current task.

## 42E.80 Critical correction

If previous wrong value had already been used for pending transaction:

invalidate candidate/confirmation.

Example:

Tuesday selected, then customer corrects Thursday.

Must return to availability.

## 42E.81 State invalidation graph

Field change can invalidate downstream state.

Example:

```text
service changes
```

invalidate:

```text
availability
slot selection
price context
provider selection
```

This is important.

## 42E.82 Dependency graph

```text
SERVICE
 ├── PRICE
 ├── PROVIDER
 └── SLOTS

LOCATION
 └── SLOTS

DATE
 └── SLOTS
```

Changing upstream field clears dependent stale values.

## 42E.83 Multi-task call

Caller can complete several actions:

```text
Ask hours
↓
Book physio
↓
Ask massage question
↓
Request SMS
```

Use task stack rather than ending after first outcome.

## 42E.84 Completed-task record

```text
COMPLETED_TASK

task_type
result
timestamp
```

At closing, summarize only relevant completed tasks.

## 42E.85 Interruptions

If caller interrupts agent:

```text
TTS_STOP
↓
PROCESS_CALLER_TURN
```

State remains unless caller changes intent.

## 42E.86 Topic interruption

During booking:

> “Wait, how much is it?”

Push current state:

```text
BOOKING
```

onto stack.

Enter:

```text
PRICE
```

Then resume.

## 42E.87 Intent replacement

During booking:

> “Actually, forget it. I just want to know your hours.”

Customer explicitly abandons booking.

Mark task:

```text
ABANDONED_BY_CUSTOMER
```

Then switch to FAQ.

Do not keep pushing booking afterward.

## 42E.88 State confidence

Some state transitions are deterministic.

Others depend on AI classification.

Store:

```text
transition_confidence
```

Low-confidence high-impact transition should require clarification.

## 42E.89 LLM responsibilities

LLM can provide:

```text
intent candidate
entities
natural response
summaries
```

LLM should not independently mutate protected transaction state.

## 42E.90 State engine responsibilities

State engine controls:

```text
allowed transitions
guards
timeouts
retries
transaction lifecycle
human transfer lifecycle
```

This separation is essential.

## 42E.91 NextAI integration

State engine provides:

```text
current_state
missing_slots
allowed_actions
```

NextAI ranks permitted next actions.

Example:

```text
state = BOOKING_DISCOVERY
missing = time
```

Allowed:

```text
ASK_TIME
HUMAN
CLOSE
```

Not:

```text
BOOK
```

## 42E.92 ConversationAI integration

NextAI chooses:

```text
ASK_TIME
```

ConversationAI generates natural wording.

State engine waits for response.

## 42E.93 ToolAI integration

State:

```text
BOOK_TOOL
```

produces structured tool request.

ToolAI executes.

Tool result becomes event.

State machine transitions accordingly.

## 42E.94 PolicyAI integration

Critical transition requires policy:

```text
CANCEL_CONFIRM
→ CANCEL_TOOL
```

Policy can block.

State:

```text
POLICY_BLOCKED
```

then appropriate explanation/human route.

## 42E.95 HumanOps integration

State engine tracks:

```text
HUMAN_ROUTE
HUMAN_QUEUE
TRANSFER
HUMAN_CONNECTED
```

HumanOps owns queue assignment.

## 42E.96 FollowUpAI integration

Terminal state can create:

```text
callback
confirmation
SMS
human task
```

based on outcome.

## 42E.97 QualityAI integration

QualityAI checks:

```text
expected state path
actual state path
```

Example:

expected:

```text
SELECT_SLOT → CONFIRM → BOOK
```

actual:

```text
SELECT_SLOT → BOOK
```

Critical defect.

## 42E.98 ObserveAI integration

Track state distribution:

```text
calls currently in AVAILABILITY
calls in HUMAN_QUEUE
calls stuck in CLARIFICATION
```

This becomes powerful live operations data.

## 42E.99 State-duration metrics

Measure:

```text
time_in_state
```

Examples:

```text
Intent discovery
Availability lookup
Human queue
```

Long durations reveal bottlenecks.

## 42E.100 State-transition dashboard

Example:

```text
GREETING            10,000
  ↓ 96%
INTENT               9,600
  ↓
SELF SERVICE         7,200
  ↓
COMPLETED            6,800
```

Visualize drop-offs.

## 42E.101 Booking state funnel

```text
BOOK_INTENT            3,100
BOOKING_DISCOVERY      3,020
AVAILABILITY           2,980
SLOTS_FOUND            2,750
SLOT_SELECTED          2,610
CONFIRMED              2,550
BOOK_SUCCESS           2,510
```

Pinpoints booking loss.

## 42E.102 Reschedule state funnel

Same model:

```text
RESCHEDULE_INTENT
→ APPOINTMENT_FOUND
→ ALTERNATIVE_FOUND
→ CONFIRM
→ SUCCESS
```

## 42E.103 Human transfer funnel

```text
HUMAN_REQUEST
→ QUEUED
→ OFFERED
→ ACCEPTED
→ CONNECTED
→ RESOLVED
```

## 42E.104 Failure-state dashboard

Track:

```text
TOOL_FAILURE
POLICY_BLOCK
IDENTITY_FAILURE
TRANSFER_FAILURE
RECONCILIATION
LOOP_DETECTED
```

by frequency and version.

## 42E.105 User story — booking state integrity

> As a customer, I want the system to book only the appointment I explicitly confirmed.

Acceptance:

```text
No BOOK_TOOL transition
without
BOOK_CONFIRMATION = TRUE.
```

## 42E.106 User story — interrupted booking

> As a caller, I want to ask a side question during booking and return to the booking without repeating my details.

Acceptance:

```text
BOOKING
→ FAQ
→ BOOKING
```

with service/time/location retained.

## 42E.107 User story — correction

> As a caller, when I correct a date, the system should stop using the old date immediately.

Acceptance:

```text
Tuesday
→ customer correction
→ Thursday active
→ Tuesday invalidated
```

## 42E.108 User story — dropped call

> As a customer, if my call drops during booking, I do not want the system to create a duplicate or uncertain appointment.

Acceptance:

```text
transaction reconciled
before
retry/follow-up
```

## 42E.109 Golden state-path tests

Example:

### FAQ

```text
CONNECTED
→ GREETING
→ INTENT
→ FAQ
→ CLOSING
→ COMPLETED
```

### Booking

```text
CONNECTED
→ GREETING
→ INTENT
→ BOOKING_DISCOVERY
→ AVAILABILITY
→ PRESENT_OPTIONS
→ SELECT
→ CONFIRM
→ BOOK
→ BOOKED
→ CLOSING
```

### Human

```text
CONNECTED
→ GREETING
→ INTENT
→ HUMAN_ROUTE
→ QUEUE
→ TRANSFER
→ HUMAN_CONNECTED
```

## 42E.110 Negative transition tests

Attempt:

```text
GREETING → CANCEL_TOOL
```

Expected:

```text
REJECTED
```

Attempt:

```text
BOOK_SELECT → BOOK_TOOL
```

without confirmation.

Expected:

```text
REJECTED
```

## 42E.111 Exhaustive transition testing

For every state:

test every:

```text
allowed event
forbidden event
timeout
error
```

State-machine testing should be systematic, not just happy-path conversation testing.

## 42E.112 Model-based testing

Represent state machine formally.

Generate test paths automatically.

Useful tools/framework patterns:

```text
statecharts
property-based testing
model-based testing
```

This can discover rare paths humans miss.

## 42E.113 Property tests

Examples:

```text
BOOKED implies scheduler_success = true
```

```text
HUMAN_CONNECTED implies AI_speaking = false
```

```text
CANCELLED implies explicit_confirmation = true
```

```text
DNC_ACTIVE prohibits outbound marketing action
```

Properties are stronger than individual scripted tests.

## 42E.114 Mutation test

Remove confirmation guard intentionally.

Test suite must fail.

If it doesn't, your tests are insufficient.

## 42E.115 Chaos test — state store outage

During normal FAQ:

may degrade.

During transaction:

critical state persists/reconciles.

No silent reset.

## 42E.116 Chaos test — duplicate event

Scheduler sends `BOOK_SUCCESS` twice.

State transition should remain:

```text
BOOKED
```

without duplicate side effects.

## 42E.117 Chaos test — out-of-order event

`BOOK_SUCCESS`

arrives after customer hangup.

Transaction remains authoritative.

Follow-up may send confirmation according to policy.

## 42E.118 Race test

Customer says:

> “Actually don't book it.”

at nearly same time booking action begins.

You need clearly defined commit boundaries.

If transaction already committed:

tell customer accurately and offer cancellation process.

Never hide transaction state.

## 42E.119 Concurrency control

Use versioning:

```text
state_version
```

On update:

```text
expected_version = 18
```

prevents two workers writing incompatible state.

## 42E.120 State locking

Avoid large distributed locks where possible.

Prefer:

optimistic concurrency  
idempotent events.

## 42E.121 State snapshot

Periodically create state snapshot for long calls.

Reduces event replay time.

## 42E.122 Replay

Given:

```text
CALL-98112
```

you should be able to reconstruct:

```text
all states
all transitions
all tools
all customer corrections
```

for RCA.

## 42E.123 Versioning

Store:

```text
state_machine_version
conversation_version
policy_version
```

Every call remains reproducible.

## 42E.124 Blue/green state flow

New state-machine version:

```text
V12
```

run in shadow against production calls.

Compare proposed transitions with V11.

Then canary.

## 42E.125 State migration

Normally allow active calls to finish on version they started with.

New calls use new version.

Avoid changing state-machine semantics mid-call.

## 42E.126 Kill switch

If booking state has critical bug:

disable:

```text
BOOK
RESCHEDULE
CANCEL
```

while continuing:

```text
FAQ
HUMAN TRANSFER
CALLBACK
```

This is far better than shutting down whole phone service.

## 42E.127 Admin/debug UI

For technical users:

```text
CALL STATE

Current:
BOOKING_CONFIRMATION

Previous:
SLOT_SELECTED

Active Intent:
BOOK

Missing Slots:
None

Selected Slot:
SLOT-778

Allowed Actions:
CONFIRM
CHANGE_SLOT
CANCEL_TASK
HUMAN
```

This makes debugging dramatically easier.

## 42E.128 State transition viewer

Graphically:

```text
GREETING ✓
  ↓
INTENT ✓
  ↓
BOOKING ✓
  ↓
AVAILABILITY ✓
  ↓
SELECT ✓
  ↓
CONFIRM ← CURRENT
  ↓
BOOK
```

Failed states can be marked separately.

## 42E.129 Operations use

If many calls are stuck in:

```text
AVAILABILITY
```

likely scheduler issue.

If stuck:

```text
INTENT
```

likely NLU/STT problem.

The state-machine dashboard becomes diagnostic.

## 42E.130 State SLO

Examples:

```text
95% FAQ calls reach resolution within X
95% booking availability checks complete within Y
```

Don't optimize raw state speed at the cost of correctness.

## 42E.131 Recommended implementation

Strong options:

```text
Custom deterministic state machine
+
Pydantic models
+
PostgreSQL event history
+
Redis current-state cache
```

Or:

```text
LangGraph
```

for conversational state orchestration, while keeping high-risk transaction guards outside free-form LLM logic.

For durable multi-hour/day activities:

```text
Temporal
```

not the live dialogue state machine itself.

## 42E.132 Boundary with Temporal

Use live call state machine for:

```text
seconds/minutes
current voice conversation
```

Use Temporal for:

```text
callback tomorrow
follow-up next week
waitlist
human task SLA
```

Keep responsibilities separate.

## 🤖 Assistant — msg #135

# Phase 42F — Missed Call, Abandoned Call, Dropped Call + Callback Recovery

This phase ensures that **every failed or incomplete inbound contact becomes a governed recovery opportunity** rather than a lost customer.

The main principle is:

> **A missed call is not one thing. Distinguish never-answered calls, queue abandonment, mid-conversation drops, transfer failures, voicemail, and customer-requested callbacks because each requires a different recovery path.**

## 42F.1 Failure taxonomy

Use separate outcomes:

```text
MISSED_CALL
ABANDONED_BEFORE_AI
ABANDONED_IN_QUEUE
CALL_DROPPED_DURING_AI
CALL_DROPPED_DURING_HUMAN
TRANSFER_FAILED
VOICEMAIL_LEFT
CALLBACK_REQUESTED
CALLBACK_FAILED
CALLBACK_MISSED_SLA
```

Never combine all of these into `FAILED_CALL`.

## 42F.2 Recovery architecture

```text
Inbound Telephony Event
        ↓
Failure Classifier
        ↓
Call State + Customer Context
        ↓
PolicyAI
        ↓
Priority Engine
        ↓
NextAI
        ↓
┌────────────────────────────┐
│ AI Callback                │
│ Human Callback             │
│ SMS                        │
│ Email                      │
│ Voicemail Processing       │
│ Wait                       │
│ Close                      │
└────────────────────────────┘
        ↓
FollowUpAI / Temporal
        ↓
Execution-Time Revalidation
        ↓
Callback / Message
        ↓
Outcome
        ↓
CRM + Reporting + QA
```

## 42F.3 Missed inbound call

A true missed inbound call means:

```text
Caller dialed
↓
Call did not reach useful conversation
```

Possible causes:

```text
telephony failure
routing outage
platform unavailable
no answer
configuration error
capacity problem
```

Store the technical cause separately from the customer-facing outcome.

## 42F.4 Missed-call object

```text
MISSED_CALL

missed_call_id
call_id
tenant_id
clinic_id

caller_token
customer_id

occurred_at
duration_before_end

reason_code
provider_reason

known_customer
existing_lead

recovery_status
priority
```

## 42F.5 Missed-call recovery flow

```text
MISSED CALL
    ↓
Known customer?
    ↓
Open appointment?
Open complaint?
Recent callback?
Lead?
    ↓
PolicyAI
    ↓
Prioritize
    ↓
NextAI
    ↓
CALLBACK / MESSAGE / CLOSE
```

## 42F.6 Do not automatically call every missed caller

Some missed calls may be:

```text
wrong number
spam
robocall
repeat dial
customer immediately called again
```

Before recovery:

```text
duplicate?
reconnected?
spam?
already handled?
DNC/preference?
```

## 42F.7 Immediate redial suppression

Customer calls twice within 30 seconds.

Do not create two callbacks.

Use deduplication:

```text
normalized caller
+
tenant
+
recent time window
```

Then merge events.

## 42F.8 Reconnect detection

If caller reconnects and completes conversation before recovery callback executes:

```text
MISS-1001
→ SUPERSEDED
```

Cancel pending recovery.

This is essential.

## 42F.9 Recovery priority

Illustrative priority:

```text
P0
Open critical service issue

P1
Customer-requested callback
Complaint follow-up
Dropped booking transaction

P2
Existing customer appointment issue
High-confidence booking intent

P3
Unknown/new prospective caller

P4
Low-confidence/spam-like call
```

Do not prioritize purely by predicted revenue.

## 42F.10 Priority inputs

Potential:

```text
call state before failure
customer explicit request
existing appointment
complaint
transaction uncertainty
lead intent
repeat attempts
time since failure
human skill requirement
```

## 42F.11 High-priority example

Call drops after customer says:

> “Yes, book Thursday at 6:30.”

Tool execution status unknown.

This is much more urgent than:

unknown caller rings for three seconds and hangs up.

## 42F.12 Abandoned-before-AI

Caller disconnects during:

```text
ringing
initial greeting
initial silence
```

Track:

```text
EARLY_ABANDON
```

Potential reasons:

latency  
wrong number  
caller changed mind  
bad greeting.

Recovery should generally be conservative.

## 42F.13 Queue abandonment

Customer explicitly entered human queue and hung up.

Store:

```text
queue_id
wait_duration
position if available
intent
language
```

This is stronger recovery evidence because customer was actively seeking help.

## 42F.14 Queue-abandonment recovery

Possible:

```text
ABANDONED_QUEUE
↓
Policy
↓
Callback eligibility
↓
Human or AI callback
```

For a billing/complaint queue, human callback may be more appropriate.

## 42F.15 Queue abandonment priority

Possible score:

```text
customer-requested-human
+
wait time
+
queue type
+
complaint
+
existing appointment issue
```

## 42F.16 Dropped AI call

Call ended while AI actively handled customer.

Persist:

```text
last stable state
active intent
slots
selected option
tool state
customer confirmation state
```

This determines recovery.

## 42F.17 Dropped-call recovery by state

Examples:

| Last state | Recovery |
|---|---|
| FAQ | Often no callback needed |
| Need discovery | Optional callback depending policy |
| Availability | Callback may help |
| Booking confirmation | High-priority recovery |
| Tool executing | Reconcile first |
| Human queue | Queue callback |
| Complaint | Human callback |

## 42F.18 Transaction-first rule

If the call dropped during:

```text
BOOK
RESCHEDULE
CANCEL
PAYMENT
```

first determine transaction result.

Only then contact customer.

Never call saying:

> “Let's book again”

until you know whether the first action succeeded.

## 42F.19 Reconciliation flow

```text
CALL DROPPED
↓
Transaction pending?
↓
YES
↓
Lookup idempotency/request ID
↓
SUCCESS / FAILED / UNKNOWN
```

If success:

send/perform appropriate confirmation.

If failed:

recover booking.

If unknown:

human/reconciliation workflow.

## 42F.20 Example

```text
Customer selected Thu 18:30
↓
Booking request sent
↓
Call disconnects
↓
Provider response lost
```

Reconciliation finds:

```text
APT-88910 exists
```

Recovery action:

```text
DO NOT BOOK AGAIN
→ confirmation follow-up
```

## 42F.21 Human-call drop

If caller disconnects while speaking to staff:

store:

```text
human_agent
queue
interaction state
```

HumanOps may own follow-up rather than AI.

## 42F.22 Transfer failure

AI attempts transfer.

Failure classes:

```text
destination busy
provider error
queue unavailable
human did not answer
telephony failure
```

Each gets different recovery.

## 42F.23 Transfer-failure flow

```text
TRANSFER_FAILED
↓
Can return safely to AI?
    YES → resume
    NO
↓
Alternate valid queue?
    YES → offer
    NO
↓
Callback
```

Never simply disconnect.

## 42F.24 Callback types

Maintain separate callback categories:

```text
CUSTOMER_REQUESTED
MISSED_CALL_RECOVERY
QUEUE_ABANDON_RECOVERY
CALL_DROP_RECOVERY
TRANSFER_FAILURE_RECOVERY
HUMAN_TASK_CALLBACK
COMPLAINT_CALLBACK
```

This allows different SLAs and policies.

## 42F.25 Callback object

```text
CALLBACK

callback_id
customer_id
call_id

callback_type
reason

requested_by

AI
CUSTOMER
HUMAN
SYSTEM

requested_at
scheduled_for

timezone

queue_id
required_skills[]
preferred_language

priority
sla_due_at

status
```

## 42F.26 Callback statuses

```text
CREATED
SCHEDULED
READY
DISPATCHED
RINGING
CONNECTED
COMPLETED

NO_ANSWER
FAILED
CANCELLED
SUPERSEDED
EXPIRED
```

## 42F.27 Customer-requested callback

This gets special treatment.

Customer:

> “Call me tomorrow at 6.”

Store exact request.

Do not convert to generic:

```text
callback tomorrow
```

Preserve:

```text
18:00 local time
```

subject to configured policy.

## 42F.28 System-generated callback

For missed-call recovery, system may choose a reasonable allowed time using:

```text
contactability
business hours
customer preferences
queue capacity
```

But this is different from explicit customer scheduling.

## 42F.29 AI vs human callback decision

Use human callback when:

```text
complaint
complex admin
restricted topic
explicit human request
repeated AI failure
```

Use AI callback when:

```text
booking
availability
general service information
lead follow-up
```

provided AI is approved for that task.

## 42F.30 Callback routing

```text
Callback due
↓
HumanOps / RouteAI
↓
AI or human
↓
language/skill routing
↓
call execution
```

## 42F.31 Callback SLA

Track separately by category.

Example:

```text
Requested callback
→ strict timing

Complaint callback
→ severity-based SLA

Missed new-lead callback
→ business-defined SLA
```

## 42F.32 SLA fields

```text
promised_for
ready_at
dialed_at
connected_at
completed_at
```

Metrics:

```text
callback_delay
callback_on_time
```

## 42F.33 Callback pre-execution checks

Immediately before dialing:

```text
customer already called back?
issue resolved?
appointment booked?
callback cancelled?
DNC changed?
channel allowed?
valid time?
duplicate active call?
```

Then execute.

## 42F.34 Callback cancellation conditions

Cancel when:

```text
customer resolves issue
customer books online
human already contacted them
customer opts out
duplicate callback exists
lead closed
```

Mark:

```text
SUPERSEDED
```

with reason.

## 42F.35 Callback no-answer

Do not automatically redial repeatedly.

Possible flow:

```text
Attempt 1
NO ANSWER
↓
Policy + attempt rules
↓
Retry later
or
approved message
or
close
```

## 42F.36 Callback attempt history

```text
CALLBACK_ATTEMPT

callback_id
attempt_no
attempt_at

route
provider

outcome
duration
```

## 42F.37 Wrong person on callback

If callback reaches someone else:

avoid exposing original caller's request.

Mark:

```text
WRONG_PERSON
```

and follow policy.

## 42F.38 Number unreachable

Provider returns:

```text
INVALID_NUMBER
DISCONNECTED
UNREACHABLE
```

Update contact quality.

Do not endlessly retry.

## 42F.39 Busy line

`BUSY` may be retriable later.

Different from invalid number.

Keep provider outcome taxonomy precise.

## 42F.40 Voicemail detection

Possible outcomes:

```text
HUMAN_ANSWER
VOICEMAIL
NO_ANSWER
BUSY
FAILED
```

If voicemail policy allows:

leave approved minimal message.

## 42F.41 Voicemail privacy

Avoid sensitive details.

Safer:

> “This is ABC Clinic returning your call. Please contact us when convenient.”

Not:

> “We're calling about your physiotherapy treatment.”

unless specifically approved.

## 42F.42 Inbound voicemail processing

If customer leaves voicemail:

```text
Audio
↓
Transcription
↓
Intent / NeedAI
↓
Priority
↓
Human/AI callback
```

Store:

```text
transcription confidence
```

Low-confidence critical details require human review.

## 42F.43 Voicemail example

Customer:

> “Please move my Friday appointment to Monday.”

System should not autonomously reschedule solely from voicemail unless specifically designed and authorized.

Safer:

create:

```text
RESCHEDULE_CALLBACK
```

## 42F.52 Drop rate by state

Very useful:

```text
GREETING             2%
INTENT               1%

```

High queue drop suggests wait problem, not AI problem.

## 42F.53 Recovery funnel

```text
1,000 Failed/Incomplete Calls
        ↓
850 Eligible for Recovery
        ↓
780 Recovery Attempted
        ↓
520 Connected
        ↓
390 Resolved
        ↓
160 Bookings
```

## 42F.54 Recovery attribution

Track:

```text
original_call_id
recovery_callback_id
final_outcome
```

Then understand:

missed call → callback → booking.

## 42F.55 Time-to-recovery

Important metric:

```text
recovery_contact_at
-
failure_at
```

Break by priority.

## 42F.56 Resolution-after-recovery

Not every callback needs conversion.

Measure:

```text
issue resolved
booking completed
information delivered
complaint handed off
```

based on original intent.

## 42F.57 Recovery cost

Track:

```text
telephony
AI
human
messages
```

Calculate:

```text
Cost per recovered call
Cost per recovered booking
```

## 42F.58 Economic value

Example:

```text
Missed call recovery
→ 150 additional appointments/month
```

This is one of the strongest business cases for inbound voice AI.

## 42F.59 Recovery by source

Break down missed calls by:

```text
Google Ads number
Website number
Main clinic line
Referral number
```

A high-value paid-acquisition source may justify faster operational response, while still respecting service fairness and policy.

## 42F.60 Lead creation from missed calls

Unknown missed caller should not automatically become a fully qualified lead.

Possible:

```text
PROSPECT_CONTACT_EVENT
```

Then if recovery connects and interest confirmed:

create lead.

Avoid junk CRM growth.

## 42F.61 Known lead recovery

If caller already has open lead:

link missed call.

Do not create duplicate lead.

## 42F.62 Existing customer recovery

If caller has upcoming appointment:

potential reason may be appointment-related.

But don't guess.

Callback agent can open with:

> “We're returning your call to ABC Clinic. How can I help?”

rather than exposing appointment details.

## 42F.63 Complaint recovery

Highest-priority human flow.

```text
Complaint call dropped
↓
Human callback
↓
Original complaint context preserved
```

No marketing.

## 42F.64 Call drop from AI misunderstanding

If:

```text
correction_count high
```

and customer hangs up:

QualityAI may classify likely AI-experience failure.

Recovery may prefer human rather than same AI.

## 42F.65 Recovery route diversity

Do not simply send customer back through exact same failing path.

Example:

Hindi STT route degraded.

Dropped Hindi calls should use:

alternate provider

or:

Hindi human.

## 42F.66 Provider-aware recovery

ObserveAI provides:

```text
Voice Provider A = DEGRADED
```

Callback should route through B if approved.

Avoid repeating incident.

## 42F.67 Scheduler-outage recovery

Missed booking during scheduler outage:

create:

```text
BOOKING_RECOVERY
```

When scheduler recovers:

NextAI reevaluates.

Do not immediately flood customers with simultaneous calls.

## 42F.68 Recovery throttling

After outage, there may be:

5,000 recovery callbacks.

Use:

```text
priority
capacity
rate limits
```

to smooth load.

## 42F.69 Callback capacity planning

Forecast:

```text
callbacks due
+
normal inbound transfer load
+
outbound campaign load
```

before scheduling large recovery batches.

## 42F.70 Human callback queue

Specialists see:

```text
Customer
Original intent
Original call time
Failure reason
AI summary
SLA
Language
```

They should not need to investigate everything manually.

## 42F.71 Callback agent opening

For system recovery:

> “Hi, this is ABC Clinic returning your recent call. How can I help?”

If the customer explicitly requested callback for a specific matter, context can be somewhat more specific while respecting privacy.

## 42F.72 Do not overstate context

Avoid:

> “You were calling about your medical issue.”

unless appropriate.

Use minimal purpose.

## 42F.73 Callback language

Use:

```text
customer-requested language
```

where supported.

If only inferred:

confirm early.

## 42F.74 Callback handoff

AI recovery starts but encounters restricted issue.

Warm transfer to human using preserved original-call context.

## 42F.75 Recovery events

Publish:

```text
call.missed
call.abandoned
call.dropped
transfer.failed

recovery.created
recovery.scheduled
recovery.cancelled

callback.dispatched
callback.connected
callback.no_answer
callback.completed
callback.overdue
```

## 42F.76 Recovery audit

Store:

```text
why recovery was created
who/what authorized it
why callback occurred
policy result
customer outcome
why journey ended
```

## 42F.77 Idempotency

Key:

```text
recovery_type
+
original_call_id
```

Prevents duplicate recovery workflow.

Callback attempts use separate idempotency keys.

## 42F.78 Event deduplication

Telephony provider may send multiple:

```text
call.completed
```

webhooks.

Event ID/provider call ID must prevent duplicate recovery.

## 42F.79 Out-of-order telephony events

Possible:

```text
CALL_COMPLETED
```

arrives before:

```text
CALL_CONNECTED
```

due webhook ordering.

Use provider timestamps/state machine rather than processing order alone.

## 42F.80 Reconnect race

Missed-call workflow schedules callback.

Customer redials one second before callback.

Execution-time check should cancel callback or suppress duplicate call.

## 42F.81 Callback/customer inbound collision

AI callback starts exactly when customer calls inbound.

Need central active-contact coordinator.

Prefer one active voice session.

Cancel/terminate duplicate according to policy/technical feasibility.

## 42F.82 Active-contact lock

Maintain:

```text
customer/contact point
active_voice_session
```

for duplicate prevention.

Do not use overly broad locking that blocks family-shared numbers incorrectly.

## 42F.83 Multiple callers behind shared number

Recovery should not assume missed call belonged to a specific person solely from ANI.

Opening should remain generic until context resolved.

## 42F.84 Unknown caller callback privacy

> “We're returning a recent call to ABC Clinic.”

Safe.

Avoid mentioning service detected from uncertain voicemail unless appropriate.

## 42F.85 Spam recovery prevention

FraudAI can return:

```text
DO_NOT_RECOVER
```

for high-confidence spam.

But low-confidence spam classifications should not block legitimate callers without appropriate controls.

## 42F.86 Callback fraud

Attackers might create repeated callback requests to expensive destinations.

Controls:

```text
number validation
destination allowlists/country rules
rate limits
fraud scoring
```

## 42F.87 Premium-number protection

Do not allow arbitrary callback destinations if they could create fraud exposure.

Use normalized authorized customer contact points.

## 42F.88 Call spoof recovery

Caller ID spoofing means outbound callback might reach actual number owner who never called.

For uncertain/high-risk cases:

use conservative opening and identity handling.

## 42F.89 Callback configuration UI

Admin configures:

```text
Missed-call recovery
ON/OFF

AI callback
ON

Human callback
ON

Maximum attempts
X

Eligible business hours
...

Queue abandonment callback
ON

Transfer-failure callback
ON
```

All changes versioned.

## 42F.90 Queue-specific recovery policy

Example:

```text
Reception
AI callback allowed

Billing
Human callback preferred

Complaint
Human callback required
```

## 42F.91 Recovery policy precedence

```text
Global safety
↓
Tenant policy
↓
Queue policy
↓
Recovery type
```

Lower-level configuration cannot override mandatory safety controls.

## 42F.92 Operations workflow

Daily operations team reviews:

```text
overdue callbacks
failed callbacks
unresolved dropped transactions
unrecovered complaints
recovery queue backlog
```

## 42F.93 Weekly recovery review

Analyze:

```text
missed-call causes
queue abandonments
drop patterns
recovery conversion
callback SLAs
```

Then improve upstream system.

Recovery should not become a substitute for fixing poor inbound reliability.

## 42F.94 Root-cause loop

Example:

```text
Missed calls ↑
↓
Reason:
Inbound gateway timeout
↓
Fix gateway
```

not:

just hire more people to callback.

## 42F.95 Missed-call cause taxonomy

```text
PROVIDER_OUTAGE
PLATFORM_ERROR
ROUTING_ERROR
CONFIG_ERROR

CALLER_HANGUP
```

Track accurately.

## 42F.96 Queue-abandon reason inference

Do not claim:

> caller abandoned because wait was too long

unless supported.

Store:

```text
wait_time

```

Use analytics to infer aggregate patterns cautiously.

## 42F.97 Callback quality score

Evaluate:

```text
timeliness
correct reason/context
language
resolution
no duplicate contact
```

Not just connection rate.

## 42F.98 Recovery QA

QualityAI checks:

```text
Was recovery appropriate?
Was callback still necessary?
Was customer privacy respected?
Was correct issue resumed?
Was duplicate action avoided?
```

## 42F.99 Customer effort metric

Recovery adds effort.

Track:

```text
original call attempts
callback attempts
repeated information
transfers
```

High effort indicates upstream problems.

## 42F.100 User story — missed call

> As a caller whose call was missed, I want the clinic to return my call promptly when appropriate without requiring me to repeatedly dial.

Acceptance:

```text
missed call captured
↓
deduplicated
↓
policy checked
↓
recovery created
↓
callback executed
↓
outcome recorded
```

## 42F.101 User story — dropped booking

> As a caller whose call drops while booking, I want the system to determine whether my appointment was created before contacting me again.

Acceptance:

```text
transaction reconciliation
must precede
new booking attempt
```

## 42F.102 User story — queue abandonment

> As a caller who does not want to wait on hold, I want to request a callback without losing my place or having to repeat my issue.

Acceptance:

```text
queue context preserved
priority preserved
summary preserved
callback completed
```

## 42F.103 User story — supervisor

> As a supervisor, I want to see overdue and high-priority recovery calls so I can intervene before customers are lost.

## 42F.104 User story — manager

> As a manager, I want to measure how many missed calls are recovered and how many recoveries lead to resolved requests or appointments.

## 42F.105 Golden recovery tests

Test:

```text
missed unknown caller
missed known customer
queue abandonment
dropped FAQ
dropped booking before confirmation
dropped booking during tool
transfer failure
complaint drop
customer reconnect
duplicate webhooks
DNC after recovery scheduled
```

## 42F.106 Test — customer books before callback

Expected:

```text
recovery callback cancelled
```

## 42F.107 Test — customer DNC after callback scheduled

Expected:

applicable outbound callback blocked at execution.

## 42F.108 Test — duplicate missed-call events

Expected:

one recovery workflow.

## 42F.109 Test — scheduler says booking succeeded after call drop

Expected:

no second booking.

Confirmation/recovery communication only.

## 42F.110 Test — shared phone number

Expected:

generic callback opening.

No customer-specific disclosure until context resolved.

## 42F.111 Test — voicemail STT low confidence

Expected:

human review or generic callback.

Do not execute transaction from uncertain transcription.

## 42F.112 Test — provider outage

Generate 500 missed calls.

Ensure:

recovery queue created correctly  
deduplicated  
rate-limited  
prioritized.

## 42F.113 Load testing

Simulate outage recovery:

```text
1,000
10,000
100,000
```

recovery records depending target scale.

Test durable timers/queues.

## 42F.114 Chaos testing

Kill callback worker during calls.

Expected:

durable workflow resumes.

No duplicated calls.

## 42F.115 Callback provider unknown state

Outbound provider request times out.

Do not immediately retry if call might already be dialing.

Reconcile provider call ID/status.

## 42F.116 Recovery SLOs

Examples:

```text
Customer-requested callback:
% executed inside agreed window

Dropped transaction:
% reconciled within threshold

Complaint callback:
% completed within priority SLA
```

Use actual business targets.

## 42F.121 Recommended implementation

```text
Telephony Webhooks
        ↓
Call Event Service
        ↓
Failure Classifier
        ↓
PostgreSQL/Event Store
        ↓
NextAI/PolicyAI
        ↓
Temporal
        ↓
Callback Worker
        ↓
Telephony Gateway
```

Use Redis for:

current state/cache,

not as sole durable recovery store.

## 42F.122 Temporal workflow example

```text
Create recovery
↓
Wait until callback time
↓
Receive events during wait
↓
At timer:
revalidate customer state
↓
If still required:
dispatch callback
↓
wait for outcome
↓
retry/fallback/complete
```

This is a strong Temporal use case.

## 42F.123 n8n role

n8n can be used for:

```text
internal recovery reports
Slack/Teams alerts
low-risk CRM notifications
```

but I would not use it as the only durable engine for high-volume customer callbacks and transaction reconciliation.
